children.title: Admissible Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Problem-class containers used to delimit the worst-case search.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Function Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-objective minimization model used as input to a performance-estimation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(\mathcal F\) be a specified class of proper functions \(f:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A single-function problem model is \[\inf_{x\in H} f(x),\qquad f\in\mathcal F.\] When attainment is required, the admissible instances satisfy \(X_\star:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H}f(x)\ne\varnothing\). A performance-estimation encoding represents an instance through finitely many sampled triples \((x_i,f_i,g_i)\), where \(f_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i\) is an admissible first-order oracle output at \(x_i\), together with interpolation conditions characterizing membership in \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single-function model minimizes one function from a prescribed class and represents queried points by compatible values and first-order data.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(\mathcal F\) is a specified class of proper extended-real-valued functions on \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{The admissible problem is }\inf_{x\in H}f(x)\text{ with }f\in\mathcal F.\)

notation.meaning: sampled point, value, and first-order datum

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the Single-Function Models container, but no source is supplied for either the model or the performance-estimation interpolation encoding.

children.title: Composite Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Problem encodings built from multiple functional components with distinct structural roles.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-term composite minimization with separately encoded smooth and proximable components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. A composite problem model is \[\inf_{x\in H}\{F(x):=f(x)+g(x)\},\] where \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) belongs to a prescribed differentiable function class and \(g:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) belongs to a prescribed proper closed convex function class. The oracle specification treats the components separately, for example through \((f(x),\nabla f(x))\) and either \((g(x),s)\) with \(s\in\partial g(x)\), or the proximal map \(\operatorname{prox}_{\gamma g}(x)\) for \(\gamma>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite model minimizes a sum whose smooth and nonsmooth components are constrained and queried separately.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(f\) is differentiable and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in H}(f(x)+g(x))\ne\varnothing\) when attainment is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=f+g\text{ is encoded through componentwise function-class and oracle constraints.}\)

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the nonsmooth component
proximal map of the scaled component

children.title: Finite-Sum Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Problem encodings organized around finitely indexed component objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-average minimization with component-indexed functions and oracle information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(n\ge 1\). A finite-sum problem model is \[\inf_{x\in H}F(x),\qquad F(x):=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_j(x),\] where every component \(f_j:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) belongs to a prescribed class \(\mathcal F_j\). Its information model specifies whether a query reveals one indexed component datum, a sampled component datum, or the full aggregate. Interpolation constraints are imposed componentwise and the aggregate values or subgradients are linked by the displayed averaging identity whenever all required component data exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-sum model minimizes the average of finitely many component functions and records which component information each query reveals.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(n\in\mathbb N\) is positive.
\(f_j\in\mathcal F_j\) for every \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_j(x)\text{ defines the aggregate objective.}\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-average definition fits the terminal container, but no source supports the component-indexed model, query alternatives, or componentwise interpolation claims.

children.title: Composite Finite-Sum Models
children.top_down_role: Models combining outer composite structure with finite-sum component organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Finite-Sum Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-sum smooth objective combined with a separately modeled regularizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(n\ge1\). A composite finite-sum model is \[\inf_{x\in H}\left\{F(x):=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_j(x)+g(x)\right\},\] where each \(f_j:H\to\mathbb R\) belongs to a prescribed differentiable class and \(g:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, closed, and convex. The information model distinguishes component queries to \(f_j\) from subgradient or proximal queries to \(g\); admissibility requires simultaneous satisfaction of all componentwise interpolation constraints and the common-point coupling in the displayed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite finite-sum model adds a separately queried convex regularizer to an average of differentiable component objectives.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(n\in\mathbb N\) is positive.
\(f_j\) is differentiable for every \(j\), and \(g\) is proper, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}f_j+g\text{ is the composite finite-sum objective.}\)

children.title: Operator Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Performance-estimation models expressed through admissible operator classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-finding model for a class of single-valued or set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(\mathcal A\) be a prescribed class of operators \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\). An operator problem model asks for \[x_\star\in H\quad\text{such that}\quad 0\in A(x_\star).\] An oracle query at \(x_i\) returns an admissible \(u_i\in A(x_i)\). A finite performance-estimation encoding consists of sampled pairs \((x_i,u_i)\) satisfying interpolation conditions for some common \(A\in\mathcal A\), algorithmic relations among the samples, and a performance criterion expressed through their inner products and squared norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator model seeks a zero of an admissible operator and encodes queries as graph points satisfying operator-class interpolation constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(\mathcal A\) is a specified class of operators from \(H\) to subsets of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\text{ solves the model exactly when }0\in A(x_\star).\)

notation.meaning: sampled point on the graph of the operator

children.title: Fixed-Point Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Performance-estimation models centered on fixed-point mappings and their residual quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-point formulation with an operator class and residual-based performance measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(\mathcal T\) be a prescribed class of mappings \(T:H\to H\). A fixed-point problem model asks for \[x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T:=\{x\in H:T(x)=x\},\qquad T\in\mathcal T.\] A query at \(x_i\) returns \(T(x_i)\), equivalently the residual \(r_i:=x_i-T(x_i)\). A finite encoding requires the sampled pairs \((x_i,T(x_i))\) to be interpolable by one mapping in \(\mathcal T\); typical exactness and performance quantities are respectively \(r_i=0\) and \(\lVert r_i\rVert\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point model seeks a point unchanged by an admissible mapping and commonly measures progress using the fixed-point residual.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(\mathcal T\) is a specified class of self-mappings of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in\operatorname{Fix}T\iff x_\star-T(x_\star)=0.\)

notation.meaning: fixed-point residual at the queried point

children.title: Operator-to-Fixed-Point Reductions
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondences that transfer operator problems into fixed-point representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-to-Fixed-Point Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resolvent reduction of monotone zero finding to fixed-point finding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximally monotone on a real Hilbert space and let \(\lambda>0\). Define the resolvent \(J_{\lambda A}:=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}:H\to H\). Then \[0\in A(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=J_{\lambda A}(x).\] Consequently, the zero set of \(A\) equals \(\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}\). Moreover, if \(y=J_{\lambda A}(x)\), then \((x-y)/\lambda\in A(y)\), so a resolvent evaluation produces a graph point of \(A\) and translates operator-oracle constraints into fixed-point relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zeros of a maximally monotone operator are exactly the fixed points of any positive-parameter resolvent of that operator.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximally monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{zer}A=\operatorname{Fix}J_{\lambda A}.\)

children.title: Constrained Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Models whose admissible instances include explicit feasibility restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Objective minimization over an explicitly represented feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subseteq H\) be nonempty, and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). A constrained problem model is \[\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\] The model specification includes both the admissible class of objectives and the representation of \(C\), such as inequalities, affine equalities, a membership oracle, or a projection oracle. Equivalently, with the indicator \(\delta_C(x)=0\) for \(x\in C\) and \(\delta_C(x)=+\infty\) otherwise, the problem is \(\inf_{x\in H}(f(x)+\delta_C(x))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained model minimizes an admissible objective over a nonempty feasible set whose representation or oracle access is specified.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty.
\(f:H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is an admissible objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}f(x)=\inf_{x\in H}\bigl(f(x)+\delta_C(x)\bigr).\)

notation.meaning: extended-real indicator of the feasible set

children.title: Set-Based Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Models organized around geometric sets, set oracles, or set-valued structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Set-Based Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility and best-approximation models specified primarily by sets rather than objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq H\) be nonempty closed sets. A set-based feasibility model asks for \[x_\star\in C:=\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}C_j,\] with the admissible instances commonly restricted by \(C\ne\varnothing\). A best-approximation variant additionally receives \(x_0\in H\) and minimizes \(\tfrac12\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2\) over \(C\). The information model specifies access to each set, for example through membership, separation, normal-cone, or projection queries.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set-based model seeks a common point of specified sets, or the nearest common point to a reference, using declared set oracles.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(m\in\mathbb N\) is positive and every \(C_j\subseteq H\) is nonempty and closed.
\(\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}C_j\ne\varnothing\) for the feasible-instance regime.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_\star\in\bigcap_{j=1}^{m}C_j\text{ is a feasible solution.}\)

notation.meaning: reference point in the best-approximation variant

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility and best-approximation variants fit the broad Set-Based Problem Models container, but no source supports the formulation or the stated membership, separation, normal-cone, and projection information interfaces.

children.title: Saddle Problem Models
children.top_down_role: Models built around coupled primal-dual or min-max structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle Problem Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-concave minimax model with a primal-dual solution criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces and let \(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) be convex in its first argument and concave in its second. A saddle problem model seeks \((x_\star,y_\star)\in X\times Y\) satisfying \[L(x_\star,y)\le L(x_\star,y_\star)\le L(x,y_\star)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X,\ y\in Y.\] Equivalently, it seeks a saddle point associated with \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{y\in Y}L(x,y)\), with oracle outputs and interpolation conditions specified for the two partial variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saddle model seeks a pair that minimizes a convex-concave saddle function in its first variable and maximizes it in its second variable.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(L:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\) is convex in its first argument and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L(x_\star,y)\le L(x_\star,y_\star)\le L(x,y_\star)\text{ for every }(x,y)\in X\times Y.\)

children.title: Constrained Saddle Regimes
children.top_down_role: Saddle formulations with additional geometric or feasibility restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Constrained Saddle Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saddle-point model with explicit primal and dual feasible sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be real Hilbert spaces, let \(C\subseteq X\) and \(D\subseteq Y\) be nonempty sets, and let \(L:C\times D\to\mathbb R\) be convex-concave. A constrained saddle regime seeks \((x_\star,y_\star)\in C\times D\) such that \[L(x_\star,y)\le L(x_\star,y_\star)\le L(x,y_\star)\qquad\text{for all }x\in C,\ y\in D.\] Its performance-estimation description combines interpolation constraints for \(L\) with the chosen membership, normal-cone, separation, or projection representation of \(C\) and \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constrained saddle regime restricts the primal and dual variables to declared feasible sets and tests the saddle inequalities only there.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real Hilbert spaces.
\(C\subseteq X\) and \(D\subseteq Y\) are nonempty.
\(L:C\times D\to\mathbb R\) is convex in its first variable and concave in its second.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_\star,y_\star)\in C\times D\text{ satisfies the constrained saddle inequalities.}\)

children.title: Encoded Information and Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: Information channels made available to an encoded method.

children.title: Value Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information models exposing objective or component values at queried points.

knowledge_statements.title: Value Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zeroth-order oracle returning function values without derivative information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(D\) be a nonempty query domain and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\). An exact value oracle for \(f\) is the mapping \[\mathcal O_f^{\mathrm{val}}:D\to\mathbb R,
\qquad \mathcal O_f^{\mathrm{val}}(x)=f(x).\] A query at \(x_i\in D\) therefore reveals only the scalar \(f_i=f(x_i)\); it does not reveal a gradient, subgradient, proximal point, or any other first-order datum. In a performance-estimation model, an algorithm using this oracle may base later queries solely on previously queried points, returned values, and permitted exogenous information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact value oracle returns only the objective value at each queried point and supplies no gradient or subgradient information.
assumptions_latex: \(D\) is a nonempty set.
\(f:D\to\mathbb R\) is the queried function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal O_f^{\mathrm{val}}(x)=f(x)\text{ for every }x\in D.\)

notation.meaning: value returned at the ith query

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact value-oracle definition is mathematically precise and definition is the correct content kind, but no cited source supports either the oracle definition or the restriction on how subsequent queries may depend on returned information.

children.title: Gradient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information models exposing smooth first-order vectors at queried points.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact gradient-information oracle for differentiable objectives in a performance-estimation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient oracle queried at a differentiability point returns the exact gradient there, but does not inherently return the function value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable on the open query domain \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g=\mathcal{O}_{\nabla f}(x)=\nabla f(x)\).

children.title: Subgradient Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information models exposing admissible nonsmooth first-order vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex subgradient oracle, allowing set-valued first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and define \(\operatorname{dom}\partial f:=\{x\in X:\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\}\). A subgradient oracle accepts \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\) and returns an arbitrary \(g\in X\) satisfying \[g\in\partial f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\text{for every }y\in X.\] The oracle contract need not prescribe which member of \(\partial f(x)\) is selected when the subdifferential contains several vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a query point having a nonempty convex subdifferential, a subgradient oracle returns any vector defining a global affine lower support to the function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
The query satisfies \(x\in\operatorname{dom}\partial f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\partial f}(x)\in\partial f(x)\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of the objective at the query
set of points at which the convex subdifferential is nonempty

children.title: Coupled Value–First-Order Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle records pairing scalar values with gradient or subgradient information.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Value–First-Order Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle returning a function value and compatible first-order datum from one query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfy \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\). A coupled value–first-order oracle returns a pair \[\mathcal{O}_{f,\partial f}(x)=(f_x,g_x)\in\mathbb{R}\times X\] such that \(f_x=f(x)\) and \(g_x\in\partial f(x)\). Consequently, the returned pair satisfies \[f(y)\geq f_x+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in X.\] If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), compatibility forces \(g_x=\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One query returns the exact objective value and a compatible subgradient; at a differentiability point the first-order component is the gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real inner-product space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.

children.title: Proximal Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information channels based on proximal responses for functions or components.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact scaled proximal oracle for a proper closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). The proximal oracle with scale \(\lambda\) maps each \(v\in X\) to the unique point \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(v):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\left\{h(x)+\frac{1}{2\lambda}\lVert x-v\rVert^2\right\}.\] Its output is equivalently characterized by \[\frac{v-p}{\lambda}\in\partial h(p).\] A query therefore supplies an implicit first-order relation at the returned point \(p\), rather than at the input \(v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal oracle minimizes the function plus a scaled squared-distance term and returns the unique minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(v)\) and \((v-p)/\lambda\in\partial h(p)\).

notation.meaning: scaled proximal mapping of the function
point returned by the proximal oracle

children.title: Projection Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information channels based on projections onto admissible sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean projection oracle for a nonempty closed convex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space \(X\). A projection oracle maps each \(v\in X\) to the unique point \[p=P_C(v):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\frac12\lVert x-v\rVert^2.\] The returned point is characterized by \[p\in C\quad\text{and}\quad \langle v-p,x-p\rangle\leq 0\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Equivalently, \(v-p\in N_C(p)\), where \(N_C(p)\) is the convex normal cone to \(C\) at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A projection oracle returns the unique feasible point nearest to the query in Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(X\) is a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=P_C(v)\) and \(\langle v-p,x-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(x\in C\).

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the feasible set
convex normal cone to the set at the projected point

children.title: Resolvent Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information channels based on resolvent evaluations of admissible operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact resolvent oracle for a maximal monotone set-valued operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) be maximal monotone, and let \(\lambda>0\). The resolvent oracle associated with \(A\) and \(\lambda\) maps each \(v\in X\) to \[p=J_{\lambda A}(v):=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}(v).\] Equivalently, its output is the unique point \(p\in X\) satisfying \[\frac{v-p}{\lambda}\in A(p).\] Maximal monotonicity ensures that this resolvent is single-valued and defined on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A resolvent oracle solves an implicit monotone inclusion and returns its unique solution for each query.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\rightrightarrows X\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=J_{\lambda A}(v)\) if and only if \((v-p)/\lambda\in A(p)\).

notation.meaning: identity operator on the ambient space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:maximal-monotone resolvent definition and Minty surjectivity are standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The resolvent definition and the full-domain single-valued conclusion for a maximal monotone operator are mathematically standard, but no source with an inspectable section, theorem, definition, or page locator is supplied.

children.title: Proximal–Resolvent Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural interfaces connecting proximal records with resolvent records.

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal–Resolvent Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identification of convex proximal mappings with subdifferential resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space, let \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\lambda>0\). Since \(\partial h\) is maximal monotone, the proximal mapping and resolvent coincide: \[\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}=(I+\lambda\partial h)^{-1}=J_{\lambda\partial h}.\] Indeed, for every \(v,p\in X\), \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{v-p}{\lambda}\in\partial h(p)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=J_{\lambda\partial h}(v).\] In particular, for the indicator \(\delta_C\) of a nonempty closed convex set \(C\), one has \(P_C=J_{N_C}=\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proximal mapping is exactly the resolvent of the convex subdifferential; projection is the indicator-function special case.
assumptions_latex: \(h:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(\lambda>0\); additionally, \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex in the projection specialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda h}=J_{\lambda\partial h}\), and \(P_C=J_{N_C}=\operatorname{prox}_{\delta_C}\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:the correspondence follows from convex optimality and the subdifferential resolvent definition

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proximal–resolvent identity and the projection specialization are standard and the representation content kind fits the correspondence leaf, but the record supplies no authoritative source or inspectable locator.

children.title: Linear-Optimization Oracles
children.top_down_role: Set-information models returning optimizers or extremal responses to linear objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Optimization Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact linear minimization oracle over a compact convex feasible region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\). A linear-optimization oracle accepts a direction \(c\in X\) and returns a point \[s=\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{LO}}(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle.\] Its verifiable optimality contract is \[s\in C\quad\text{and}\quad \langle c,s\rangle\leq\langle c,x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] Compactness guarantees existence; if the minimizing face contains multiple points, the oracle may return any one of them unless a tie-breaking rule is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given a direction, a linear-optimization oracle returns any feasible point minimizing the associated linear functional.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
The oracle is exact and accepts every direction \(c\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{LO}}(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:exact linear minimization oracle over a compact convex set is standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact linear-optimization-oracle contract is mathematically precise, and compactness guarantees attainment, but the record has no authoritative citation with a specific locator.

children.title: Separation Oracles
children.top_down_role: Set-information models returning separating certificates for queried points.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation certificate for membership queries to a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\). A strong separation oracle queried at \(z\in X\) either certifies \(z\in C\), or returns \((a,\beta)\in X\times\mathbb{R}\) with \(a\neq0\) such that \[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta<\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] The returned affine inequality is directly checkable against any representation of \(C\) supporting maximization of \(\langle a,\cdot\rangle\), and it proves that the query lies strictly outside \(C\). Scaling \((a,\beta)\) by any positive scalar yields the same separating certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The oracle confirms membership or returns a hyperplane placing the entire convex set strictly apart from the query.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The requested contract is strong, rather than weak or approximate, separation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Either \(z\in C\), or \(\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta<\langle a,z\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:finite-dimensional strong separation for a point outside a closed convex set is standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated strong-separation contract is standard in finite dimensions, but no authoritative locator is supplied. In addition, the terminal container is an oracle type, so the complete record functions as a definition of a separation oracle rather than as a certificate record, even though an individual negative response is a certificate.

children.title: Optimization–Separation Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Relationships between extremal linear information and separating information.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization–Separation Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shared contract exposing linear optimization and strong separation over one convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real inner-product space \(X\). An optimization–separation interface for \(C\) consists of two callable maps sharing the same set: \[\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{LO}}(c)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\langle c,x\rangle\] for each \(c\in X\), and a separation map \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SEP}}(z)\) that either reports \(z\in C\) or returns \((a,\beta)\) satisfying \[\langle a,x\rangle\leq\beta<\langle a,z\rangle\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\] This record specifies the joint interface only; it does not assert complexity-equivalent reductions between the two oracle types.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The interface gives algorithms both linear minimization and membership-or-separation access to the same compact convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, compact, and convex.
Both component oracles are exact and refer to the same set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{LO}}\) and \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathrm{SEP}}\) jointly expose optimization and separation contracts for \(C\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:the record combines the exact contracts of the two component oracles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The joint interface is clearly delimited and appropriately avoids claiming polynomial-time equivalence, but it is unsupported by any source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Randomized Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle models whose returned information includes internal randomization.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle whose response law includes internal randomization without an inherent unbiasedness requirement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a measurable query space and \(Y\) a measurable response space. A randomized oracle is specified by a probability kernel \(K(\cdot\mid q)\) from \(Q\) to \(Y\): when queried at \(q\in Q\), it returns a random response \(Y_q\) satisfying \[\mathbb{P}(Y_q\in B\mid q)=K(B\mid q)\] for every measurable \(B\subseteq Y\). Equivalently, one may write \(Y_q=\Phi(q,U)\) for an auxiliary random seed \(U\). Randomization alone imposes no unbiasedness, variance, independence-across-calls, or accuracy condition; such properties must be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized oracle returns an answer drawn from a query-dependent distribution; randomness alone guarantees neither accuracy nor unbiasedness.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) and \(Y\) are measurable spaces.
\(K\) is a probability kernel from queries to responses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{L}(Y_q\mid q)=K(\cdot\mid q)\).

notation.meaning: conditional response distribution at a query

children.title: Stochastic Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle models exposing sampled information from an underlying problem distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with a conditional second-moment bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. A stochastic first-order oracle queried at \(x\in\operatorname{dom}F\) returns a random vector \(G(x,\xi)\) such that, relative to the information \(\mathcal{F}\) available before the query, \[g(x):=\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid\mathcal{F}]\in\partial F(x),\qquad \mathbb{E}[\lVert G(x,\xi)-g(x)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal{F}]\leq\sigma^2.\] The bound holds almost surely. The parameter \(\sigma\geq0\) records oracle noise; \(\sigma=0\) recovers exact subgradient information almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic first-order oracle returns a conditionally unbiased subgradient estimate whose conditional variance is uniformly bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
The query \(x\) is \(\mathcal{F}\)-measurable and belongs to \(\operatorname{dom}F\).
The displayed conditional moments exist and \(\sigma<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[G(x,\xi)\mid\mathcal{F}]\in\partial F(x)\) and \(\mathbb{E}[\lVert G-g(x)\rVert^2\mid\mathcal{F}]\leq\sigma^2\).

notation.meaning: information available before the oracle call

children.title: Inexact Oracles
children.top_down_role: Oracle models permitting controlled error or uncertainty in returned records.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic inexact first-order oracle with separately verifiable value and gradient errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable on a normed space \(X\). An \((\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_g)\)-inexact first-order oracle is a map returning \((\widetilde f(x),\widetilde g(x))\in\mathbb R\times X^*\) at each query \(x\in X\), such that \[|\widetilde f(x)-f(x)|\leq \varepsilon_f,\qquad \|\widetilde g(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_*\leq \varepsilon_g.\] The exact oracle is recovered when \(\varepsilon_f=\varepsilon_g=0\). In a performance-estimation problem, the displayed inequalities are imposed on every queried point and become constraints on admissible oracle transcripts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact oracle returns approximate function values and gradients whose errors obey declared tolerances; these error bounds become constraints in the performance-estimation problem.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at every queried point.
\(\varepsilon_f,\varepsilon_g\geq 0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\widetilde f(x)-f(x)|\leq\varepsilon_f\) and \(\|\widetilde g(x)-\nabla f(x)\|_*\leq\varepsilon_g\).

notation.meaning: continuous dual of the normed space X
declared value and gradient error tolerances

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: absolute-error inexact first-order oracle is a standard deterministic model

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and content kind fit the leaf, but absolute value-and-gradient error bounds are only one of several inequivalent inexact-oracle models. A specific authoritative locator is required to establish that this is the intended local model.

children.title: Stochastic Inexactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Information models combining sampling variability with imperfect oracle responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic Inexactness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional bias-and-variance regimes for stochastic approximate first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_k)_{k\geq0}\) be the transcript filtration, let \(x_k\) be \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable, and let the oracle return \(G_k\). A stochastic inexactness regime is specified by predictable bounds \(b_k,\sigma_k\geq0\) satisfying \[\bigl\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]-\nabla f(x_k)\bigr\|_*\leq b_k,\qquad \mathbb E\!\left[\left.\|G_k-\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_*^2\right|\mathcal F_k\right]\leq\sigma_k^2.\] The unbiased regime has \(b_k=0\); bounded-variance, diminishing-noise, and deterministic-inexact regimes correspond respectively to bounded \(\sigma_k\), \(\sigma_k\to0\), and \(\sigma_k=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stochastic inexactness is classified through conditional bias and variance bounds, with unbiased, bounded-variance, vanishing-noise, and deterministic regimes obtained as special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(x_k\) is \(\mathcal F_k\)-measurable and \(G_k\) is conditionally square-integrable.
\(f\) is differentiable at \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]-\nabla f(x_k)\|_*\leq b_k\) and \(\mathbb E[\|G_k-\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_*^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma_k^2\).

notation.meaning: information available before the kth oracle response

children.title: Linear-Operator Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information models exposing forward actions of linear operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Operator Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward oracle access to a bounded linear operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be normed spaces and let \(A:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear. A forward linear-operator oracle for \(A\) accepts any query \(x\in X\) and returns \(y=Ax\in Y\). An algorithm with this oracle may use previously returned vectors and declared problem data, but it does not receive a matrix or other explicit representation of \(A\). Consequently, every admissible transcript satisfies the linear consistency relations \(y_i=Ax_i\) for all queried indices \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward linear-operator oracle evaluates an otherwise implicit bounded linear map at queried vectors, and every transcript must be consistent with one common operator.
assumptions_latex: \(A:X\to Y\) is a fixed bounded linear operator.
Each query satisfies \(x_i\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_i=Ax_i\in Y\) for every forward query \(x_i\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: black-box application of a bounded linear map is standard

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically plausible and fits the leaf, but no inspectable source supports the black-box access restrictions or their use as a PEP transcript model.

children.title: Adjoint Oracles
children.top_down_role: Information models exposing actions of adjoint operators.

knowledge_statements.title: Adjoint Oracles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle access to the adjoint associated with a fixed forward operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be Hilbert spaces, let \(A:X\to Y\) be bounded and linear, and let \(A^*:Y\to X\) denote its adjoint. An adjoint oracle accepts \(y\in Y\) and returns \(z=A^*y\in X\), where \[\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,A^*y\rangle_X\qquad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Thus an admissible transcript \((y_i,z_i)\) must be consistent with the unique adjoint of the same operator \(A\), rather than with an independently chosen linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adjoint oracle returns the action of the unique adjoint of the forward operator, characterized by the Hilbert-space inner-product identity.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Hilbert spaces.
\(A:X\to Y\) is bounded and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z=A^*y\) and \(\langle Ax,y\rangle_Y=\langle x,z\rangle_X\) for all \(x\in X\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: adjoint characterization is standard functional analysis

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Hilbert-space adjoint definition is standard and the content kind fits, but the oracle-access and common-operator transcript interpretation lacks a cited locator.

children.title: Paired Forward–Adjoint Access
children.top_down_role: Information models coordinating forward and adjoint records for a common linear map.

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Forward–Adjoint Access
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency conditions coupling forward and adjoint oracle transcripts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be Hilbert spaces. A transcript has paired forward–adjoint access when there exists one bounded linear operator \(A:X\to Y\) such that every forward response and adjoint response satisfy \[u_i=Ax_i,\qquad z_j=A^*y_j.\] Equivalently, in addition to linearity within each family, all queried pairs obey the cross-consistency equations \[\langle u_i,y_j\rangle_Y=\langle x_i,z_j\rangle_X\qquad\text{for all }i,j.\] These equations couple the two oracle channels and are necessary for representing them by a common forward–adjoint pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Paired access requires forward and adjoint replies to arise from one common operator; cross-inner-product identities provide directly checkable transcript constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are Hilbert spaces.
All forward and adjoint replies are generated by one bounded linear operator \(A:X\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle u_i,y_j\rangle_Y=\langle x_i,z_j\rangle_X\) for every forward index \(i\) and adjoint index \(j\).

notation.meaning: forward query-response pair with u_i=A x_i
adjoint query-response pair with z_j=A^* y_j
adjoint of the common forward operator A

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: cross-consistency follows from the defining adjoint identity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition container is appropriate, and the cross-inner-product equations are necessary. The asserted equivalence requires explicit transcript linear-consistency and bounded-extension hypotheses, especially for infinite families, and no source establishes the intended sufficiency statement.

children.title: Method-Encoding Models
children.top_down_role: Structural classes of admissible dependence on previously revealed information.

children.title: Fixed-Step Encodings
children.top_down_role: Trajectory encodings with iteration coefficients fixed before execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Step Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical PEP representation of predetermined first-order updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a differentiable objective queried at \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\), a fixed-step first-order encoding prescribes scalars \(h_{i,j}\) before oracle execution and imposes \[x_i=x_0-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}h_{i,j}g_j,\qquad g_j=\nabla f(x_j),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.\] The coefficients may depend on the iteration indices and declared class parameters, but not on realized oracle values. Hence each iterate belongs to the affine span generated by \(x_0\) and the preceding gradients, and the method constraints are linear equalities among transcript vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-step encoding expresses each iterate as a predetermined linear combination of earlier gradients, yielding linear transcript constraints suitable for performance estimation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0,\ldots,x_N\).
The coefficients \(h_{i,j}\) are fixed before oracle responses are observed.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fixed-step first-order span encoding is standard in PEP literature

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind and formula fit fixed-step PEP encodings, and the displayed TeX is properly delimited. An authoritative PEP source with a specific locator is still required for the exact encoding class and its transcript interpretation.

children.title: Oblivious Encodings
children.top_down_role: Trajectory encodings whose coefficients do not depend on observed oracle history.

knowledge_statements.title: Oblivious Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-independent method coefficients determined only from declared information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a horizon \(N\) and declared side information \(\theta\), such as known smoothness or convexity parameters. A method encoding is oblivious if, for every iteration \(i\), all coefficients defining \(x_i\) are deterministic functions of \((i,N,\theta)\) and are independent of the realized transcript \(\mathcal T_{i-1}=\{(x_j,f_j,g_j):0\leq j<i\}\). Thus two problem instances sharing \((N,\theta)\) use identical coefficients through iteration \(N\), even when their oracle responses differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An oblivious encoding chooses all method coefficients from iteration indices, horizon, and declared parameters, never from the observed oracle transcript.
assumptions_latex: The horizon \(N\) and declared information \(\theta\) are fixed before execution.
The oracle transcript is not included in \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h_{i,j}=H_{i,j}(i,N,\theta)\) with \(h_{i,j}\) independent of \(\mathcal T_{i-1}\).

notation.meaning: oracle transcript available before iteration i

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: transcript-independent coefficients are the usual meaning of oblivious method encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits, but “oblivious” has varying meanings across PEP and oracle-complexity literature. No source fixes the intended dependence on horizon, declared parameters, or randomization for this leaf.

children.title: Fixed-Step Oblivious Regimes
children.top_down_role: Encodings simultaneously restricted to predetermined steps and history-independent coefficients.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Step Oblivious Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined regime producing affine, transcript-independent PEP method constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A first-order method lies in the fixed-step oblivious regime over horizon \(N\) when there exist coefficients \(h_{i,j}=H_{i,j}(N,\theta)\), selected before any oracle call, such that \[x_i=x_0-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}h_{i,j}g_j,\qquad i=1,\ldots,N.\] Here \(\theta\) contains only declared problem-class data, and neither \(H_{i,j}\) nor \(h_{i,j}\) depends on realized function values, gradients, randomness, or acceptance tests. For fixed coefficients, these update relations are affine equalities and can be inserted directly into a Gram-based performance-estimation formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-step oblivious regime combines predetermined gradient-span updates with complete independence from realized oracle information, producing affine constraints in the PEP transcript.
assumptions_latex: The finite horizon \(N\) and declared data \(\theta\) are fixed in advance.
Exact first-order responses \(g_j=\nabla f(x_j)\) are available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i=x_0-\sum_{j<i}H_{i,j}(N,\theta)g_j\) with coefficients independent of the realized transcript.

children.title: Adaptive Encodings
children.top_down_role: Method representations whose parameters depend on information revealed during execution.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Method encodings whose decisions are measurable functions of the observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T_i=\{(x_j,f_j,g_j):0\leq j\leq i\}\) denote the transcript after iteration \(i\). An adaptive first-order encoding specifies the next query by \[x_{i+1}=\Phi_i(\mathcal T_i,\theta),\] where \(\Phi_i\) is measurable and \(\theta\) is declared side information. Scalar coefficients, search directions, restarts, and stopping decisions may therefore depend on observed oracle responses, but not on future responses. In a performance-estimation formulation, the graph of each decision rule or valid consequences of that graph must be encoded as additional transcript constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive encoding selects each new query from the information observed so far, so its PEP model must encode the decision rule or valid consequences.
assumptions_latex: Each oracle response in \(\mathcal T_i\) is available before \(x_{i+1}\) is selected.
Each decision rule \(\Phi_i\) is measurable with respect to the transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{i+1}=\Phi_i(\mathcal T_i,\theta)\) and depends on no future oracle response.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: nonanticipative transcript-measurable decisions define adaptivity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits adaptive encodings, but the measurable spaces underlying the transcript and decision maps are not specified, and no cited source supports the asserted graph-constraint treatment in PEP.

children.title: Line-Search Encodings
children.top_down_role: Method representations incorporating accepted-step conditions or search-generated parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Armijo–Wolfe acceptance conditions encoded as transcript inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(x_i\in\mathbb R^d\), and define \(f_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i=\nabla f(x_i)\). Given a direction \(d_i\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i<0\), an Armijo–weak-Wolfe line-search encoding introduces \(\alpha_i>0\), sets \(x_{i+1}=x_i+\alpha_i d_i\), defines \(f_{i+1}=f(x_{i+1})\) and \(g_{i+1}=\nabla f(x_{i+1})\), and imposes \[f_{i+1}\leq f_i+c_1\alpha_i g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i,\qquad g_{i+1}^{\mathsf T}d_i\geq c_2 g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i,\] where \(0<c_1<c_2<1\). These relations encode the accepted step without explicitly representing every rejected trial point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Armijo–weak-Wolfe line-search encoding introduces the accepted positive step length and imposes the update, sufficient-decrease, and weak-curvature conditions directly on the accepted oracle transcript.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at \(x_i\) and \(x_{i+1}\).
\(d_i\in\mathbb R^d\) satisfies \(g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{i+1}=x_i+\alpha_i d_i\) satisfies the Armijo and weak-Wolfe inequalities.

notation.meaning: function value f(x_k) at an accepted query point
gradient \(\nabla f(x_k)\) at an accepted query point

children.title: Adaptive Line-Search Regimes
children.top_down_role: Encodings combining history-responsive choices with line-search information.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Line-Search Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipative step selection certified by transcript-level acceptance conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, define \(f_j=f(x_j)\) and \(g_j=\nabla f(x_j)\), and let \(\mathcal T_i=\{(x_j,f_j,g_j):0\leq j\leq i\}\) be the accepted transcript available at iteration \(i\). Given declared side information \(\theta\), an iterative method is in an adaptive line-search regime when \(d_i=D_i(\mathcal T_i,\theta)\) is selected nonanticipatively, trial step lengths are tested using newly observed oracle data, and an accepted \(\alpha_i>0\) produces \(x_{i+1}=x_i+\alpha_i d_i\). In an Armijo–weak-Wolfe regime, each accepted step additionally satisfies \[f_{i+1}\leq f_i+c_1\alpha_i g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i,\qquad g_{i+1}^{\mathsf T}d_i\geq c_2g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i,\] where \(g_i^{\mathsf T}d_i<0\) and \(0<c_1<c_2<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive Armijo–weak-Wolfe line-search regime chooses each direction from the accepted transcript, tests trial step lengths using new oracle information, and certifies the accepted step through sufficient-decrease and weak-curvature inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable at every accepted query point.
\(D_i\) is measurable with respect to the accepted transcript and uses no future oracle response.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{i+1}=x_i+\alpha_i d_i\) and each accepted step satisfies the Armijo and weak-Wolfe conditions.

notation.meaning: accepted transcript available when the direction is selected

children.title: Parameter-Free Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations for methods operating without prior numerical knowledge of selected problem parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adaptive encodings independent of unknown numerical problem-class parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\lambda\) denote numerical instance parameters, such as a smoothness constant, strong-convexity modulus, gradient bound, or distance to a solution. A method encoding is parameter-free relative to \(\lambda\) if its initialization, query rules, and stopping rule have the form \[x_0=I(\theta),\qquad x_{i+1}=\Phi_i(\mathcal T_i,\theta),\qquad \tau=S(\mathcal T_0,\mathcal T_1,\ldots;\theta),\] where none of \(I,\Phi_i,S\) takes \(\lambda\) as input. The rules may estimate scale from the observed transcript, provided they do not use the unknown parameter directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-free encoding never takes designated unknown problem constants as inputs, though it may infer operational scales adaptively from observed oracle data.
assumptions_latex: The unknown parameter vector \(\lambda\) is distinguished from declared side information \(\theta\).
Each adaptive rule is nonanticipative with respect to the transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\), \(\Phi_i\), and \(S\) are independent of the designated unknown parameters \(\lambda\).

notation.meaning: algorithmic stopping time or output index

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exclusion of unknown class parameters is the customary parameter-free predicate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but parameter-free status is meaningful only relative to a precisely designated set of unavailable parameters. The infinite-transcript expression for S also needs a stopping-time/nonanticipativity formulation, and no authoritative PEP locator supports the proposed definition.

children.title: Universal Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations designed to cover multiple regularity classes or parameter regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform finite-horizon PEP encoding across a parameterized union of oracle classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{\mathcal F_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) be function classes with compatible first-order oracles, and let \(H_N\) denote an oracle transcript through iteration \(N\). A universal encoding is a fixed collection of algebraic and measurability constraints \(\mathcal E_N(H_N)\) whose form and coefficients do not depend on \(\theta\), such that every transcript generated by the encoded method on every \(f\in\mathcal F_\theta\) satisfies \(\mathcal E_N(H_N)\). If the encoding is exact, every transcript satisfying \(\mathcal E_N\) and the interpolation conditions for some \(\mathcal F_\theta\) is realizable by that method on an instance in \(\mathcal F_\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal encoding uses one parameter-independent constraint system for all classes in a family; exactness additionally requires every feasible encoded transcript to be realizable.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is fixed.
The classes \(\mathcal F_\theta\) share a common transcript format and oracle semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal E_N\) is valid simultaneously for every \(\theta\in\Theta\), and exactness identifies feasible encoded transcripts with realizable method transcripts.

notation.meaning: first-order oracle transcript through iteration N
index set of admissible problem classes

children.title: Parameter-Free Universal Regimes
children.top_down_role: Encodings combining absent parameter knowledge with adaptation across problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Universal Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous PEP regime for methods not given class constants or target accuracy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For classes \(\{\mathcal F_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), a method is in a parameter-free universal regime through horizon \(N\) when each decision satisfies \(x_{k+1}=\Phi_k(H_k,U_k)\), where \(\Phi_k\) is independent of \(\theta\), class constants, and a prescribed accuracy. Its worst-case performance is therefore represented by the single robust quantity \[\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\ \sup_{f\in\mathcal F_\theta}\ \mathbb E\!\left[\mathcal P(H_N,f)\right],\] subject to one universal method encoding and the interpolation constraints associated with the selected \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method receives neither class parameters nor target accuracy, and one robust performance problem covers every admissible class parameter.
assumptions_latex: \(H_k\) contains only observations available by time \(k\).
\(U_k\) is internal randomness independent of unavailable problem parameters.
\(\mathcal P\) is an integrable terminal performance criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method rules are common to all \(\theta\in\Theta\), while the worst case takes the supremum over both \(\theta\) and instances.

notation.meaning: internal random seed at iteration k

Meaning of universal regime may vary between adaptive-method frameworks.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the regime leaf, but the asserted interpretation of parameter-free universality and its reduction to the displayed robust PEP require a direct source. Different adaptive or universal-method frameworks impose materially different information restrictions.

children.title: Randomized Method Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations that retain random choices or distributions within the encoded trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Method Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kernel representation of randomized first-order decisions in a finite-horizon PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space, let \(H_k\) be the transcript available before decision \(k+1\). A randomized method encoding is specified by stochastic kernels \(K_k(\cdot\mid H_k)\) such that \[\mathbb P\!\left(x_{k+1}\in B\mid H_k\right)=K_k(B\mid H_k)\] for every Borel set \(B\) in the decision space. Equivalently, after adjoining independent seeds \(U_k\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,1]\), one may write \(x_{k+1}=\Phi_k(H_k,U_k)\) with measurable \(\Phi_k\). A randomized PEP imposes these conditional-law constraints and evaluates an expectation or a specified tail functional of the terminal performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomized decisions are encoded by conditional probability kernels, equivalently by measurable history-and-seed maps, and performance is evaluated probabilistically.
assumptions_latex: The decision space is a standard Borel space.
Each \(K_k\) is a measurable stochastic kernel.
All terminal quantities used by the criterion are measurable and integrable when expectation is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditional distribution of each iterate is determined by the encoded kernel, permitting expected or tail performance evaluation.

children.title: History-Dependent Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations whose future coefficients depend on previously observed records.

knowledge_statements.title: History-Dependent Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonanticipative encoding in which every decision may use the complete observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_k=(x_0,y_0,\ldots,x_k,y_k)\), where \(y_i\) is the oracle response observed at \(x_i\). A deterministic history-dependent encoding consists of measurable maps \(\Phi_k\) satisfying \(x_{k+1}=\Phi_k(H_k)\) for \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\). The rule is nonanticipative: \(x_{k+1}\) may depend on every component of \(H_k\), but not on \(y_{k+1}\) or later observations. In an algebraic PEP, each equality or membership constraint used to describe \(\Phi_k\) may involve only variables indexed at most \(k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A history-dependent method chooses each new query from the entire observed past while excluding current and future oracle information.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is fixed.
Oracle responses \(y_k\) are observed after querying \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each \(x_{k+1}\) is measurable with respect to the information generated by \(H_k\) and is nonanticipative.

notation.meaning: complete observed history through response k

children.title: Randomized History-Dependent Regimes
children.top_down_role: Encodings coupling random choices with dependence on accumulated information.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized History-Dependent Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adapted randomized regime combining full-history dependence with conditional sampling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathscr F_k=\sigma(H_k)\) be the information available after the \(k\)-th oracle response. A method belongs to a randomized history-dependent regime when, for each \(k<N\), its next query has an \(\mathscr F_k\)-measurable conditional law \(K_k(\cdot\mid H_k)\), or equivalently \(x_{k+1}=\Phi_k(H_k,U_k)\), where \(U_k\) is independent of \(\mathscr F_k\). Thus the sampling rule may adapt to the complete realized history but cannot depend on future oracle responses or future random seeds. The associated certificate must bound the chosen expectation or tail criterion under every admissible kernel-constrained trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each randomized query may adapt to the full realized past, but its fresh randomness and conditional law cannot use future information.
assumptions_latex: The decision and transcript spaces are standard Borel spaces.
Fresh seeds \(U_k\) are independent of \(\mathscr F_k\).
The certified probabilistic performance criterion is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{k+1}\) is adapted to \(\sigma(\mathscr F_k,U_k)\), and its conditional law given \(\mathscr F_k\) equals \(K_k(\cdot\mid H_k)\).

children.title: Stationary Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations with iteration-invariant structural coefficients or transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-invariant method encoding with a single update rule reused at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(s_k\) be the method state and \(y_k\) the oracle response generated from the current query. A stationary encoding is an iteration model for which there exists one time-independent relation \(\mathcal R\) satisfying \[(s_k,y_k,s_{k+1})\in\mathcal R,\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1.\] If the method is deterministic, this may be written \(s_{k+1}=T(s_k,y_k)\) for a single map \(T\). Fixed algorithmic coefficients may be included in \(T\), but iteration-dependent coefficients or explicitly time-indexed update maps are excluded unless the iteration counter is itself included in the state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary encoding repeats one update relation at every iteration; time variation is allowed only when represented within the state.
assumptions_latex: The state and oracle-response spaces do not change with \(k\).
All fixed algorithmic parameters are included in the definition of \(\mathcal R\) or \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The same relation \(\mathcal R\), or the same deterministic map \(T\), governs every transition.

notation.meaning: oracle response used in transition k

children.title: State-Space Encodings
children.top_down_role: Representations organized around latent state, observable records, and structured transitions.

knowledge_statements.title: State-Space Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional latent-state realization of an iterative first-order method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A state-space encoding of a deterministic first-order method consists of a state space \(\mathcal S\), initialization \(s_0=I(x_0)\), query map \(x_k=C_k(s_k)\), oracle response \(y_k=\mathcal O_f(x_k)\), and transition map \(s_{k+1}=T_k(s_k,y_k)\). The externally visible transcript is obtained by eliminating the latent states from \[s_0=I(x_0),\qquad x_k=C_k(s_k),\qquad y_k=\mathcal O_f(x_k),\qquad s_{k+1}=T_k(s_k,y_k).\] The encoding is exact when these equations generate precisely the method’s admissible finite-horizon transcripts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A method is represented by a latent state, a query map, an oracle response, and a state transition; exactness means no transcripts are lost or added.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is fixed.
All maps have compatible domains and codomains.
The oracle \(\mathcal O_f\) returns the information used by the method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating \(s_0,\ldots,s_N\) yields the visible method constraints; exactness makes this projection equal to the admissible transcript set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The state-space representation fits the leaf and introduces the needed maps, but no source supports the general PEP realization or the stated projection-based exactness convention.

children.title: Stationary State-Space Regimes
children.top_down_role: State-space representations with iteration-invariant transition structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary State-Space Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Time-invariant finite-state realization used uniformly over the PEP horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method lies in a stationary state-space regime when there are fixed spaces and fixed maps \(C\) and \(T\) such that, for every \(k<N\), \[x_k=C(s_k),\qquad y_k=\mathcal O_f(x_k),\qquad s_{k+1}=T(s_k,y_k).\] Neither \(C\) nor \(T\) depends explicitly on \(k\). Constant stepsizes, momentum coefficients, or preconditioners may be embedded in \(T\). A schedule depending on \(k\) is stationary only after augmenting \(s_k\) with sufficient variables, such as a counter, to reproduce that schedule through the same transition map.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One fixed query map and one fixed state transition govern all iterations; varying schedules require enough extra state to make the realization time invariant.
assumptions_latex: The state and oracle-response spaces are fixed across iterations.
Algorithmic constants are fixed throughout the horizon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The entire finite-horizon method is represented by repeated application of the same state-space transition.

children.title: Initial-Data Normalizations
children.top_down_role: Normalization families that make worst-case comparisons well posed.

children.title: Initial-Distance Normalizations
children.top_down_role: Worst-case comparison regimes normalized by distance from initial data to a reference solution.

knowledge_statements.title: Initial-Distance Normalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP initial-data constraint fixing or bounding distance from the initial point to a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(x_0\in X\), and let \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\). An initial-distance normalization with scale \(D>0\) imposes \[\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\le D.\] When the problem class and performance criterion are homogeneous under spatial rescaling, one may set \(D=1\) after replacing every primal displacement by \(D^{-1/2}\) times that displacement. A bound obtained for the normalized problem must then be rescaled according to the homogeneity degree of the chosen performance criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The initial point is constrained to lie within squared distance D of a minimizer; homogeneous problems may be rescaled to D equal to one.
assumptions_latex: A minimizer \(x_\star\) exists.
Normalization to one is used only when the instance class and criterion admit the stated scaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\le D\), with unit normalization available under spatial homogeneity.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the squared initial distance

children.title: Radius Normalizations
children.top_down_role: Worst-case comparison regimes normalized by a prescribed geometric radius.

knowledge_statements.title: Radius Normalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent unsquared-radius convention for bounding the initial point’s displacement from a solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space, let \(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\), and choose \(R>0\). The radius normalization imposes \[\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R.\] Under a homogeneous spatial rescaling, define \(\widehat x=(x-x_\star)/R\); then \(\lVert\widehat x_0\rVert\le1\). If the performance measure \(\mathcal P\) has spatial homogeneity degree \(q\), so that scaling displacements by \(R\) multiplies \(\mathcal P\) by \(R^q\), a unit-radius certificate \(\mathcal P\le B\) yields \(\mathcal P\le R^qB\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The initial displacement is bounded by radius R; homogeneous instances can use unit radius and restore the factor determined by the performance measure’s degree.
assumptions_latex: A minimizer \(x_\star\) exists.
The asserted rescaling is used only for a spatially homogeneous class and criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\), and unit-radius bounds rescale by \(R^q\) when the criterion has degree \(q\).

notation.meaning: spatial homogeneity degree of the performance measure

children.title: Distance–Radius Equivalence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings in which distance bounds and radius bounds provide interchangeable comparison scales.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance–Radius Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic equivalence between squared-distance and unsquared-radius initial normalizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a normed space and let \(x_0,x_\star\in X\). For every \(R>0\), setting \(D=R^2\) gives the pointwise equivalence \[\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\le D\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R.\] Consequently, PEPs that differ only by these two forms of the initial bound have identical feasible instances under the substitutions \(D=R^2\) and \(R=\sqrt D\). In particular, unit squared-distance and unit-radius normalizations coincide. This equivalence concerns distance from the selected minimizer and does not by itself imply a diameter bound on a feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A squared-distance bound D and a radius bound R describe the same initial constraint when D equals R squared; this does not make either constraint a global feasible-set diameter bound.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a normed space.
\(x_0,x_\star\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under \(D=R^2\), \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\le D\iff\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\).

children.title: Objective-Gap Normalizations
children.top_down_role: Comparison regimes scaled by an initial or reference objective-value gap.

knowledge_statements.title: Objective-Gap Normalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initial-data constraint bounding suboptimality of the starting point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) attain its minimum value \(f_\star\), and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). An objective-gap normalization with scale \(\Delta>0\) imposes \[0\le f(x_0)-f_\star\le\Delta.\] If the function class and method are invariant under positive vertical scaling, define \(\widehat f=(f-f_\star)/\Delta\); then \(\inf\widehat f=0\) and \(0\le\widehat f(x_0)\le1\). A bound for the normalized objective is transferred back by multiplying every objective-value gap by \(\Delta\), while iterates remain unchanged when the method’s parameter scaling is compatible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initial suboptimality is bounded by Δ; under compatible vertical homogeneity it can be normalized to one and objective gaps rescaled by Δ.
assumptions_latex: The minimum value \(f_\star\) is finite and attained.
\(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\Delta>0\).
Unit normalization is used only under compatible vertical scaling of the class and method.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\le f(x_0)-f_\star\le\Delta\), with \(0\le\widehat f(x_0)\le1\) after admissible vertical normalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Normalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization of an initial composite stationarity residual in a performance-estimation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and lower semicontinuous on a finite-dimensional normed space, and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}F\). For a prescribed scale \(R>0\), the residual-normalized instance class is defined by \[\operatorname{dist}_{*}(0,\partial F(x_0))\le R.\] Equivalently, there exists \(v_0\in\partial F(x_0)\) with \(\lVert v_0\rVert_{*}\le R\). Dividing the objective by \(R\) produces the unit normalization \(\operatorname{dist}_{*}(0,\partial(F/R)(x_0))\le1\), without changing the minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance is residual-normalized when the smallest initial subgradient norm is bounded; rescaling the objective converts any positive residual bound to one.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is finite-dimensional and equipped with a norm and its dual norm.
\(F\) is proper and lower semicontinuous, and \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}_{*}(0,\partial F(x_0))\le R\), equivalently \(\operatorname{dist}_{*}(0,\partial(F/R)(x_0))\le1\).

notation.meaning: limiting subdifferential of F at x

knowledge_statements.title: Gap–Residual Comparison Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided comparison for differentiable smooth strongly convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex with respect to a Hilbert norm, where \(0<\mu\le L\), and let \(x_*\) minimize \(f\). Then every \(x\in X\) satisfies \[\frac{1}{2L}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^{2}\le f(x)-f(x_*)\le\frac{1}{2\mu}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^{2}.\] Thus an objective-gap normalization and a gradient-residual normalization are quantitatively interchangeable when both curvature bounds are fixed. Without strong convexity, only the left inequality is guaranteed in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For smooth strongly convex objectives, the objective gap lies between fixed multiples of the squared gradient norm; without strong convexity, the upper comparison may fail.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable, \(L\)-smooth, and \(\mu\)-strongly convex.
\(0<\mu\le L\), and \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\frac{1}{2L}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^{2}\le f(x)-f(x_*)\le\frac{1}{2\mu}\lVert\nabla f(x)\rVert^{2}\) for every \(x\in X\).

children.title: Bounded-Domain Normalizations
children.top_down_role: Comparison regimes controlled by the size or diameter of the admissible domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Domain Normalizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Diameter normalization for feasible-domain performance-estimation classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a nonempty subset of a finite-dimensional normed space. A bounded-domain normalization with scale \(D>0\) imposes \[\operatorname{diam}(Q):=\sup_{x,y\in Q}\lVert x-y\rVert\le D.\] Under the change of variables \(z=x/D\), the transformed domain \(Q/D:=\{x/D:x\in Q\}\) has diameter at most one. If only distances from an initial point are used, the weaker radius normalization \(\sup_{x\in Q}\lVert x-x_0\rVert\le D\) may be imposed instead and must not be identified with the diameter convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-domain regime fixes either a domain diameter or an explicitly distinguished initial-point radius; spatial rescaling reduces the selected positive bound to one.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is nonempty and contained in a finite-dimensional normed space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{diam}(Q)\le D\) implies \(\operatorname{diam}(Q/D)\le1\).
