children.title: Separation Transformations
children.top_down_role: Transfer from aggregate records to structurally separated records.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residualization between aggregate convex interpolation and a prescribed differentiable convex component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let aggregate data \(\{(x_i,g_i,f_i)\}_{i=1}^m\) be given in \(\mathbb R^d\). Let \(f^{(1)}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and convex, with
\[
f^{(1)}(x_i)=f_i^{(1)},
\qquad \nabla f^{(1)}(x_i)=g_i^{(1)}.
\]
Define residual data by
\[
f_i^{(2)}=f_i-f_i^{(1)},
\qquad g_i^{(2)}=g_i-g_i^{(1)}.
\]
A proper convex function \(f^{(2)}:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) interpolates the residual data if and only if \(f=f^{(1)}+f^{(2)}\) satisfies \(f(x_i)=f_i\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the prescribed component is differentiable and convex, subtracting its sampled values and gradients converts aggregate convex interpolation exactly into residual convex interpolation, and summing the two functions reverses the transformation.
assumptions_latex: \(x_i,g_i,g_i^{(1)}\in\mathbb R^d\) and \(f_i,f_i^{(1)}\in\mathbb R\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\).
\(f^{(1)}:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) is differentiable and convex, with the prescribed values and gradients.
\(f^{(2)}:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interpolation of \((x_i,g_i-g_i^{(1)},f_i-f_i^{(1)})\) by \(f^{(2)}\) is equivalent to interpolation of \((x_i,g_i,f_i)\) by \(f^{(1)}+f^{(2)}\).

notation.meaning: Residual sampled value and first-order datum.

children.title: Component Transformations
children.top_down_role: Changes of representation that expose, merge, or reindex component-level records.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise transformation of finite oracle records before aggregation in a decomposed objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=\sum_{r=1}^{m}f_r\), and let \(\mathcal R_r=\{(x_i,g_{r,i},v_{r,i})\}_{i\in I}\) be interpolable by \(f_r\). For positive scalars \(a_r\), constants \(b_r\), and a common affine change \(y=T x+c\) with invertible \(T\), define \(\widetilde f_r(y)=a_r f_r(T^{-1}(y-c))+b_r\). The transformed component record is \(\widetilde x_i=T x_i+c\), \(\widetilde g_{r,i}=a_rT^{-*}g_{r,i}\), and \(\widetilde v_{r,i}=a_rv_{r,i}+b_r\). Each transformed record is interpolable by its corresponding \(\widetilde f_r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive rescaling, constant shifting, and an invertible affine coordinate change transform each component’s values and subgradients while preserving componentwise interpolability.
assumptions_latex: \(m<\infty\) and every \(\mathcal R_r\) is interpolable by \(f_r\).
\(a_r>0\) for every \(r\).
\(T\) is an invertible linear operator on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{(\widetilde x_i,\widetilde g_{r,i},\widetilde v_{r,i})\}_{i\in I}\) is interpolable by \(\widetilde f_r\) for every \(r\).

notation.meaning: Inverse of the adjoint of T.

children.title: Aggregate–Component Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between aggregate interpolation data and componentwise realizability.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregate–Component Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility equations connecting component oracle records to the record of their sum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f=\sum_{r=1}^{m}f_r\), component records \(\{(x_i,g_{r,i},v_{r,i})\}\) and an aggregate record \(\{(x_i,g_i,v_i)\}\) are compatible precisely when, for every \(i\), \[g_i=\sum_{r=1}^{m}g_{r,i},\qquad v_i=\sum_{r=1}^{m}v_{r,i}.\] If every component record is interpolated by \(f_r\), these identities make the aggregate record interpolable by \(f\). Conversely, any chosen decomposition \(g_i=\sum_r g_{r,i}\) with \(g_{r,i}\in\partial f_r(x_i)\) and \(v_{r,i}=f_r(x_i)\) yields the aggregate oracle data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Component values and subgradients must sum to their aggregate counterparts; component interpolation plus these coupling identities realizes the aggregate sum objective.
assumptions_latex: \(f_r\) are proper convex functions on a common finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(x_i\in\bigcap_{r=1}^{m}\operatorname{dom}f_r\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) and \(v_i=f(x_i)\) for every \(i\).

notation.meaning: Subgradient and value of component r at sample i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-way construction from component subgradients and values to aggregate data is correct, and condition fits the leaf. However, no source supports the PEP compatibility formulation or clarifies the intended scope of the phrase “compatible precisely when.”

children.title: Conjugate Transformations
children.top_down_role: Transfer of interpolation structure through convex conjugation.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate transformation of convex subgradient oracle records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, closed, and convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, with conjugate \(f^*(g)=\sup_x\{\langle g,x\rangle-f(x)\}.\) A record triple \((x_i,g_i,v_i)\) satisfying \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) transforms into \((g_i,x_i,v_i^*)\) for \(f^*\), where \[v_i^*=\langle x_i,g_i\rangle-v_i.\] Indeed, the transformation is characterized by the equivalences \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), \(x_i\in\partial f^*(g_i)\), and \(f(x_i)+f^*(g_i)=\langle x_i,g_i\rangle\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation exchanges sample points and subgradients, while the transformed value equals their pairing minus the original function value.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex.
\(v_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_i\in\partial f^*(g_i)\) and \(f^*(g_i)=\langle x_i,g_i\rangle-v_i\) for every \(i\).

children.title: Envelope Transformations
children.top_down_role: Transfer of interpolation structure through envelope representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Envelope Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation from proximal-point records to Moreau-envelope value-gradient records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper, closed, convex function \(f\) and \(\lambda>0\), define the Moreau envelope \(e_\lambda f(x)=\inf_y\{f(y)+(2\lambda)^{-1}\|x-y\|^2\}.\) If \(p_i\) and \(g_i\) satisfy \(g_i\in\partial f(p_i)\) and \(x_i=p_i+\lambda g_i\), then \(p_i\) is the unique proximal point at \(x_i\), and the transformed envelope record is \[e_\lambda f(x_i)=f(p_i)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|g_i\|^2,\qquad \nabla e_\lambda f(x_i)=g_i.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient record at a proximal point becomes a differentiable Moreau-envelope record after shifting the point by the scaled subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(\lambda>0\).
\(g_i\in\partial f(p_i)\) and \(x_i=p_i+\lambda g_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_i=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(x_i)\), \(\nabla e_\lambda f(x_i)=g_i\), and \(e_\lambda f(x_i)=f(p_i)+(\lambda/2)\|g_i\|^2\).

notation.meaning: Moreau envelope of f with parameter lambda.

children.title: Resolvent Transformations
children.top_down_role: Transfer of operator interpolation structure through resolvent representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Transformations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Graph transformation between a monotone operator and its resolvent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be a maximal monotone operator on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space and let \(\lambda>0\). Its resolvent is \(J_{\lambda A}=(I+\lambda A)^{-1}\). Every graph record \((p_i,a_i)\) with \(a_i\in A(p_i)\) transforms to the resolvent record \((x_i,p_i)\), where \(x_i=p_i+\lambda a_i\). Conversely, \[p_i=J_{\lambda A}(x_i)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a_i=\lambda^{-1}(x_i-p_i)\in A(p_i).\] Thus the transformation is bijective at the level of finite graph records.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a scaled operator value to its base point converts an operator graph record into a resolvent input-output record, and the conversion is reversible.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_i\in A(p_i)\) if and only if \(p_i=J_{\lambda A}(p_i+\lambda a_i)\).

notation.meaning: Resolvent of the scaled operator lambda A.

children.title: Dual–Resolvent Correspondences
children.top_down_role: Structural links among conjugate, envelope, and resolvent representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual–Resolvent Correspondences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moreau correspondence between primal and conjugate proximal-resolvent records.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be proper, closed, and convex, let \(\lambda>0\), and set \(p=J_{\lambda\partial f}(x)\) and \(g=(x-p)/\lambda\). Then \(g\in\partial f(p)\), hence \(p\in\partial f^*(g)\), and \[g=J_{\lambda^{-1}\partial f^*}(x/\lambda),\qquad J_{\lambda\partial f}(x)+\lambda J_{\lambda^{-1}\partial f^*}(x/\lambda)=x.\] Therefore a primal resolvent record determines, and is determined by, the corresponding conjugate resolvent record.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal proximal point and its scaled residual form a conjugate subgradient pair and satisfy Moreau’s primal-dual resolvent decomposition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.
\(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p+\lambda g=x\), \(g\in\partial f(p)\), and \(g=J_{\lambda^{-1}\partial f^*}(x/\lambda)\).

notation.meaning: Scaled primal residual and dual resolvent output.

children.title: Realizability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating exact interpolation from necessary-only or dimension-restricted descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Necessary-Only Interpolation Descriptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between necessary relaxations and exact finite interpolation descriptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I_{\mathcal F}(I)\) be the set of finite records \(\{(x_i,g_i,v_i)\}_{i\in I}\) realizable by some \(f\in\mathcal F\), and let \(\mathcal N_{\mathcal F}(I)\) be the records satisfying a proposed family of necessary inequalities. Necessity gives \(\mathcal I_{\mathcal F}(I)\subseteq\mathcal N_{\mathcal F}(I).\) The description is necessary-only when the inclusion is strict: \[\mathcal I_{\mathcal F}(I)\subsetneq\mathcal N_{\mathcal F}(I).\] In that case, feasibility of the inequalities is not a realizability certificate and can produce nonattainable PEP instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A necessary-only interpolation system contains every realizable record but also admits at least one record that no function in the target class realizes.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
\(\mathcal N_{\mathcal F}(I)\) is defined by inequalities valid for every record realized by \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I_{\mathcal F}(I)\subsetneq\mathcal N_{\mathcal F}(I)\) implies that inequality feasibility does not certify interpolation.

notation.meaning: Exactly realizable records for class F.
Records satisfying the proposed necessary conditions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary fits the terminal container, and the set-theoretic definition is coherent. A class-specific source or witness is required to substantiate strict inclusion and the claimed occurrence of nonattainable PEP instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Restricted Realizability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank condition for realizing a finite scalar-Gram record in a prescribed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_1,\ldots,z_q\) denote all vector quantities in a finite oracle record, and let \(G\in\mathbb S^q\) prescribe their inner products by \(G_{ab}=\langle z_a,z_b\rangle.\) The vector portion of the record is realizable in \(\mathbb R^d\) if and only if \[G\succeq0\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{rank}(G)\le d.\] Consequently, interpolation inequalities expressed through \(G\) yield dimension-\(d\) realizability only when this rank restriction and all class-specific scalar conditions also hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A prescribed Gram record is realizable in dimension d exactly when its Gram matrix is positive semidefinite and has rank at most d.
assumptions_latex: \(q<\infty\) and \(d\in\mathbb N\).
\(G\) specifies every required pairwise inner product among the record vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) has a factorization \(G=Z^\top Z\) with \(Z\in\mathbb R^{d\times q}\) if and only if \(G\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\le d\).

notation.meaning: Gram matrix of all vector quantities in the record.

source_refs.source_title: First-Order Methods in Optimization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The PSD-and-rank characterization is mathematically correct and condition fits the leaf, but the cited general dimension section does not specifically support Gram factorization or dimension-restricted PEP realizability.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Class Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint realizability condition for records constrained by multiple function or operator classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For classes \(\mathcal F_1,\ldots,\mathcal F_s\) on a common domain, a finite record \(R=\{(x_i,g_i,v_i)\}_{i\in I}\) is mixed-class compatible when \[\exists f\in\bigcap_{k=1}^{s}\mathcal F_k\quad\text{such that}\quad v_i=f(x_i),\quad g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\quad(i\in I).\] Hence compatibility implies membership in every individual interpolation set. The converse requires a joint interpolation theorem: separate witnesses \(f_k\in\mathcal F_k\) for the same record do not by themselves provide one witness in the intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-class compatibility requires one function satisfying every class restriction and realizing the entire record; separate class-specific witnesses are generally insufficient.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(s\) are finite.
\(\mathcal F_k\) share the same ambient space and oracle semantics.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R\) is mixed-class compatible exactly when \(R\in\mathcal I_{\cap_{k=1}^{s}\mathcal F_k}(I)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record gives a coherent definition of joint realization by one witness and condition fits the leaf. A source is still needed for the mixed-class interpolation framing and the boundary between separate and joint sufficiency.

knowledge_statements.title: Noninterpolable Oracle Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite oracle data violating convex subgradient interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), consider the two oracle triples \[(x_1,g_1,v_1)=(0,1,0),\qquad (x_2,g_2,v_2)=(1,0,0).\] If a convex function \(f\) interpolated them, the subgradient inequality at the first sample would require \(v_2\ge v_1+g_1(x_2-x_1)=1\), contradicting \(v_2=0\). Equivalently, monotonicity would require \((g_1-g_2)(x_1-x_2)\ge0\), whereas the displayed record gives \(-1<0\). Thus even finite, dimension-one oracle data need not be convexly interpolable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two records at 0 and 1 with reversed subgradients violate both the subgradient inequality and monotonicity, so no convex interpolant exists.
assumptions_latex: Interpolation means \(v_i=f(x_i)\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for a convex \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No proper convex function interpolates both \((0,1,0)\) and \((1,0,0)\).

notation.meaning: Sample point, proposed subgradient, and proposed function value.

children.title: Function-Value Records
children.top_down_role: Scalar records representing sampled objective or component values.

knowledge_statements.title: Function-Value Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar variables representing sampled objective values in a finite-dimensional PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite index set \(I\), sample points \(x_i\), and an objective \(f:\mathcal H\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the function-value record is the scalar vector \[v=(v_i)_{i\in I},\qquad v_i=f(x_i).\] In a finite-dimensional performance-estimation formulation, the entries \(v_i\) are scalar decision variables. They are coupled to the Gram representation through interpolation inequalities, algorithmic relations, initial conditions, and the performance criterion, rather than through additional Gram rows or columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Function-value records are scalar variables equal to objective values at sampled points and coupled to the Gram matrix through PEP constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite.
\(x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f\) for every recorded finite value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v\in\mathbb R^{|I|}\) records exactly the sampled values \(f(x_i)\).

notation.meaning: Function value at sample point x_i.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition fits Function-Value Records and the sampled-value vector is correctly specified. The PEP-specific claims about decision variables and coupling without Gram rows or columns require a scalar-Gram formulation source.

children.title: Auxiliary Scalar Records
children.top_down_role: Scalar variables representing parameters, residual magnitudes, bounds, or certificate quantities.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary Scalar Records
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-value scalar variables used to encode PEP constraints and objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite performance-estimation problem with Gram variable \(G\) and function-value vector \(v\), an auxiliary scalar record is a finite vector \(s\in\mathbb R^r\) whose entries are neither sampled function values nor inner products represented directly in \(G\). Its entries may encode epigraph bounds, residual bounds, radii, or scalarized performance measures. Admissibility is specified by explicit constraints \[\Phi_\ell(G,v,s)\le0\quad(\ell=1,\ldots,L),\qquad \Psi_j(G,v,s)=0\quad(j=1,\ldots,J).\] In scalar-Gram PEP formulations whose scalar couplings are affine, the forms \(\Phi_\ell\) and \(\Psi_j\) are affine in their represented scalar arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Auxiliary scalar records hold non-value scalar quantities, such as bounds or radii, and connect to Gram and value variables through explicit constraints; in affine scalar-Gram formulations, those coupling constraints are affine.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) and \(v\) already encode vector inner products and sampled function values.
\(r,L,J<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s\) is valid exactly when all stated coupling constraints \(\Phi_\ell(G,v,s)\le0\) and \(\Psi_j(G,v,s)=0\) hold.

children.title: Scalar Record Couplings
children.top_down_role: Structural dependencies linking function values with other scalar records.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalar Record Couplings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine coupling of scalar PEP records to entries of a common Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s\in\mathbb R^p\) collect function values and auxiliary scalar records, and let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) be the Gram matrix of the point and oracle vectors. A scalar-record coupling is a finite system
\[a_k^{\mathsf T}s+\langle A_k,G\rangle\le b_k,\qquad k=1,\ldots,q,\]
together with optional affine equalities of the same form. Consequently, interpolation conditions, algorithmic scalar identities, initial bounds, and the performance criterion can be represented without introducing additional ambient-space vectors whenever each relevant squared norm or inner product is an entry or affine combination of entries of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scalar records couple to geometry through affine constraints involving scalar variables and Gram-matrix entries, thereby encoding interpolation, algorithmic identities, initial conditions, and performance measures.
assumptions_latex: \(s\in\mathbb R^p\) contains all scalar records used by the finite PEP.
\(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) contains the inner products of all represented vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k^{\mathsf T}s+\langle A_k,G\rangle\le b_k\) gives an affine scalar–Gram coupling for every indexed constraint \(k\).
review_flags: PEP-specific scalar–Gram formulation requires a direct performance-estimation source
standard_field_rationale: finite-dimensional quadratic records become affine functions of Gram entries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation is mathematically coherent and fits the Scalar Record Couplings container, but it makes PEP-specific claims about interpolation, algorithmic identities, initialization bounds, and performance criteria without an inspectable source. A direct performance-estimation reference with a section, theorem, or page locator is required.

children.title: Point Gram Models
children.top_down_role: Gram representations built from sampled points or iterates.

knowledge_statements.title: Point Gram Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram representation of finitely many iterates relative to a reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_\star,x_1,\ldots,x_n\) lie in a real Hilbert space and set \(u_i=x_i-x_\star\). The point Gram model is
\[P_{ij}=\langle u_i,u_j\rangle,\qquad 1\le i,j\le n.\]
Then \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\), and every squared point distance is affine in its entries:
\[\|x_i-x_j\|^2=P_{ii}+P_{jj}-2P_{ij}.\]
Conversely, every \(P\in\mathbb S_+^n\) admits vectors \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\in\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}P}\) satisfying \(P_{ij}=\langle u_i,u_j\rangle\); taking \(x_\star=0\) and \(x_i=u_i\) realizes the corresponding centered points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite matrix records all inner products and pairwise squared distances among iterates centered at a reference point, and every such matrix has a realization whose dimension equals its rank.
assumptions_latex: \(x_\star,x_1,\ldots,x_n\) belong to one real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\succeq0\), and every such \(P\) is realizable in \(\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}P}\).

children.title: Oracle-Vector Gram Models
children.top_down_role: Gram representations built from gradients, subgradients, residuals, or other oracle vectors.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Vector Gram Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram representation of gradients, subgradients, residuals, or other oracle-returned vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) be vectors returned by a first-order or monotone-operator oracle in a common real Hilbert space. Their oracle-vector Gram model is
\[Q_{ij}=\langle g_i,g_j\rangle,\qquad 1\le i,j\le n.\]
Thus \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\), with \(Q_{ii}=\|g_i\|^2\). Conversely, every \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^n\) admits vectors \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\in\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}Q}\) whose mutual inner products equal the entries of \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle vectors are represented by a positive-semidefinite matrix containing all mutual inner products and squared norms, and every such matrix has a realization whose dimension equals its rank.
assumptions_latex: \(g_1,\ldots,g_n\) lie in one real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\succeq0\), and every such \(Q\) is realizable by oracle vectors in dimension \(\operatorname{rank}Q\).

notation.meaning: vector returned by the oracle at index i

children.title: Point–Oracle Cross-Gram Structure
children.top_down_role: Cross terms linking point records to oracle-vector records.

knowledge_statements.title: Point–Oracle Cross-Gram Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint Gram constraint linking centered points with oracle-returned vectors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For centered point vectors \(u_i=x_i-x_\star\) and oracle vectors \(g_j\), define \(P_{ik}=\langle u_i,u_k\rangle\), \(Q_{j\ell}=\langle g_j,g_\ell\rangle\), and \(C_{ij}=\langle u_i,g_j\rangle\). Their joint Gram matrix is
\[G=\begin{pmatrix}P&C\\ C^{\mathsf T}&Q\end{pmatrix}\succeq0.\]
Hence the cross block \(C\) cannot generally be chosen independently of \(P\) and \(Q\). Conversely, any positive-semidefinite block matrix of this form has a simultaneous realization by point and oracle vectors in a real Euclidean space of dimension at most \(\operatorname{rank}G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Point–oracle inner products form the off-diagonal block of one positive-semidefinite Gram matrix, coupling point and oracle Gram models through joint realizability.
assumptions_latex: All centered point vectors and oracle vectors lie in one real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\begin{pmatrix}P&C\\C^{\mathsf T}&Q\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) is necessary and sufficient for simultaneous finite-dimensional realization.

children.title: Centered Gram Models
children.top_down_role: Gram representations organized relative to a reference point or origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Centered Gram Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation-invariant Gram coordinates obtained by subtracting a fixed anchor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given points \(z_0,z_1,\ldots,z_n\) in a real Hilbert space, choose \(z_0\) as anchor and define \(v_i=z_i-z_0\). The centered Gram model is
\[G^{\mathrm c}_{ij}=\langle z_i-z_0,z_j-z_0\rangle,\qquad 1\le i,j\le n.\]
It satisfies \(G^{\mathrm c}\succeq0\) and is invariant under the common translation \(z_i\mapsto z_i+a\). Moreover, all pairwise squared distances are recovered through \(\|z_i-z_j\|^2=G^{\mathrm c}_{ii}+G^{\mathrm c}_{jj}-2G^{\mathrm c}_{ij}\), using the convention that the centered vector for index \(0\) is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting a fixed anchor yields a positive-semidefinite, translation-invariant Gram matrix from which every pairwise squared distance can be recovered.
assumptions_latex: \(z_0,z_1,\ldots,z_n\) lie in one real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G^{\mathrm c}\succeq0\), is translation invariant, and determines every \(\|z_i-z_j\|^2\).

children.title: Difference Gram Models
children.top_down_role: Gram representations organized around pairwise or sequential differences.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference Gram Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram coordinates for selected differences of an underlying vector family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) lie in a real Hilbert space, let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^n\) be their Gram matrix, and let \(B=[b_1,\ldots,b_r]\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\). Define selected linear combinations, including differences when the columns of \(B\) are incidence vectors, by
\[d_\ell=\sum_{i=1}^n B_{i\ell}v_i,\qquad \ell=1,\ldots,r.\]
Their difference Gram matrix satisfies
\[G^\Delta_{k\ell}=\langle d_k,d_\ell\rangle,\qquad G^\Delta=B^{\mathsf T}GB\succeq0.\]
Thus inner products and squared norms of the selected steps or displacements are obtained by a positive-semidefinite congruence transformation of the base Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selected vector differences or linear combinations have Gram matrix B-transpose G B, preserving positive semidefiniteness and encoding inner products between steps or displacements.
assumptions_latex: \(v_1,\ldots,v_n\) lie in one real Hilbert space.
\(B\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G^{\Delta}=B^{\mathsf T}GB\succeq0\), with entries equal to inner products among the selected differences or linear combinations.

notation.meaning: Gram matrix of the base vectors
coefficient or incidence matrix defining the selected combinations

children.title: Block Gram Models
children.top_down_role: Partitioned Gram representations for multiple variable or oracle groups.

knowledge_statements.title: Block Gram Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A joint Gram matrix partitioned according to vector type or problem component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Partition a finite vector family as \(V=(V^{(1)},\ldots,V^{(r)})\), where every block lies in the same real Hilbert space. Its block Gram model is
\[G=V^{\mathsf T}V=\bigl[G_{ab}\bigr]_{a,b=1}^r,\qquad G_{ab}=(V^{(a)})^{\mathsf T}V^{(b)}.\]
Then \(G\succeq0\), each diagonal block \(G_{aa}\) is the Gram matrix of one vector type, and each off-diagonal block records cross-inner-products. Conversely, any positive-semidefinite block matrix with compatible block sizes has a joint Euclidean realization, so its diagonal and cross blocks are jointly consistent rather than independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A block Gram matrix jointly represents several vector families; diagonal blocks store within-family products and off-diagonal blocks store cross-products under one PSD constraint.
assumptions_latex: All vector blocks \(V^{(a)}\) lie in a common real Hilbert space.
The block sizes are mutually compatible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=[G_{ab}]_{a,b=1}^r\succeq0\) is exactly the joint Gram representation of the partitioned vector family.

notation.meaning: matrix whose columns form vector block a
cross-Gram block between vector blocks a and b

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Worst-Case Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical finite-dimensional semidefinite formulation of a deterministic worst-case performance problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s\in\mathbb R^p\) collect scalar records and \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) collect all vector inner products. A primal worst-case PEP model has the form
\[\sup_{s,G}\ \bigl(c^{\mathsf T}s+\langle C,G\rangle\bigr)\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_k^{\mathsf T}s+\langle A_k,G\rangle\le b_k\ \ (k=1,\ldots,q),\quad G\succeq0.\]
The affine constraints encode exact class interpolation conditions, algorithmic relations, and initialization restrictions. When these constraints are necessary and sufficient for interpolation and all algorithmic vectors are included in \(G\), the optimum equals the worst attainable value of the chosen performance measure over the modeled method and problem class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal PEP maximizes a linear performance measure over scalar records and a PSD Gram matrix constrained by interpolation, algorithm, and initialization relations.
assumptions_latex: The modeled interpolation conditions are necessary and sufficient for the selected function or operator class.
All scalar and vector quantities used by the finite method are represented in \(s\) and \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed semidefinite program has optimal value equal to the modeled finite-horizon worst-case performance.
review_flags: A direct source for exact finite-dimensional PEP reduction and interpolation sufficiency is required

children.title: Dual Bound Models
children.top_down_role: Dual semidefinite formulations used to organize worst-case upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Bound Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conic dual model producing an upper bound on a primal worst-case PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the primal model
\[\sup_{s,\,G\succeq0}\ c^{\mathsf T}s+\langle C,G\rangle\quad\text{subject to}\quad a_k^{\mathsf T}s+\langle A_k,G\rangle\le b_k,\]
with free \(s\), its Lagrange dual bound model is
\[\inf_{y\ge0}\ \sum_{k=1}^q b_k y_k\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{k=1}^q y_k a_k=c,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^q y_kA_k-C\succeq0.\]
Every dual-feasible multiplier vector \(y\) therefore supplies a valid upper bound on the primal worst-case value. Equality of primal and dual optimal values additionally requires an applicable conic strong-duality qualification.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative multipliers satisfying scalar balance and a PSD matrix inequality yield an upper bound; under conic strong duality, the best bound equals the primal value.
assumptions_latex: The primal scalar variable \(s\) is unrestricted.
The primal affine inequalities and objective have the displayed sign convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every dual-feasible \(y\), \(c^{\mathsf T}s+\langle C,G\rangle\le\sum_k b_ky_k\) holds for every primal-feasible \((s,G)\).

notation.meaning: multipliers for the primal affine inequalities

review_flags: The supplied locators do not directly identify semidefinite conic duality with this sign convention

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed dual and weak-duality conclusion are internally consistent for the stated primal sign convention, and duality is the correct content kind. children.title: Dual Certificate Models
children.top_down_role: Structured dual objects intended for conversion into checkable certificates.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Certificate Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite, directly checkable certificate for a claimed PEP upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a claimed bound \(\tau\), a dual certificate is a pair \((y,S)\) satisfying
\[y_k\ge0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^q y_ka_k=c,\qquad S=\sum_{k=1}^q y_kA_k-C\succeq0,\qquad \sum_{k=1}^q b_ky_k\le\tau.\]
It is verified using scalar arithmetic and a positive-semidefiniteness check. For every primal-feasible \((s,G)\), summing the affine constraints with weights \(y_k\) and using \(\langle S,G\rangle\ge0\) yields \(c^{\mathsf T}s+\langle C,G\rangle\le\tau\). Thus certificate feasibility validates the bound independently of a numerical optimizer's termination report.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative multipliers and a PSD slack matrix certify an upper bound through finite equality, inequality, and positive-semidefiniteness checks.
assumptions_latex: The primal PEP has the affine-inequality form used in the dual bound model.
\(G\succeq0\) for every primal-feasible record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility of \((y,S)\) certifies \(c^{\mathsf T}s+\langle C,G\rangle\le\tau\) for every primal-feasible \((s,G)\).
review_flags: A direct PEP or semidefinite-certificate source is needed for this certificate formulation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite multiplier-and-PSD-slack object is correctly classified as a certificate and is mathematically consistent with the preceding primal-dual convention. children.title: Bound–Certificate Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between dual objective bounds and certificate content.

knowledge_statements.title: Bound–Certificate Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between valid SDP dual certificates and optimal worst-case bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(p_\star\) and \(d_\star\) be the optimal values of a primal PEP semidefinite program and its dual bound model. Weak duality gives
\[p_\star\le d_\star,\]
and every dual-feasible point with objective at most \(\tau\) is a certificate of the valid bound \(p_\star\le\tau\). If the primal or dual satisfies a conic constraint qualification ensuring strong duality and the dual optimum is attained, then \(p_\star=d_\star\) and an optimal dual solution certifies the sharp bound. Without attainment, bounds arbitrarily close to \(d_\star\) may exist although no certificate realizes the exact value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every feasible dual point certifies a bound; under strong duality and dual attainment, an optimal certificate realizes the exact primal worst-case value.
assumptions_latex: The primal and dual PEPs form a valid conic dual pair.
For exact correspondence, strong duality holds and the dual optimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Dual feasibility implies \(p_\star\le\tau\); under the additional qualification and attainment assumptions, an optimal certificate has value \(\tau=p_\star=d_\star\).

notation.meaning: value of a feasible dual certificate

review_flags: A precise semidefinite strong-duality and attainment source is required

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly separates weak duality, strong duality, and dual attainment, and duality is the appropriate knowledge kind. A precise conic or semidefinite duality source with a theorem or section locator is required for the exact bound–certificate correspondence and nonattainment statement.

children.title: Multiple-Component PEP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple-Component PEP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite PEP representation for objectives or operators assembled from several components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a model with components indexed by \(r=1,\ldots,R\). For each component \(r\), let \(s^{(r)}\) collect its scalar records and let \(g_i^{(r)}\) denote its oracle vector at the shared evaluation point \(x_i\). Form one Gram matrix \(G\succeq0\) containing all represented iterate differences and all vectors \(g_i^{(r)}\). Impose the interpolation constraints for each component separately, together with the affine identities that couple the component records through the shared iterates and the modeled algorithm. If every component class has a necessary-and-sufficient finite interpolation description affine in the scalar records and entries of \(G\), then the combined constraints and \(G\succeq0\) form a finite semidefinite representation of the coupled worst-case problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiple-component PEP retains separate records and interpolation constraints for each component while coupling them through shared iterates, algorithmic identities, and one joint Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: Each component class has a finite interpolation description affine in scalar records and Gram entries.
All component oracle vectors and shared iterate differences are included in one joint Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The componentwise interpolation systems, coupling identities, and \(G\succeq0\) form a finite semidefinite model of the coupled worst-case problem.

children.title: Operator PEP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Operator PEP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite sampled-transcript representation for deterministic operator-based performance estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:\mathcal H\rightrightarrows\mathcal H\) belong to an operator class \(\mathfrak T\). An operator PEP introduces samples \((x_i,y_i)_{i\in I}\) satisfying \(y_i\in T(x_i)\), linear relations encoding the algorithm, and a Gram matrix \(G\succeq0\) for all sampled vectors. If \(\mathcal I_{\mathfrak T}\) is a necessary-and-sufficient finite interpolation system for \(\mathfrak T\), the worst-case value of a criterion \(\Phi\) is represented by \[\sup\{\Phi(G):G\succeq0,\ \mathcal I_{\mathfrak T}(G),\ \mathcal A(G),\ \mathcal N(G)\}.\] Here \(\mathcal A\) and \(\mathcal N\) encode the algorithm and normalization constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator PEP maximizes a performance criterion over a positive semidefinite Gram matrix constrained by operator interpolation, algorithmic relations, and normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal H\) is a real Hilbert space and \(I\) is finite.
\(\mathcal I_{\mathfrak T}\) characterizes finite interpolation by operators in \(\mathfrak T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP})=\sup\{\Phi(G):G\succeq0,\mathcal I_{\mathfrak T}(G),\mathcal A(G),\mathcal N(G)\}\), subject to rank compatibility.

children.title: Coupled Component–Operator Models

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Component–Operator Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint Gram formulation coupling component functions and set-valued operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_k\in\mathcal F_k\) for \(k=1,\ldots,q\), let \(T_\ell\in\mathfrak T_\ell\) for \(\ell=1,\ldots,r\), and collect sampled iterates, subgradients, and operator values in one Gram matrix \(G\succeq0\). A coupled component–operator PEP imposes simultaneously the component interpolation constraints \(\mathcal I_{\mathcal F_k}\), operator interpolation constraints \(\mathcal I_{\mathfrak T_\ell}\), and coupling equations \(\mathcal C\) identifying shared iterates and enforcing inclusions or algorithmic updates. Its finite model is \[\sup\{\Phi(G,F):G\succeq0,\ \mathcal I_{\mathcal F_k}(G,F),\ \mathcal I_{\mathfrak T_\ell}(G),\ \mathcal C(G,F),\ \mathcal N(G,F)\}.\]

All sampled vectors lie in a common real Hilbert space.

children.title: Expectation-Level PEP Models
children.top_down_role: Performance models whose criteria or constraints are organized through expectations.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation-Level PEP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-moment PEP for expected performance of randomized first-order methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\), let a randomized method generate a finite transcript \(Z(\omega)\), and let \(M=\mathbb E[Z Z^{\mathsf T}]\succeq0\) denote its second-moment Gram matrix. An expectation-level PEP replaces pathwise quadratic expressions by linear functionals of \(M\), imposes expected interpolation, oracle, algorithm, and normalization constraints \(\mathcal K(M,m)\), and computes \[\sup\{\mathbb E[\Phi(Z)]:M\succeq0,\ \mathcal K(M,m)\},\] where \(m=\mathbb E[Z]\). The model is exact only when its moment constraints characterize realizable transcript laws; otherwise it is an upper relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expected worst-case performance is optimized over first and second transcript moments; the model is exact only when those moments are jointly realizable.
assumptions_latex: The randomized transcript has finite second moments.
The performance criterion is expressible through the retained moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed moment problem bounds the expected worst-case criterion, with equality under moment-law realizability.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the leaf, but generic first and second moments do not automatically encode conditional, pathwise, or interpolation constraints. A source must specify the stochastic PEP construction and the conditions under which the retained moments yield an upper relaxation or an exact model.

children.title: Randomized Oracle Models
children.top_down_role: PEP models for random oracle outputs, samples, coordinates, or method choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Oracle Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional moment conditions for stochastic first-order oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_i\) be the history before oracle call \(i\), let \(x_i\) be \(\mathcal F_i\)-measurable, and let the oracle return \(g_i\). A conditionally unbiased stochastic first-order oracle with variance bound \(\sigma_i^2\) satisfies \[\mathbb E[g_i\mid\mathcal F_i]=s_i,\qquad s_i\in\partial f(x_i),\qquad \mathbb E[\|g_i-s_i\|^2\mid\mathcal F_i]\leq\sigma_i^2\quad\text{a.s.}\] A randomized-oracle PEP encodes these conditional relations, together with interpolation and update constraints, at every call. Other oracle models are obtained by explicitly replacing unbiasedness or the variance inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Before each call, the iterate is history-measurable; the oracle is conditionally unbiased for a valid subgradient and has bounded conditional variance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper and convex on a real Hilbert space.
Each oracle output is conditionally square-integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g_i-s_i\mid\mathcal F_i]=0\) and \(\mathbb E[\|g_i-s_i\|^2\mid\mathcal F_i]\leq\sigma_i^2\) almost surely.

children.title: Distribution-Aware PEP Models

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Aware PEP Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP retaining specified probability-law information beyond generic moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi\sim P\) drive a randomized method and suppose specified distributional information \(\mathcal D(P)\) is part of the problem class. A distribution-aware PEP optimizes \[\sup_{P,\,Z}\ \mathbb E_P[\Phi(Z(\xi))]\] subject to \(\mathcal D(P)\), pathwise interpolation and algorithm constraints, and prescribed dependence between \(\xi\) and the transcript. For finite support \(\{\xi_s\}_{s=1}^S\) with probabilities \(p_s\), this becomes a scenario model with \(p_s\geq0\), \(\sum_s p_s=1\), scenario Gram matrices \(G_s\succeq0\), shared-data coupling constraints, and objective \(\sum_s p_s\Phi_s(G_s)\).

The expected criterion is finite for every feasible law.

children.title: Exactness and Relaxation Status
children.top_down_role: Structural mechanisms governing equivalence between the infinite-dimensional search and its finite representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolation-Based Exactness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exactness criterion for a finite Gram PEP based on necessary-and-sufficient interpolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite transcript template and ambient dimension \(d\). Suppose every constraint used to form the finite PEP is necessary for a realizable transcript, and the interpolation conditions are also sufficient: every feasible scalar table and Gram matrix \(G\succeq0\) with \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d\) is generated by an admissible problem instance and algorithm transcript having the same criterion value. Then the finite PEP and the original worst-case problem have equal optimal values. If sufficiency is absent, the finite model yields only an upper bound; if the rank restriction is dropped, exactness is asserted only in a sufficiently large or unrestricted dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Necessary-and-sufficient interpolation plus transcript realizability and compatible Gram rank makes the finite PEP value equal the original worst-case value.
assumptions_latex: Finite interpolation constraints are necessary and sufficient for the chosen problem class.
Algorithmic constraints preserve exactly the admissible transcript relations.
\(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d\) is enforced or guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_{\mathrm{finite}})=\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_{\mathrm{original}})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property accurately states the intended exactness mechanism and distinguishes fixed-dimensional from unrestricted-dimensional formulations, but equality of optimal values is a nontrivial PEP exactness claim requiring a specific interpolation/realizability theorem or authoritative section.

children.title: Gram-Rank Constraints
children.top_down_role: Rank restrictions attached to finite Gram representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Rank Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank predicate ensuring realization of a PEP Gram matrix in fixed dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) be the vectors represented in a PEP and let \(G\in\mathbb S^m\) satisfy \(G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\). Realizability in \(\mathbb R^d\) is equivalent to \[G\succeq0\qquad\text{and}\qquad \operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d.\] Thus a fixed-dimensional Gram PEP must retain the nonconvex rank constraint. Omitting it enlarges the feasible set to transcripts realizable in some dimension at most \(m\), and therefore generally produces an upper relaxation for the dimension-\(d\) worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gram matrix is realizable by vectors in dimension d exactly when it is positive semidefinite and has rank at most d.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a real symmetric \(m\times m\) matrix.
The represented vectors use the Euclidean inner product.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is a Gram matrix of vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\) if and only if \(G\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d\).

children.title: Ambient-Dimension Requirements
children.top_down_role: Dimension requirements for realizing candidate Gram data.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Requirements
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension threshold for realizing all vectors represented by a feasible Gram point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a finite PEP whose Gram matrix has order \(m\). A particular feasible point \(G\succeq0\) is realizable in an ambient Euclidean space of dimension \(d\) precisely when \(d\geq\operatorname{rank}(G)\). Consequently, if the semidefinite formulation contains no rank constraint, the uniform requirement \(d\geq m\) guarantees realization of every feasible Gram matrix. A smaller sufficient requirement is \(d\geq r_*\), where \(r_*\) is the supremum of feasible Gram ranks; for an optimizer alone, it suffices that some optimal Gram matrix have rank at most \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimension must cover the relevant Gram rank; dimension m realizes every feasible m-by-m Gram matrix, while an optimizer may require less.
assumptions_latex: The PEP represents \(m\) vectors through a real positive semidefinite Gram matrix.
No additional geometric structure restricts their factorization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d\geq\operatorname{rank}(G)\) is necessary and sufficient for realizing \(G\), and \(d\geq m\) is uniformly sufficient.

children.title: Rank–Dimension Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between Gram rank and the available ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Dimension Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility relation between SDP feasibility, Gram rank, and fixed-dimensional PEP exactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal G\subseteq\mathbb S_+^m\) be the feasible Gram set of a finite PEP and let the original problem be posed in dimension \(d\). The Gram formulation is dimension-compatible at a feasible point \(G\) exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d\). It is globally dimension-compatible when this holds for every \(G\in\mathcal G\), and value-compatible when \[\sup_{G\in\mathcal G}\Phi(G)=\sup_{G\in\mathcal G,\,\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d}\Phi(G).\] Global compatibility implies value compatibility, but value compatibility may hold merely because a rank-compatible optimizer or maximizing sequence exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Global compatibility requires every feasible Gram rank to fit the dimension; equality of optimal values needs only a compatible optimizer or maximizing sequence.
assumptions_latex: \(\Phi\) is the finite PEP objective on \(\mathcal G\).
Non-rank constraints exactly describe the intended finite transcripts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global rank compatibility implies value compatibility, while the converse need not hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property correctly distinguishes pointwise, global, and value compatibility, but the PEP-specific value-equivalence claim and its maximizing-sequence qualification have no cited support.

children.title: Attained Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case objects represented by actual feasible optimizers.

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite feasible transcript certifying attainment of a worst-case PEP value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)\) be an original worst-case problem. An attained-extremizer certificate consists of a feasible finite PEP point \((G,F)\), a compatible factorization \(G=P^{\mathsf T}P\) in the prescribed dimension, and interpolating problem objects whose algorithmic transcript equals the columns of \(P\). It certifies attainment when \[\Phi(G,F)=V.\] If \(V\) is independently upper-bounded by a valid dual certificate with the same value, the reconstructed instance and transcript provide a verifiable matching lower bound and hence an attained worst-case extremizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-compatible optimal Gram point, reconstructed interpolating instance, and matching dual upper bound certify an actually attained worst-case value.
assumptions_latex: The finite interpolation system permits reconstruction of admissible problem objects.
The Gram factorization respects the prescribed ambient dimension.
A valid upper certificate establishes the same value \(V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The reconstructed feasible instance attains \(\Phi=V\), so the worst-case supremum is a maximum.

notation.meaning: optimal Gram and scalar interpolation data

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits the terminal container, and the lower-bound reconstruction plus matching upper certificate has the intended role. A source is still required for the interpolation reconstruction and its use as an attained PEP extremizer certificate.

children.title: Limiting Extremizer Sequences
children.top_down_role: Extremal behavior represented only through feasible limiting families.

knowledge_statements.title: Limiting Extremizer Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a maximizing sequence representing a sharp value when no feasible extremizer attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z\) be a nonempty feasible set and let \(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)<+\infty\). A limiting extremizer sequence is a sequence \((z_n)_{n\geq1}\subseteq\mathcal Z\) such that \[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Phi(z_n)=V.\] In a finite PEP, each \(z_n\) may be encoded by realizable interpolation data \((G_n,F_n)\) satisfying the applicable rank, algorithm, and normalization constraints. Such a sequence establishes sharpness of \(V\), but it does not establish attainment unless some \(z\in\mathcal Z\) satisfies \(\Phi(z)=V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A limiting extremizer sequence is a feasible sequence whose performance converges to the supremum; it establishes sharpness but does not by itself establish attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Z\neq\varnothing\).
\(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi(z_n)\to V\), while attainment additionally requires some \(z\in\mathcal Z\) with \(\Phi(z)=V\).

notation.meaning: set of realizable problem instances and transcripts

children.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural settings separating attained worst cases from limiting-only behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of extremizer attainment despite a finite sharp PEP supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal Z\neq\varnothing\) and let \(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)<+\infty\). Nonattainment means that \[\Phi(z)<V\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal Z,\qquad \sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)=V.\] A maximizing sequence \((z_n)\subseteq\mathcal Z\) then satisfies \(\Phi(z_n)\to V\), but no member attains \(V\). Possible boundary mechanisms include failure of compactness of the feasible transcript set, approach to an excluded parameter value, or failure of the admissible or interpolable class to contain a relevant limit. Equality of primal and dual optimal values alone does not assert the existence of an attaining feasible transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sharp supremum is nonattained when every feasible transcript has strictly smaller performance, even though feasible performances approach the supremum. This can arise from noncompactness or exclusion of relevant limits.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Z\neq\varnothing\).
\(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal Z}\Phi(z)<+\infty\).
No \(z\in\mathcal Z\) satisfies \(\Phi(z)=V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case value \(V\) is a supremum but not a maximum on \(\mathcal Z\).

knowledge_statements.title: Relaxation-Only Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes valid upper-bounding PEP relaxations from interpolation-exact finite-dimensional formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the set of Gram-value data realizable by admissible functions and iterates, and let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible set of a tractable relaxation with \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal F\). For a performance functional \(\Phi\), the relaxed value \(U=\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)\) satisfies \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal R}\Phi(z)\leq U\). If no realization theorem establishes equality of the two suprema, or if \(\mathcal F\setminus\mathcal R\) contains a point attaining a strictly larger value, then the formulation is relaxation-only: \(U\) is a valid upper bound but not an exact worst-case characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation-only PEP enlarges the realizable data set and therefore gives an upper bound, without certifying that its optimum is attainable by an admissible problem instance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal F\).
\(\Phi\) is well-defined on \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal R}\Phi(z)\leq\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)\), with exactness requiring an additional realization argument.

notation.meaning: Set of realizable finite PEP data

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:set inclusion immediately yields validity, while exactness requires realizability
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, and set inclusion supports the upper-bound inequality. However, absence of a realization theorem establishes only that exactness is unverified, not that the relaxation is mathematically inexact; strict inequality or a nonrealizable relaxed optimizer with a strictly larger value would establish inexactness. No inspectable PEP-specific source is cited.

children.title: Structured Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions preserving the navigation-level formulation while exploiting repeated or invariant structure.

children.title: Span-Restricted Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions confining iterates or oracle vectors to generated spans.

knowledge_statements.title: Span-Restricted Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite PEP reduction obtained by restricting all sampled vectors to their generated subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given sampled vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\) in a real Hilbert space, set \(S=\operatorname{span}\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\) and choose an orthonormal basis matrix \(Q\) for \(S\). Every sampled vector has coordinates \(a_i\in\mathbb R^r\) such that \(v_i=Qa_i\), where \(r=\dim S\leq m\), and its Gram matrix obeys \(G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=a_i^{\mathsf T}a_j\). Consequently, any finite PEP whose constraints and objective depend only on these inner products and sampled scalar values has an equivalent formulation over \(\mathbb R^r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All sampled PEP vectors may be represented in their own span; inner products and scalar data are preserved, so no larger ambient Hilbert space is needed.
assumptions_latex: The formulation uses finitely many sampled vectors.
Vector dependence occurs only through their inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite formulation admits an equivalent realization in \(\mathbb R^r\), where \(r=\dim S\leq m\).

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis matrix for the span

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:finite Gram data are preserved by orthonormal coordinates on the generated span

children.title: Low-Rank Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions exploiting low-rank Gram or state representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension reduction through a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix of bounded rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) encode all inner products among the vectors of a finite PEP. If \(\operatorname{rank}G=r\), then there exists \(V\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\) with \(G=V^{\mathsf T}V\); the columns of \(V\) realize the same inner products in \(\mathbb R^r\). Conversely, every realization in \(\mathbb R^d\) produces a Gram matrix satisfying \(\operatorname{rank}G\leq d\). Thus imposing \(\operatorname{rank}G\leq r\) is precisely the finite-dimensional realizability restriction for dimension at most \(r\), although it is generally nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-r positive-semidefinite Gram matrix is exactly realizable by vectors in r dimensions; dimension restrictions therefore become nonconvex rank constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\).
All vector information used by the formulation is encoded by \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is realizable in \(\mathbb R^r\) if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}G\leq r\).

notation.meaning: Matrix whose columns realize the sampled vectors

children.title: Span–Rank Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which span restrictions support low-rank representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Span–Rank Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition linking span restriction, Gram rank, and ambient realization dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sampled vectors \(v_1,… ,v_m\) with Gram matrix \(G\), one has \(\operatorname{rank}G=\dim\operatorname{span}\{v_1,… ,v_m\}\). Hence a span-restricted representation in a space of dimension \(r\) is compatible with the Gram formulation exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}G\leq r\). If an optimization model simultaneously prescribes a span of dimension at most \(r\) and permits a feasible matrix with larger rank, that matrix has no compatible realization under the prescribed span restriction. Without an ambient dimension bound, every feasible \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) is realizable in dimension \(\operatorname{rank}G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The dimension of the sampled-vector span equals the Gram rank, so span and rank restrictions must use the same effective dimension bound.
assumptions_latex: \(G_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle\) for \(1\leq i,j\leq m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\operatorname{span}\{v_i\}_{i=1}^m=\operatorname{rank}G\), and dimension-\(r\) realizability is equivalent to \(\operatorname{rank}G\leq r\).

notation.meaning: Gram matrix of the sampled vectors
Prescribed span or ambient dimension bound

children.title: Symmetry Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions based on interchangeable indices, coordinates, components, or trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex reduction by averaging feasible PEP data over a finite or compact symmetry group.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite or compact group \(\Gamma\) act linearly on a convex feasible set \(\mathcal F\), and suppose \(\gamma z\in\mathcal F\) and \(\Phi(\gamma z)=\Phi(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathcal F\) and \(\gamma\in\Gamma\). With normalized Haar measure \(\mu\), define \(\bar z=\int_\Gamma \gamma z\,d\mu(\gamma)\). Then \(\bar z\in\mathcal F\), \(\gamma\bar z=\bar z\) for all \(\gamma\in\Gamma\), and, when \(\Phi\) is linear, \(\Phi(\bar z)=\Phi(z)\). Therefore optimizing \(\Phi\) over \(\mathcal F\) is equivalent to optimizing it over the fixed-point set \(\mathcal F^\Gamma\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex group-invariant PEP with a linear invariant objective, averaging over the group produces an equally good feasible point fixed by every symmetry.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\) is convex and invariant under a finite or compact group \(\Gamma\).
\(\Phi\) is linear and \(\Gamma\)-invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)=\sup_{z\in\mathcal F^\Gamma}\Phi(z)\).

notation.meaning: Points in the feasible set fixed by the group

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:convex group averaging preserves feasibility and invariant linear objectives
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits symmetry reduction, but the compact-group averaging statement requires conditions ensuring that the action is measurable or continuous, that the integral exists in the data space, and that the averaged point remains feasible; convexity alone is insufficient without an appropriate finite-dimensional or closedness framework. No source is cited to settle these hypotheses or the PEP application.

children.title: Invariance Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions based on transformations that preserve the performance problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Invariance Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restriction to invariant coordinates or fixed subspaces when the complete PEP data model is equivariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be a linear idempotent map on a finite-dimensional data space, with \(T(\mathcal F)\subseteq\mathcal F\), and let the objective satisfy \(\Phi(Tz)=\Phi(z)\) for every \(z\in\mathcal F\). Then each feasible point can be replaced without loss by the invariant point \(Tz\in\operatorname{Fix}(T)\). Consequently, \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)=\sup_{z\in\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(T)}\Phi(z)\). The reduction is valid only when initialization, interpolation constraints, algorithmic recurrences, performance criterion, and any dimension restrictions are all preserved by \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An idempotent transformation permits restriction to its fixed subspace only when it preserves every constraint and leaves the performance value unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(T^2=T\) and \(T(\mathcal F)\subseteq\mathcal F\).
\(\Phi\circ T=\Phi\) on \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimization over \(\mathcal F\) is equivalent to optimization over \(\mathcal F\cap\operatorname{Fix}(T)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:an objective-preserving feasible retraction yields an exact fixed-point reduction
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle kind fits the leaf. Given an objective-preserving feasible idempotent map, the fixed-point restriction follows as stated, but no inspectable source supports either the abstract reduction or its asserted PEP-specific preservation requirements.

children.title: Orbit-Quotient Representations
children.top_down_role: Reduced representations formed by grouping equivalent configurations.

knowledge_statements.title: Orbit-Quotient Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation of invariant PEP data and objectives on the orbit space of a symmetry action.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a group \(\Gamma\) act on a feasible set \(\mathcal F\), and write \(\pi:\mathcal F\to\mathcal F/\Gamma\) for the orbit map. If every feasibility predicate and the objective \(\Phi\) are constant on each orbit, then there exist well-defined quotient predicates and a function \(\widehat\Phi\) satisfying \(\Phi=\widehat\Phi\circ\pi\). The original problem therefore has the representation \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)=\sup_{[z]\in\mathcal F/\Gamma}\widehat\Phi([z])\). A coordinate model of the quotient is exact only if its chosen invariants separate all feasible orbits relevant to the constraints and objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When constraints and performance are constant along symmetry orbits, the PEP can be written over orbit classes; invariant coordinates must distinguish all relevant feasible orbits.
assumptions_latex: \(\Gamma\) acts on \(\mathcal F\).
Feasibility data and \(\Phi\) are constant on \(\Gamma\)-orbits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)=\sup_{[z]\in\mathcal F/\Gamma}\widehat\Phi([z])\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:orbit-constant functions factor uniquely through the orbit projection
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind is appropriate, and an orbit-constant objective factors through the orbit map. The stronger assertion about exact coordinate models and orbit-separating invariants needs a precise source and hypotheses; none is provided.

children.title: Stationary Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions exploiting iteration-independent extremal or certificate structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary ansatz for PEP variables indexed by time within a homogeneous interior regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For time-indexed PEP data \(z_0,\ldots,z_N\), a stationary reduction is admissible on an index set \(I\subseteq\{0,… ,N\}\) when there exists a shift operator \(S\) such that \(z_{k+1}=Sz_k\) whenever \(k,k+1\in I\), every interior constraint is preserved by \(S\), and the objective depends on the retained data through shift-invariant quantities or specified endpoints. For Gram data, stationarity may be imposed as \(G_{i+1,j+1}=G_{ij}\) for all admissible interior pairs. These equalities reduce variables but are exact only if an optimizer satisfying them exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary reduction identifies time-shifted interior data through one shift rule; it is lossless only when the original PEP possesses a stationary optimizer.
assumptions_latex: The interior algorithmic and interpolation constraints are unchanged by an index shift.
Endpoint-dependent data are retained separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Interior variables may satisfy \(z_{k+1}=Sz_k\), and Gram entries may satisfy \(G_{i+1,j+1}=G_{ij}\), subject to optimizer existence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is plausible for this leaf, but the proposed stationary ansatz and Toeplitz-like Gram equalities are context dependent and are not consequences of time-homogeneous constraints alone. A source is required to define the intended PEP regime and justify when the restriction is lossless.

children.title: Time-Homogeneous Reductions
children.top_down_role: Reductions exploiting repeated transition structure across time.

knowledge_statements.title: Time-Homogeneous Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Repeated-step representation for algorithms and PEP constraints with iteration-independent local rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose an iterative method has state \(s_k\) and an iteration-independent update relation \(s_{k+1}=F(s_k,u_k)\), while each oracle pair \((s_k,u_k)\) obeys the same local admissibility predicate \(C(s_k,u_k)\). A time-homogeneous PEP represents every interior step by repeated copies of \(F\) and \(C\), using shared method parameters rather than iteration-specific coefficients. This representation preserves the original finite-horizon problem when those parameters are genuinely constant and all initial, terminal, and cross-time interpolation constraints are retained; time homogeneity alone does not identify the values of different iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A time-homogeneous PEP reuses one update rule, one local constraint template, and shared parameters at every interior iteration while retaining boundary and cross-time constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(F\), \(C\), and the method parameters are independent of \(k\).
Initial, terminal, and cross-time constraints are represented separately.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each interior step is represented by the same relations \(s_{k+1}=F(s_k,u_k)\) and \(C(s_k,u_k)\).

notation.meaning: Oracle output or auxiliary input at time k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:iteration-independent recurrences admit a shared-template finite-horizon representation
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Finite-Horizon Boundary Effects
children.top_down_role: Initial or terminal effects that limit homogeneous reductions.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Boundary Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explains why stationary interior reductions need not extend to initialization or terminal performance constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a horizon \(k=0,… ,N\) with time-homogeneous interior constraints \(C_k=C\). Initialization restricts \(z_0\) through a set \(B_0\), while the performance criterion or stopping condition restricts \(z_N\) through \(B_N\). Unless \(B_0\), \(B_N\), and the objective are invariant under the same time shift as the interior constraints, the complete finite-horizon feasible set is not shift-invariant. Therefore equalities such as \(z_{k+1}=Sz_k\) or \(G_{i+1,j+1}=G_{ij}\) may be imposed only on compatible interior indices; extending them across the boundaries can change the optimum or make the model infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Initialization and terminal performance break time-shift symmetry, so stationary equalities valid in the interior may be invalid at either end of a finite horizon.
assumptions_latex: Interior constraints are time homogeneous.
Initialization or terminal data are not shift invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The full finite-horizon PEP need not be stationary even when every interior step is time homogeneous.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:noninvariant boundary constraints destroy global shift invariance
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is appropriate, and noninvariant endpoint restrictions can destroy global shift invariance. A PEP-specific source or example with a precise locator is required to support the scope and the claim that extending the equalities can alter the optimum or feasibility.

children.title: Beyond Basic Semidefinite PEP
children.top_down_role: Adjacent conic and polynomial certificate frameworks whose exactness status may differ from classical interpolation-based PEP.

knowledge_statements.title: Strengthened Semidefinite Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Semidefinite PEP relaxation augmented by additional valid linear or conic constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the basic semidefinite PEP have feasible set \(\mathcal F_0=\{(G,f):G\succeq0,\ A(G,f)=b,\ C(G,f)\leq0\}\), containing every realizable data pair. If additional inequalities \(L_j(G,f)\leq0\) are valid for every realizable pair, the strengthened model uses \(\mathcal F_1=\mathcal F_0\cap\bigcap_j\{L_j\leq0\}\). For a maximization PEP, its bound satisfies \(\sup_{\mathcal R}\Phi\leq\sup_{\mathcal F_1}\Phi\leq\sup_{\mathcal F_0}\Phi\). Strengthening preserves validity, and it is exact only when the remaining feasible data attain precisely the realizable worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding valid semidefinite or linear constraints shrinks the basic PEP relaxation and can improve its upper bound without excluding realizable instances.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal R\subseteq\mathcal F_0\).
Every added inequality \(L_j\leq0\) holds on \(\mathcal R\).
\(\Phi\) is maximized over the feasible data.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{\mathcal R}\Phi\leq\sup_{\mathcal F_1}\Phi\leq\sup_{\mathcal F_0}\Phi\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale:adding constraints valid on the realizable set preserves an upper bound and can only tighten it

knowledge_statements.title: Sum-of-Squares Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial nonnegativity certificate used to bound a polynomially encoded performance-estimation problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a polynomial PEP have feasible set \(K=\{z:g_i(z)\geq0,\ h_j(z)=0\}\) and polynomial performance \(p(z)\). A degree-\(2d\) sum-of-squares upper-bound certificate for \(p^*\leq\gamma\) is an identity \(\gamma-p(z)=\sigma_0(z)+\sum_i\sigma_i(z)g_i(z)+\sum_j q_j(z)h_j(z)\), where each \(\sigma_i\) is a sum-of-squares polynomial and every product respects the degree limit \(2d\). Evaluating the identity on \(K\) gives \(p(z)\leq\gamma\). Representing \(\sigma_i\) by positive-semidefinite Gram matrices converts the search for such a certificate into a semidefinite program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS identity expresses the performance gap as nonnegative constraint multiples plus equality multiples, yielding a verifiable upper bound and an SDP search problem.
assumptions_latex: The PEP objective and constraints are polynomial in \(z\).
Each \(\sigma_i\) is sum of squares.
All terms satisfy the selected degree bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed identity certifies \(p^*=\sup_{z\in K}p(z)\leq\gamma\).

children.title: Integral Quadratic Constraint Models
children.top_down_role: Performance models organized through integral quadratic constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Quadratic Constraint Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon hard IQCs for a causal oracle in feedback with a first-order method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta:\ell_2^m\to\ell_2^p\) be causal, let \(u=\Delta(y)\), and let a stable linear filter \(\Psi\), initialized at zero, produce \(z_k=\Psi[y;u]_k\in\mathbb R^r\). Given \(M=M^\top\in\mathbb S^r\), the pair \((\Psi,M)\) defines a hard integral quadratic constraint for \(\Delta\) when, for every input sequence and every finite \(N\geq0\), \[\sum_{k=0}^{N} z_k^\top Mz_k\geq0.\] A finite IQC model is a collection \(\{(\Psi_i,M_i)\}_{i=1}^q\); nonnegative multipliers \(\lambda_i\) preserve validity through \(M_i\mapsto\lambda_iM_i\) and summation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hard IQC requires every finite sum of a filtered input-output quadratic form to be nonnegative; nonnegative combinations of valid IQCs remain valid.
assumptions_latex: \(\Delta\) is causal and the trajectories under consideration make every filtered finite-horizon sum well defined.
Each filter \(\Psi_i\) starts from its prescribed zero state.
Each multiplier satisfies \(\lambda_i\geq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^q\lambda_i\sum_{k=0}^{N}z_{i,k}^\top M_i z_{i,k}\geq0\) for every \(N\geq0\).

notation.meaning: Causal oracle or nonlinearity being modeled
Linear filter defining the ith IQC signal

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Integral Quadratic Constraint Models leaf and the content kind is appropriate, but no inspectable source is cited.
