knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Affine Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremizing feasible instances whose objective is a finite convex piecewise-affine function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a performance-estimation problem with feasible instance class \(\mathcal F\), performance functional \(P\), and worst-case value \(W=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}P(I)\). A piecewise-affine extremizer is an instance \(I_*\in\mathcal F\) attaining \(P(I_*)=W\) whose objective has the form \[f_*(x)=\max_{1\le k\le m}\{a_k^Tx+b_k\}\] on its finite-dimensional ambient space, for some \(m<\infty\). If the supremum is not attained, a sequence of such instances is an asymptotically piecewise-affine extremizing family when its performance values converge to \(W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-affine extremizer attains the worst-case performance using an objective that is the maximum of finitely many affine functions.
assumptions_latex: The performance-estimation problem and feasible class \(\mathcal F\) are fixed.
The objective convention is proper finite convex piecewise-affine on the relevant domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(I_*)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}P(I)\) with \(f_*\) piecewise affine.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits this extremal-object leaf and distinguishes attained from asymptotic extremizers, but no PEP source establishes the intended finite-dimensional, convex piecewise-affine convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Quadratic Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extremizing feasible instances represented by finitely many quadratic pieces under a fixed gluing convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a performance-estimation problem with feasible class \(\mathcal F\), functional \(P\), and value \(W=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}P(I)\). A convex piecewise-quadratic extremizer is an instance \(I_*\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \(P(I_*)=W\) whose objective admits a finite representation \[f_*(x)=\max_{1\le k\le m}\left\{\tfrac12x^TQ_kx+a_k^Tx+b_k\right\},\qquad Q_k\succeq0.\] More generally, a partition-based definition may be used only when the quadratic pieces agree continuously on shared boundaries and the resulting function belongs to the prescribed function class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-quadratic extremizer attains the worst case with an objective assembled from finitely many convex quadratic pieces.
assumptions_latex: The performance-estimation problem and function class are fixed.
The displayed maximum representation is compatible with all required smoothness or strong-convexity conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(I_*)=W\) and \(f_*\) is convex piecewise quadratic.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf, but piecewise-quadratic conventions are not unique, and no source establishes that the maximum-of-convex-quadratics convention is the intended PEP extremizer family.

children.title: Quadratic Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case instances represented by quadratic objectives or quadratic local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Quadratic Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case instances attained within the subclass of convex quadratic objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a performance-estimation problem with feasible instance class \(\mathcal F\), performance functional \(P\), and value \(W=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}P(I)\). A quadratic extremizer is an instance \(I_*\in\mathcal F\) attaining \(P(I_*)=W\) whose objective is \[f_*(x)=\tfrac12x^TQx+q^Tx+r,\qquad Q\succeq0.\] If the prescribed class is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth, the spectral conditions are \(\mu I\preceq Q\preceq LI\). The definition is relative to the fixed algorithm, initialization constraints, horizon, and performance criterion encoded by \(\mathcal F\) and \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic extremizer is a feasible convex quadratic instance that attains the worst-case value for the fixed algorithm and performance criterion.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm, horizon, initialization constraints, and performance criterion are fixed.
The quadratic objective satisfies the spectral restrictions of the prescribed function class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(I_*)=\sup_{I\in\mathcal F}P(I)\) with a quadratic objective.

notation.meaning: Symmetric Hessian of the quadratic objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and spectral restrictions are mathematically appropriate, but no source identifies the algorithmic regime in which a quadratic instance attains the full worst-case value.

children.title: Spectral Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case instances organized through eigenvalues, modes, or spectral distributions.

knowledge_statements.title: Spectral Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional quadratic extremizers described through the spectral data of their Hessians.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a first-order method, a horizon \(N\), an admissible spectral interval \([\mu,L]\), and a performance functional \(\mathcal P_N\). A spectral extremizer is a quadratic instance \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle-\langle b,x\rangle+c\), together with an admissible initial point, such that \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\), \(\sigma(Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]\), and the generated trajectory attains the quadratic worst-case value:
\[
\mathcal P_N(f,x_0)=\sup_{\widetilde Q=\widetilde Q^{\mathsf T},\,\sigma(\widetilde Q)\subseteq[\mu,L]}\mathcal P_N(f_{\widetilde Q},\widetilde x_0),
\]
where the supremum includes all initial data satisfying the prescribed normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spectral extremizer is an admissible quadratic whose Hessian spectrum and initial data make the method attain its quadratic worst-case performance.
assumptions_latex: \(N\in\mathbb N\) is fixed and the method is well defined through iteration \(N\).
\(0\leq\mu\leq L<\infty\).
The admissible initial data obey a fixed normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_N(f,x_0)\) equals the worst-case value over the prescribed quadratic spectral class.

notation.meaning: symmetric Hessian of the quadratic instance

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses performance-estimation spectral extremizers.
Exact extremizer convention may depend on the method, normalization, and performance criterion.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition fits the Spectral Extremizers leaf, but no cited source supports this performance-estimation convention. The displayed supremum varies the Hessian and initial point without explicitly varying or fixing the quadratic linear and constant terms, and the notation f_{\widetilde Q} and \widetilde x_0 is not fully defined. A method-, normalization-, and criterion-specific source is required to determine the intended admissible class.

children.title: Eigenmode-Concentration Regimes
children.top_down_role: Extremal regimes dominated by selected spectral modes.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenmode-Concentration Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concentration of a quadratic worst-case trajectory on a small set of Hessian eigenspaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q=Q^{\mathsf T}\) have spectral projectors \(P_\lambda\), and let \(e_0=x_0-x_\star\). Its initial-error spectral measure is
\[
\nu_{e_0}=\sum_{\lambda\in\sigma(Q)}\lVert P_\lambda e_0\rVert^2\delta_\lambda.
\]
An eigenmode-concentration regime of order \(r\) holds when there is a set \(S\subseteq\sigma(Q)\) with \(|S|\leq r\) such that \(P_\lambda e_0=0\) for every \(\lambda\notin S\). Equivalently, \(\operatorname{supp}(\nu_{e_0})\subseteq S\). For any fixed-step linear first-order recurrence on the quadratic, every error vector then remains in \(\bigoplus_{\lambda\in S}\operatorname{range}(P_\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The regime holds when the initial error occupies at most r Hessian eigenspaces; a fixed-step linear quadratic trajectory remains confined to those modes.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\) is a finite-dimensional real symmetric matrix.
The quadratic method induces a linear recurrence whose coefficients commute with \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k\in\bigoplus_{\lambda\in S}\operatorname{range}(P_\lambda)\) for every generated index \(k\).

notation.meaning: orthogonal projector onto the lambda-eigenspace of Q
spectral measure induced by the initial error

review_flags: No supplied locator supports the performance-estimation interpretation of eigenmode concentration.
The recurrence class must be specialized for method-specific use.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition and invariant-subspace conclusion are mathematically plausible for finite-dimensional symmetric quadratics when every recurrence operator preserves Q-eigenspaces. No citation supports the performance-estimation interpretation, however, and the phrase fixed-step linear first-order recurrence is broader than the stated commuting-coefficient hypothesis makes precise. A source is needed to identify the intended recurrence class.

children.title: Composite Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case instances with decomposed objective or oracle structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case instances for methods applied to a smooth-plus-proximable composite objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix classes \(\mathcal F\) and \(\mathcal H\), a method \(M
earrow\) applicable to objectives \(F=f+h\), a horizon \(N\), and a normalized admissible-instance set \(\mathcal I\). A composite extremizer is an instance \((f,h,x_0)\in\mathcal I\), with \(f\in\mathcal F\) and \(h\in\mathcal H\), for which the trajectory generated by \(M\) is well defined and
\[
\mathcal P_N(f+h,x_0)=\sup_{(\widetilde f,\widetilde h,\widetilde x_0)\in\mathcal I}\mathcal P_N(\widetilde f+\widetilde h,\widetilde x_0).
\]
The instance includes compatible gradient-oracle data for \(f\) and subgradient or proximal-oracle data for \(h\) at every sampled point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composite extremizer is a normalized smooth-plus-proximable instance whose method trajectory attains the prescribed worst-case performance.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) specifies the function classes, initialization normalization, and oracle compatibility.
The supremum is attained by at least one admissible instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f,h,x_0)\) attains the worst-case value of \(\mathcal P_N\) over \(\mathcal I\).
review_flags: No supplied locator defines composite extremizers in a performance-estimation framework.
Attainment and oracle conventions require a class-specific source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is appropriate for the Composite Extremizers leaf, but no source supports the proposed extremizer and oracle conventions. The expression \(M\nearrow\) is unexplained and appears erroneous, while the admissible smooth, proximable, interpolation, and attainment requirements are delegated almost entirely to \(\mathcal I\). A class-specific PEP source is required.

children.title: Operator Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case instances represented through extremal operators or inclusions.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case monotone-operator instances for splitting or fixed-point methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathfrak A\) be an admissible class of operator tuples \(A=(A_1,\ldots,A_m)\) on a real Hilbert space, and let \(M\) be an operator method run for \(N\) oracle calls. Given normalized initial data and a performance functional \(\mathcal R_N\), an operator extremizer is an admissible tuple and initial state for which all queried graph pairs satisfy \((x_i,u_i)\in\operatorname{gra}(A_j)\) for the queried operator and
\[
\mathcal R_N(A,x_0)=\sup_{(\widetilde A,\widetilde x_0)\in\mathfrak I}\mathcal R_N(\widetilde A,\widetilde x_0),
\]
where \(\mathfrak I\) incorporates the operator-class constraints and normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An operator extremizer is an admissible operator tuple and initial state that attain the worst-case residual of a specified operator method.
assumptions_latex: Each \(A_j\) has the monotonicity, maximality, or regularity required by the chosen class.
The method's resolvent or graph-oracle calls are well defined.
The displayed supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A,x_0)\) attains the worst-case value of \(\mathcal R_N\) over \(\mathfrak I\).

notation.meaning: operator residual or performance measure after N calls

review_flags: The supplied monotone-operator locators do not support the extremizer definition itself.
Operator class, oracle model, and residual require method-specific sourcing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected definition role fits Operator Extremizers, but the supremum ranges over \(\mathfrak I\) although only \(\mathfrak A\) is introduced as the operator-tuple class and the relationship between them is not defined. The graph-query, resolvent, regularity, normalization, and residual conventions are method dependent and unsupported by a cited locator.

children.title: Set Extremizers
children.top_down_role: Worst-case instances driven by extremal feasible sets, constraints, or projections.

knowledge_statements.title: Set Extremizers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case closed-convex-set instances for projection and feasibility methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathfrak C\) be an admissible family of tuples \(C=(C_1,\ldots,C_m)\) of nonempty closed convex subsets of a real Hilbert space. Fix a projection or feasibility method \(M\), horizon \(N\), normalized instance set \(\mathfrak I\), and performance measure \(\mathcal D_N\). A set extremizer is \((C,x_0)\in\mathfrak I\) whose projections and normal-cone samples are consistent with every method step and which satisfies
\[
\mathcal D_N(C,x_0)=\sup_{(\widetilde C,\widetilde x_0)\in\mathfrak I}\mathcal D_N(\widetilde C,\widetilde x_0).
\]
Thus the geometry of the sets, together with the initial state, realizes the prescribed worst case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set extremizer is an admissible closed-convex-set configuration and initial state that attain a projection or feasibility method's worst case.
assumptions_latex: Every \(C_j\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
All projections invoked by \(M\) are defined.
The worst-case supremum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((C,x_0)\) attains the worst-case value of \(\mathcal D_N\) over \(\mathfrak I\).

notation.meaning: distance, feasibility, or fixed-point performance measure

review_flags: No supplied locator treats set extremizers or their performance-estimation certificates.
The admissible geometry and performance measure are method dependent.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A definition is suitable for the Set Extremizers leaf, but no cited source establishes this PEP notion. The relationship between the introduced family \(\mathfrak C\) and normalized instance set \(\mathfrak I\) is not specified, and the performance measure ranges over materially different distance, feasibility, and fixed-point criteria. Method-specific sourcing is required.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Dimensional Tight Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact worst-case attainment by an instance supported on a line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a method \(M\), horizon \(N\), normalized instance class \(\mathcal I_d\) in each dimension \(d\geq1\), and performance measure \(\mathcal P_N\). A one-dimensional tight instance is an element \(I_1\in\mathcal I_1\) such that
\[
\mathcal P_N(I_1)=\sup_{d\geq1}\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_d}\mathcal P_N(I).
\]
Equivalently, after an isometric embedding into any ambient Hilbert space, every point and oracle vector of the realizing transcript lies in one affine line, while its performance equals the unrestricted worst-case value. Tightness refers to exact equality, not merely approximation of the supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-dimensional tight instance lies on a line and exactly attains the method's worst-case value over all admissible dimensions.
assumptions_latex: The instance classes are invariant under isometric embeddings.
The unrestricted worst-case supremum is finite and attained in dimension one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_1}\mathcal P_N(I)=\sup_{d\geq1}\sup_{I\in\mathcal I_d}\mathcal P_N(I)\).

notation.meaning: normalized admissible instances in dimension d

review_flags: The supplied one-dimensional-optimization locators concern scalar algorithms, not one-dimensional PEP tightness.
A source establishing the dimensional tightness convention is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition matches the dimensional-tightness topic, but the available one-dimensional optimization references do not support exact PEP tightness across all dimensions. The claimed equivalence between membership in \(\mathcal I_1\) and an embedded transcript lying in one affine line also depends on how points, displacements, and oracle vectors are represented. A PEP dimensional-realization source is required.

children.title: Low-Rank Instances
children.top_down_role: Extremal instances admitting low-rank Gram or state representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Low-Rank Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance-estimation instances admitting a low-rank Gram realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,
\ldots,z_m\) be all vector quantities in a finite performance-estimation transcript and let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) be their Gram matrix, \(G_{ij}=\langle z_i,z_j\rangle\). For a prescribed integer \(r\), the transcript is a low-rank instance of order \(r\) when \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq r\). If the transcript is feasible for the interpolation and method constraints and attains the performance-estimation optimum, it is a low-rank extremal instance. Such a transcript has an isometric realization by vectors in \(\mathbb R^r\), possibly in a smaller space when the rank is below \(r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A low-rank instance has a feasible transcript Gram matrix of rank at most r; an extremal one also attains the performance-estimation optimum.
assumptions_latex: The transcript contains finitely many vector variables.
\(G\succeq0\) satisfies all required interpolation and method constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq r\) permits a realization of the transcript in \(\mathbb R^r\).

notation.meaning: sampled iterate, gradient, subgradient, or auxiliary vector
Gram matrix of all transcript vectors

review_flags: Supplied rank-one-update locators are unrelated to Gram-rank performance-estimation instances.
A PEP reconstruction or rank-reduction source is required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and rank-realization statement are standard finite Gram-matrix facts and fit the Low-Rank Instances leaf. Nevertheless, no cited source supports the PEP-specific convention that all relevant transcript vectors are included in this Gram matrix or the use of its rank as the instance dimension. The supplied rank-one-update references are not relevant evidence.

children.title: Span-Limited Instances
children.top_down_role: Extremal instances confined to method-generated spans.

knowledge_statements.title: Span-Limited Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instances whose complete sampled transcript occupies a prescribed finite-dimensional span.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(z_1,
\ldots,z_m\) collect every displacement, oracle output, and auxiliary vector used by a performance-estimation transcript. The instance is span-limited of order \(s\) if there exist vectors \(v_1,
\ldots,v_s\) such that
\[
z_i\in\operatorname{span}\{v_1,
\ldots,v_s\}\qquad(i=1,
\ldots,m).
\]
The definition applies to the entire transcript rather than only to the iterates. Equivalently, the transcript Gram matrix has rank at most \(s\). When the transcript attains the performance-estimation optimum, it is a span-limited extremal instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A span-limited instance has every sampled vector in one subspace of dimension at most s; equivalently, its transcript Gram matrix has rank at most s.
assumptions_latex: The transcript has finitely many vector quantities.

All relevant oracle and method vectors are included among \(z_1,
\ldots,z_m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\dim\operatorname{span}\{z_1,
\ldots,z_m\}\leq s\), equivalently \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\leq s\).

notation.meaning: vector quantities in the full sampled transcript
Gram matrix of the transcript vectors

review_flags: No supplied locator defines span-limited performance-estimation instances.
Whether auxiliary vectors belong to the span convention needs source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement is plausible and the definition role fits the leaf, but no source establishes which displacements, oracle outputs, or auxiliary variables belong to the complete transcript. As written, span-limited order and low Gram rank are mathematically equivalent, making the distinction from the sibling Low-Rank Instances dependent entirely on an unsupported local convention.

children.title: Rank–Span Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility regimes linking low rank to span limitations.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank–Span Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition between a PEP Gram rank bound and prescribed linear-span restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G\in\mathbb S^m\) represent a transcript \((z_1,
\ldots,z_m)\), and encode each required relation \(z_i=\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}z_j\) by its coefficient vector \(c_i=e_i-
\sum_{j<i}a_{ij}e_j\). A rank–span regime with ambient dimension bound \(d\) is feasible exactly when there exists \(G\) satisfying
\[
G\succeq0,
\qquad Gc_i=0\ \text{for every prescribed span relation},
\qquad \operatorname{rank}(G)\leq d,
\]
together with all interpolation, normalization, and method constraints of the performance-estimation problem. The nullspace equations ensure that every Gram realization obeys the prescribed vector relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank–span feasibility requires a positive semidefinite transcript Gram matrix satisfying all constraints, annihilating each span-relation vector, and having rank at most the ambient dimension.
assumptions_latex: All span coefficients \(a_{ij}\) are fixed data.
The remaining PEP constraints are expressible in the Gram and scalar variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A realization in \(\mathbb R^d\) respecting every prescribed span relation exists exactly when the displayed constrained Gram matrix exists.

notation.meaning: coefficient vector encoding a prescribed linear relation

review_flags: No supplied locator establishes the rank–span feasibility characterization for PEP transcripts.
The exact constraint encoding should be checked against the project's Gram convention.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A condition is the correct role for Rank–Span Feasibility Regimes, and \(Gc_i=0\) is the natural Gram encoding of a fixed vector relation. No source validates the project's precise Gram convention, however. The stated existence condition also mentions scalar PEP variables in the assumptions but quantifies only the matrix \(G\), so the exact feasibility formulation requires source-guided clarification.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension-Growing Extremal Instances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case families whose minimal exact realization dimension diverges with the horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each horizon \(N\), let \(\mathcal E_N\) be the set of admissible instances attaining the exact worst-case value, and define
\[
d_N=\inf_{I\in\mathcal E_N}\dim\operatorname{span}(I),
\]
with \(d_N=+\infty\) when \(\mathcal E_N\) is empty. A family of dimension-growing extremal instances is a choice \(I_N\in\mathcal E_N\) whose exact realization dimensions are unbounded and for which \(d_N\to\infty\) along the stated horizon sequence. In a Gram formulation, \(\dim\operatorname{span}(I)\) equals the rank of the complete transcript Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These are exact worst-case families for which the smallest dimension capable of realizing an extremizer grows without bound as the iteration horizon increases.
assumptions_latex: Exact extremizers exist for every horizon in the stated sequence.
The dimension counts the span of the complete sampled transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_N\to\infty\) along the specified sequence of horizons.

notation.meaning: minimum exact realization dimension at horizon N
chosen extremal instance at horizon N

review_flags: No supplied locator addresses horizon-dependent realization dimension of PEP extremizers.
The intended definition may use approximate rather than exact extremizers.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is reasonable for this topic, but no source supports the exact-extremizer convention or divergence of minimal transcript dimension. The phrase along the stated horizon sequence does not actually introduce that sequence, and the definition becomes vacuous when exact extremizers fail to exist. A source is needed to determine whether exact or approximate extremizers and which limiting sequence are intended.

children.title: Gram-Factor Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of vectors or coordinates from feasible Gram data.

knowledge_statements.title: Gram-Factor Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recovery of explicit transcript vectors from a feasible positive semidefinite Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a feasible matrix \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) and an ordered list of transcript labels. Compute \(r=\operatorname{rank}(G)\) and a factorization \(G=V^{\mathsf T}V\) with \(V\in\mathbb R^{r\times m}\), for example from the positive-eigenvalue decomposition. For each label \(i\), output the column \(z_i=Ve_i\in\mathbb R^r\). Then
\[
\langle z_i,z_j\rangle=e_i^{\mathsf T}V^{\mathsf T}Ve_j=G_{ij}
\]
for all \(i,j\). A numerical implementation chooses a rank tolerance and must report it with the factor; exact reconstruction uses the algebraic rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor a feasible positive semidefinite Gram matrix and use the factor's columns as explicit transcript vectors, preserving every encoded inner product.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
The ordering of Gram rows and columns matches the transcript labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
The output vectors satisfy \(\operatorname{Gram}(z_1,
\ldots,z_m)=G\) in dimension \(r=\operatorname{rank}(G)\).

notation.meaning: reconstructed vector assigned to transcript label i

review_flags: The reconstruction is standard linear algebra, but no supplied locator directly supports the PEP Gram-factor interface.
Numerical rank-tolerance conventions require a dedicated source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Algorithm is the correct content kind, and factoring a positive semidefinite Gram matrix into explicit vectors is standard linear algebra. No cited locator supports the PEP label-to-factor reconstruction interface, and the numerical rank-tolerance requirement is not specified sufficiently to define an implementation. A direct Gram-reconstruction or PEP source is required.

children.title: Trajectory Reconstruction
children.top_down_role: Recovery of an extremal iterate and oracle trajectory.

knowledge_statements.title: Trajectory Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assembly of an explicit method trajectory from factored vectors and scalar PEP data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input reconstructed transcript vectors, sampled scalar values, the method coefficients, and the transcript's label map. Select the labeled initial point \(x_0\), oracle vectors, and auxiliary vectors. Recursively compute each method state using its defining update, and at every step compare the computed state with the correspondingly labeled reconstructed vector. Attach each scalar value \(f_i\) to its sample \((x_i,g_i)\). If all update equalities hold and the samples satisfy the selected function or operator interpolation conditions, output the resulting finite trajectory and an interpolating admissible instance; otherwise output inconsistency. The output preserves the objective or residual value encoded by the transcript.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Use factored vectors, scalar samples, and method updates to assemble a trajectory; accept it only when update and interpolation constraints are consistent.
assumptions_latex: The Gram factor and scalar transcript solve the same performance-estimation problem.
A valid interpolation theorem or reconstruction rule is available for the selected instance class.
All transcript labels and method coefficients are supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful reconstruction returns an admissible instance whose sampled method trajectory realizes the certified transcript performance.

notation.meaning: sampled scalar function value at x_i

review_flags: No supplied locator gives a class-specific PEP trajectory-reconstruction algorithm.
The interpolation and explicit-instance construction steps depend on the chosen function or operator class.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-to-Trajectory Consistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consistency condition for reconstructing vectors from a positive-semidefinite Gram factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb{S}_+^m\) be the Gram matrix of formal vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_m\), and let \(G=P^{\mathsf T}P\), where column \(p_i\) of \(P\) represents \(v_i\). Suppose every trajectory vector has prescribed coefficients \(x_k=\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ki}v_i\). The factor and trajectory are consistent precisely when the reconstructed vectors \(\widehat x_k=\sum_{i=1}^m a_{ki}p_i\) use the same coefficients and satisfy every certified affine relation. Then \(\langle\widehat x_k,\widehat x_\ell\rangle=a_k^{\mathsf T}Ga_\ell\), so all Gram-expressible method updates, initial conditions, and performance quantities are preserved.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Gram factor yields a consistent trajectory when reconstruction uses the certified coefficients, thereby preserving every affine update and all encoded inner products.

knowledge_statements.title: Interpolating-Function Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite reconstruction certificate for a closed proper convex interpolant from sampled first-order data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite and let \((x_i,g_i,f_i)\in\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(f_i\ge f_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\) for all \(i,j\in I\). Define \[f(x)=\max_{j\in I}\{f_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle\}.\] Then \(f\) is finite-valued, closed, and convex; moreover, \(f(x_i)=f_i\) and \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\) for every \(i\in I\). Thus the displayed maximum reconstructs an explicit convex objective realizing the sampled values and subgradients, and constitutes a verifiable worst-case interpolation certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Operator Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximal-monotone reconstruction from a finite monotone input-output table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite-dimensional real Hilbert space and let \(S=\{(x_i,u_i):i\in I\}\subset H\times H\) be finite. If \(\langle u_i-u_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\ge0\) for all \(i,j\in I\), then \(S\) is a monotone relation and is contained in the graph of at least one maximal monotone operator \(T:H\rightrightarrows H\). Consequently, choosing any maximal monotone extension of \(S\) reconstructs an operator satisfying \(u_i\in T(x_i)\) at every sampled point. The pairwise inequalities and graph inclusions form a finite certificate that the reconstructed operator realizes the recorded oracle responses.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any finite monotone input-output table admits a maximal-monotone extension realizing all recorded operator responses.

knowledge_statements.title: Composite Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separate reconstruction of convex components from componentwise first-order samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be finite. Define \[f_r(x)=\max_{j\in I}\{f_j^{(r)}+\langle g_j^{(r)},x-x_j\rangle\},\qquad F=f_1+f_2.\] Then each \(f_r\) is closed convex with \(f_r(x_i)=f_i^{(r)}\) and \(g_i^{(r)}\in\partial f_r(x_i)\). knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Horizon Exact Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact equality between a certified bound and worst-case performance at each fixed horizon.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a method \(M\), problem class \(\mathcal F\), admissible initialization set \(\mathcal I\), performance measure \(\Phi_N\), and horizon \(N\in\mathbb N\). Let \(U_N\) be a certified upper bound and define \[W_N=\sup\{\Phi_N(M,f,z_0):f\in\mathcal F,\ z_0\in\mathcal I\}.\] The certificate is finite-horizon exactly tight at \(N\) when \(U_N=W_N\). Equivalently, validity gives \(W_N\le U_N\), while for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there is an admissible instance with performance at least \(U_N-\varepsilon\). If the supremum is attained, the latter may be replaced by one instance achieving \(U_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bound is exactly tight at a fixed iteration count when it equals the supremal admissible performance, whether or not a worst case is attained.

\(U_N\) is valid for every admissible instance

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Rate Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightness of the decay or growth order, without requiring the optimal leading constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U_N>0\) be a valid worst-case upper bound and \(W_N\ge0\) the corresponding worst-case value for horizons \(N\ge1\). For a positive comparison sequence \(r_N\), the bound is asymptotically rate-tight at scale \(r_N\) when \[0<\liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac{W_N}{r_N}\le\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac{U_N}{r_N}<\infty.\] Since validity implies \(W_N\le U_N\), this condition places both quantities in \(\Theta(r_N)\). In particular, for \(r_N=N^{-p}\), the exponent \(p\) cannot be improved uniformly over the stated problem and method classes, although the certified multiplicative constant may remain nonoptimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rate tightness means the certified bound and true worst case have the same asymptotic order, while their leading constants may differ.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le W_N\le U_N\) for every \(N\ge1\)
\(r_N>0\) for every \(N\ge1\)

knowledge_statements.title: Leading-Constant Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of first-order asymptotic constants relative to a prescribed rate scale.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\le W_N\le U_N\) denote the worst-case value and a valid upper bound, and let \(r_N>0\) be the target asymptotic scale. Assume both normalized sequences converge to finite values. The certificate is leading-constant tight relative to \(r_N\) when \[\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{W_N}{r_N}=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{U_N}{r_N}=C\] for some \(C\in(0,\infty)\). Equivalently, \(W_N=C r_N+o(r_N)\) and \(U_N=C r_N+o(r_N)\). This is stronger than rate tightness because it excludes a persistent multiplicative gap between the certified bound and realizable worst-case performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Leading-constant tightness requires the upper bound and true worst case to share the same nonzero first-order asymptotic coefficient.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Minimax Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality between a method's certified worst case and the minimax risk under a fixed oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a problem class \(\mathcal F\), oracle model \(\mathcal O\), horizon \(N\), and loss \(L\). Let \(\mathfrak A_N(\mathcal O)\) be the admissible algorithms using at most \(N\) adaptive oracle calls, and define \[R_N^*=\inf_{A\in\mathfrak A_N(\mathcal O)}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}L(A,f).\] For a particular method \(M\in\mathfrak A_N(\mathcal O)\) with valid certificate \(U_N\), oracle-minimax tightness holds when \[U_N=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}L(M,f)=R_N^*.\] Thus the certificate is attainable in the worst-case sense and no algorithm obeying the same oracle-information restrictions has a smaller worst-case loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle-minimax tightness means a method attains its certified worst case and matches the best possible risk among all algorithms using the same oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Formulation Relaxation Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of exact tightness caused by replacing realizable trajectories with a larger feasible certificate set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal T_N\) be the set of realizable length-\(N\) method trajectories, let \(\mathcal R_N\supseteq\mathcal T_N\) be the feasible set of a relaxed performance-estimation formulation, and let \(\Phi_N\) be its objective. Define \[W_N=\sup_{t\in\mathcal T_N}\Phi_N(t),\qquad U_N^{\mathrm{rel}}=\sup_{r\in\mathcal R_N}\Phi_N(r).\] The formulation relaxation gap is \(\Delta_N^{\mathrm{rel}}=U_N^{\mathrm{rel}}-W_N\ge0\). Exact tightness fails through this mechanism when \(\Delta_N^{\mathrm{rel}}>0\); equivalently, relaxed near-maximizers cannot be approximated, in objective value, by realizable trajectories. Equality of the feasible sets is sufficient, but not necessary, for a zero gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relaxation gap is the excess of the relaxed optimum over the supremum attainable by genuine method trajectories.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Dimension Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tightness obstruction caused by a rank requirement exceeding the permitted ambient dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a Gram-based certificate have optimal value \(U_N\), and let \(G\in\mathbb S_+^m\) encode all formal trajectory vectors. Reconstruction in \(\mathbb R^d\) requires \(\operatorname{rank}(G)\le d\). Define \[U_{N,d}=\sup\{\Phi(G):G\text{ is certificate-feasible and }\operatorname{rank}(G)\le d\}.\] The ambient-dimension gap is \(\Delta_{N,d}^{\mathrm{dim}}=U_N-U_{N,d}\ge0\). If every optimizer, and every sequence approaching \(U_N\), has rank exceeding \(d\), then \(\Delta_{N,d}^{\mathrm{dim}}>0\); the unrestricted certificate cannot be reconstructed as a \(d\)-dimensional worst-case trajectory. A factor of rank at most \(d\) achieving \(U_N\) certifies zero dimension gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dimension gap occurs when optimal certificate Gram matrices require rank above the allowed space dimension, preventing an equally bad low-dimensional reconstruction.

knowledge_statements.title: Method-Class Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mismatch between the analyzed method family and the algorithm family claimed by a tightness conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M\subseteq\mathfrak A\) be two method classes under the same problem class, oracle, horizon, and loss. Define \[R_N(\mathfrak C)=\inf_{M\in\mathfrak C}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}L(M,f)\] for \(\mathfrak C\in\{\mathfrak M,\mathfrak A\}\). Since \(\mathfrak M\subseteq\mathfrak A\), one has \(R_N(\mathfrak A)\le R_N(\mathfrak M)\). The method-class gap is \(\Delta_N^{\mathrm{meth}}=R_N(\mathfrak M)-R_N(\mathfrak A)\ge0\). If it is positive, a certificate optimal over \(\mathfrak M\) cannot establish minimax optimality over \(\mathfrak A\); it proves optimality only within the smaller analyzed family.

knowledge_statements.title: Information Gap

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates equality of optimal values from existence of a finite worst-case instance attaining that value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be the feasible set of a PEP and let \(V=\sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)<+\infty\). A nonattainment gap occurs when \[\Phi(z)<V\quad\text{for every }z\in\mathcal F,\qquad \sup_{z\in\mathcal F}\Phi(z)=V.\] Equivalently, there may exist a maximizing sequence \((z_m)_{m\ge1}\subset\mathcal F\) with \(\Phi(z_m)\to V\), while no feasible transcript or interpolating problem instance realizes \(V\). Thus an exact optimal value alone does not provide an attained worst-case example.

children.title: Numerical Gap

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies unresolved numerical error through certified primal and dual bounds for a solved PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider a maximization-form PEP with exact value \(V\). If a validated feasible primal point gives \(L\le V\) and a validated dual certificate gives \(V\le U\), define the numerical gap by \[\Delta_{\mathrm{num}}=U-L\ge 0.\] The computation certifies \(V\in[L,U]\), and it certifies absolute accuracy \(\varepsilon\ge0\) whenever \(\Delta_{\mathrm{num}}\le\varepsilon\). A solver-reported objective difference without independently checked primal feasibility, dual feasibility, and rigorous evaluation of both objectives is not by itself such a certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A numerical gap is the width of a validated primal–dual bracket on the exact PEP value, not merely a solver-reported residual.
assumptions_latex: The PEP is posed as a maximization problem with exact value \(V\).
The value \(L\) comes from a validated feasible primal point, and \(U\) comes from a validated dual certificate.
The requested absolute tolerance satisfies \(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The inequalities \(L\le V\le U\) hold, and \(U-L\le\varepsilon\) certifies absolute accuracy \(\varepsilon\).

children.title: Limit–Solver Discrepancies

knowledge_statements.title: Limit–Solver Discrepancies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies failure of exchanging an approximation limit with optimization or numerical solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V_m=\sup_{z\in\mathcal F_m}\Phi_m(z)\) be exact values of approximating PEPs and let \(\widehat V_m\) be their computed values. A limit–solver discrepancy occurs if either \(\widehat V_m-V_m\not\to0\), or the limiting model has value \(V_\infty\) but \[\lim_{m\to\infty}V_m\ne V_\infty.\] Consequently, convergence of solver outputs does not establish convergence to the intended limiting worst-case value unless numerical errors vanish and the feasible sets and objectives converge strongly enough to justify passage of the supremum through the limit.

The relevant limits exist whenever an inequality between them is asserted.

knowledge_statements.title: Smooth Gradient-Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Gram representation for fixed-step gradient methods on smooth convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For convex differentiable \(f\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, sampled triples \((x_i,g_i,f_i)\) are interpolable when, for all \(i,j\), \[f_i\ge f_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle+\frac{1}{2L}\lVert g_i-g_j\rVert^2.\] A fixed-step gradient method satisfies \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h_k g_k\), with prescribed \(h_k\ge0\), and an optimizer sample satisfies \(g_\star=0\). Under a normalization such as \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert^2\le R^2\), maximizing a linear performance measure over these constraints becomes a semidefinite PEP by replacing all vector inner products with entries of a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth convex gradient-method worst cases admit an SDP representation using exact interpolation inequalities, linear method relations, normalization, and a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, convex, differentiable, and has \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient with \(L>0\).
The stepsizes \(h_0,\ldots,h_{N-1}\) are fixed before the PEP is solved.
The performance criterion is linear in sampled function values and inner products.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-horizon worst-case problem has a Gram-matrix semidefinite representation.

notation.meaning: sampled point, gradient, and function value

knowledge_statements.title: Strongly Convex Gradient-Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram formulation using exact interpolation for smooth strongly convex functions with fixed gradient steps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0\le\mu<L\). Samples \((x_i,g_i,f_i)\) are interpolable by an \(L\)-smooth, \(\mu\)-strongly convex function exactly when, for every \(i,j\), \[f_i\ge f_j+\langle g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle+\frac{1}{2(1-\mu/L)}\left(\frac{1}{L}\lVert g_i-g_j\rVert^2+\mu\lVert x_i-x_j\rVert^2-\frac{2\mu}{L}\langle g_i-g_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\right).\] Together with \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h_k g_k\), \(g_\star=0\), normalization, and a linear criterion, these inequalities yield a semidefinite Gram-matrix PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strongly convex gradient-method PEPs use exact smooth–strongly-convex interpolation inequalities and fixed-step recurrences to obtain an SDP worst-case formulation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, \(\mu\)-strongly convex, and differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
\(0\le\mu<L\), and the stepsizes are prescribed.
The objective and normalization are Gram-representable.

children.title: Adaptive-Stepsize PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance-estimation models for stepsizes selected from evolving method information.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive-Stepsize PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents stepsizes chosen from observed history rather than fixed before execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\), an adaptive policy is a family of maps \(A_k\) satisfying \[\alpha_k=A_k(H_k),\qquad H_k=(x_0,f_0,g_0,\ldots,x_k,f_k,g_k).\] A PEP for this policy maximizes the selected performance criterion over interpolable oracle data while enforcing both the method update and the graph constraints of each \(A_k\). Replacing \(\alpha_k\) by an unconstrained scalar models a larger method class and can overestimate performance. Because products such as \(\alpha_k g_k\) are decision-dependent, the exact adaptive PEP need not be an SDP without additional representability or lifting assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adaptive-stepsize PEP must encode the stepsize as a function of available history; treating it as a free scalar changes the method class.
assumptions_latex: At iteration \(k\), the policy uses only the recorded history \(H_k\).
Oracle samples satisfy the interpolation conditions of the selected function class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact performance estimation requires the constraints \(\alpha_k=A_k(H_k)\); omitting them yields a relaxation.

notation.meaning: oracle history available before choosing step \(k\)

review_flags: Source needed for adaptive-policy PEP representability and relaxation claims

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly separates a history-dependent policy from free stepsize variables and appropriately warns that decision-dependent products need not yield an SDP, but these representability and relaxation claims have no source.

children.title: Line-Search PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite PEP encoding of exact line search along the negative gradient direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable convex \(f\), exact gradient-direction line search chooses \(\alpha_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\alpha\ge0}f(x_k-\alpha g_k)\) and sets \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\). If \(\alpha_k>0\), convexity of the univariate restriction gives the condition \[\langle g_{k+1},g_k\rangle=0.\] If \(\alpha_k=0\), the boundary condition is \(\langle g_{k+1},g_k\rangle\le0\). A line-search PEP combines these relations with function-class interpolation and normalization; an exact formulation must also preserve the common scalar \(\alpha_k\) in the update rather than retaining only orthogonality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact line-search PEPs encode minimization along each gradient ray, including update consistency and the appropriate interior orthogonality or boundary condition.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and differentiable on every searched ray.
The search domain is \([0,+\infty)\), and an exact minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The line-search rule implies the stated first-order ray-optimality condition and must be encoded jointly with the iterate update.

notation.meaning: accepted point on the negative-gradient ray

review_flags: Dedicated source needed for exact line-search PEP encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The interior orthogonality condition, boundary sign, and common-stepsize update are internally consistent for exact ray search, but no source supports this exact PEP encoding.

children.title: Accepted-Step Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Accepted-Step Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes accepted and rejected trials needed to model backtracking rules exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(c\in(0,1)\), contraction \(\beta\in(0,1)\), and initial trial \(\bar\alpha_k>0\). In Armijo backtracking, the accepted step is \(\alpha_k=\bar\alpha_k\beta^{m_k}\), where \(m_k\) is the least nonnegative integer satisfying \[f(x_k-\alpha_k g_k)\le f(x_k)-c\alpha_k\lVert g_k\rVert^2.\] If \(m_k>0\), exact encoding also requires rejection of the preceding trial: \[f(x_k-\alpha_k\beta^{-1}g_k)>f(x_k)-c\alpha_k\beta^{-1}\lVert g_k\rVert^2.\] Encoding only the accepted inequality relaxes the backtracking policy.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact backtracking PEP records both Armijo acceptance and, when applicable, failure of the immediately preceding larger trial.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_k\).
\(c,\beta\in(0,1)\), and backtracking terminates at a finite \(m_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The acceptance inequality plus predecessor rejection characterizes the first accepted trial on the geometric grid.

notation.meaning: index of the first accepted trial

review_flags: Authoritative source needed for exact accepted-step PEP encoding

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The acceptance condition and rejection of the immediately preceding grid point correctly characterize the first accepted Armijo trial, and condition is an appropriate content kind. An authoritative source for its exact use in a PEP is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram representation for fixed-step subgradient descent on Lipschitz convex objectives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and suppose sampled subgradients satisfy \(\lVert g_i\rVert\le G\). With a Gram-representable normalization and linear performance criterion, maximizing over these inequalities and a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix gives the finite-horizon subgradient PEP.

children.title: Projected-Subgradient PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Subgradient PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation of subgradient updates followed by metric projection onto a nonempty closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space. Projected subgradient descent satisfies \[x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-h_k g_k),\qquad g_k\in\partial f(x_k).\] Define \(r_k=x_k-h_k g_k-x_{k+1}\). The projection is characterized by \[x_{k+1}\in C,\qquad \langle r_k,z-x_{k+1}\rangle\le0\quad\text{for every }z\in C.\] A finite PEP combines convex-function interpolation, subgradient norm bounds, normalization, and projection inequalities involving the represented feasible points. Enforcing these inequalities only on finitely many sampled points is exact only when the resulting data are jointly realizable by one nonempty closed convex set; otherwise the formulation is a relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected-subgradient PEPs combine subgradient interpolation with the variational characterization of projection and must ensure that the sampled feasibility data describe one common closed convex set.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty closed convex subset of a real Hilbert space.
\(f\) is convex and subdifferentiable at every iterate \(x_k\).
The stepsizes satisfy \(h_k\ge0\) and are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each projected update is certified by \(x_{k+1}\in C\) together with \(\langle r_k,z-x_{k+1}\rangle\le0\) for every \(z\in C\).

notation.meaning: metric projection onto the nonempty closed convex set C

children.title: Projection-Induced Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes inactive and active projections in projected-subgradient performance estimation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. For a trial point \(y_k=x_k-\alpha_k g_k\), define \(x_{k+1}=P_C(y_k)\) and \(r_k=(y_k-x_{k+1})/\alpha_k\), where \(\alpha_k>0\). The projection constraints are equivalently \(r_k\in N_C(x_{k+1})\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_k(g_k+r_k)\). The step is in the inactive regime exactly when \(y_k\in C\), equivalently \(r_k=0\). It is in the active regime when \(y_k\notin C\), in which case \(r_k\neq0\) is a boundary normal. A projected-subgradient PEP must retain these normal-cone constraints; deleting them reduces the model to an unconstrained subgradient PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection is inactive when the trial point is feasible and active otherwise; the active regime introduces a nonzero normal-cone residual that must appear in the PEP.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(g_k\in\partial f(x_k)\) and \(\alpha_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y_k\in C\iff r_k=0\), while \(y_k\notin C\Rightarrow r_k\in N_C(x_{k+1})\setminus\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible set

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Descent PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP representation of deterministic mirror descent in primal-dual coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(h\) be differentiable and strictly convex on the relevant domain. A horizon-\(N\) mirror-descent PEP introduces samples \((x_i,f_i,g_i)\) with \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\), together with the method constraints
\[x_{i+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\left\{\alpha_i\langle g_i,x\rangle+D_h(x,x_i)\right\},\qquad i=0,\ldots,N-1.\]
Equivalently, there exist \(n_{i+1}\in N_C(x_{i+1})\) satisfying \(\nabla h(x_{i+1})=\nabla h(x_i)-\alpha_i(g_i+n_{i+1})\). Maximizing a prescribed terminal performance measure over these constraints, the initial condition, and valid interpolation constraints defines the mirror-descent PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mirror-descent PEP maximizes a terminal criterion over interpolable oracle samples constrained by the mirror update, equivalently by its dual-coordinate normal-cone equation.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\), and each oracle vector satisfies \(g_i\in\partial f(x_i)\).
\(h\) is differentiable and strictly convex, and every displayed subproblem attains a minimizer.
\(\alpha_i>0\) for \(i=0,\ldots,N-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PEP feasible set is characterized by interpolation, initialization, and the displayed mirror-descent update constraints.

notation.meaning: normal cone to C at x

children.title: Bregman-Geometry PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman-Geometry PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines PEPs whose geometry is encoded by sampled Bregman divergences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A Bregman-geometry performance-estimation problem over a finite index set \(I\) is an extremal problem whose variables include sampled points \(x_i\), values \(h_i=h(x_i)\), gradients \(s_i=\nabla h(x_i)\), and divergences
\[D_{ij}=h_i-h_j-\langle s_j,x_i-x_j\rangle,\qquad i,j\in I.\]
Its feasible set imposes interpolation conditions for the chosen class of distance-generating functions, algorithmic relations written using \(D_{ij}\) or \(s_i-s_j\), and an initial Bregman-radius bound. Its objective is a specified worst-case performance measure. Unlike an exclusively Euclidean Gram formulation, the geometry-defining samples are optimization variables constrained by the function class of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman-geometry PEP optimizes worst-case performance jointly over algorithm samples and an admissible distance-generating function encoded through sampled divergences and gradients.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and all sampled points lie in the differentiability domain of \(h\).
\(h\) belongs to a specified convex function class admitting finite-sample interpolation conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{ij}=h_i-h_j-\langle s_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\) is retained as geometry-dependent PEP data subject to interpolation.

notation.meaning: sampled Bregman divergence from x_j to x_i
sampled gradient of the distance-generating function

children.title: Geometry-Sensitive Performance Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Sensitive Performance Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows how strong convexity of the mirror map controls the standard mirror-descent bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, let \(x_*\) minimize \(f\) on \(C\), and suppose \(h\) is \(\sigma\)-strongly convex with respect to a norm \(\|\cdot\|\). For mirror descent with constant step \(\alpha>0\), subgradients satisfying \(\|g_k\|_*\le G\), and weighted average \(\bar x_N=N^{-1}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}x_k\), the geometry-sensitive guarantee is
\[f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)\le \frac{D_h(x_*,x_0)}{\alpha N}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2\sigma}.\]
Thus the performance regime is determined by the initial Bregman radius, the dual-norm oracle bound, and the strong-convexity modulus of the chosen geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mirror-descent performance depends on the initial Bregman radius, dual-norm subgradient bound, and strong-convexity modulus, not solely on Euclidean distance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex, \(x_*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\), and \(\|g_k\|_*\le G\).
\(h\) is differentiable and \(\sigma\)-strongly convex relative to \(\|\cdot\|\).
Mirror descent uses the constant step \(\alpha>0\) for \(N\ge1\) iterations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x_N)-f(x_*)\le D_h(x_*,x_0)/(\alpha N)+\alpha G^2/(2\sigma)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bundle-Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP encoding of stabilized bundle methods for convex minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For convex \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), a bundle-method PEP records oracle triples \((y_j,f_j,g_j)\) and the cutting-plane model \(m_k(x)=\max_{j\in B_k}\{f_j+\langle g_j,x-y_j\rangle\}\). Given a center \(c_k\) and parameter \(\tau_k>0\), the trial point satisfies
\[y_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_x\left\{m_k(x)+\frac{1}{2\tau_k}\|x-c_k\|^2\right\}.\]
After evaluating \(f_{k+1}=f(y_{k+1})\), a prescribed serious/null-step rule selects \(c_{k+1}\). Maximizing a terminal gap over convex interpolation, model construction, proximal optimality, center updates, and initialization defines the corresponding bundle-method PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bundle-method PEP encodes oracle cuts, the stabilized model subproblem, and serious/null center updates, then maximizes a terminal error over all convex interpolants.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex, with \(g_j\in\partial f(y_j)\).
Each bundle \(B_k\) is a specified subset of previously queried indices.
\(\tau_k>0\), and the serious/null-step test is fixed in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case terminal criterion is optimized subject to convex interpolation and the complete stabilized bundle recursion.

children.title: Cutting-Plane PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Cutting-Plane PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for an exact polyhedral cutting-plane model with a prescribed query rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and let queried oracle data satisfy \(g_j\in\partial f(x_j)\). Define the lower model
\[m_k(x)=\max_{0\le j\le k}\{f_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle\}.\]
A cutting-plane PEP imposes convex interpolation on \((x_j,f_j,g_j)\), the query rule \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}m_k(x)\), and the associated epigraph optimality constraints. Because \(m_k(x)\le f(x)\) on \(C\), the model value \(\ell_k=\min_{x\in C}m_k(x)\) is a valid lower bound on \(f_*\). The PEP maximizes a specified error, such as \(f(x_N)-\ell_N\), over all admissible oracle data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cutting-plane PEP uses all sampled affine minorants, enforces minimization of their maximum, and exploits the model minimum as a verifiable lower bound.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and each \(g_j\in\partial f(x_j)\).
Every model-minimization subproblem attains its minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(m_k\le f\) on \(C\) and \(\ell_k\le f_*\), so \(f(x_N)-\ell_N\) is a valid computable upper bound on suboptimality.

notation.meaning: minimum value of the cutting-plane model on C

children.title: General Model-Based PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: General Model-Based PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines finite-horizon PEPs for methods driven by lower models and regularized model subproblems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A finite-horizon model-based PEP for minimizing \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is an extremal problem over oracle samples and models \(m_k(\cdot;x_k)\) satisfying a specified fidelity class. Its method constraints have the form
\[x_{k+1}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{m_k(x;x_k)+R_k(x,x_k)\},\]
where \(R_k\) is a prescribed stabilizer, together with any acceptance or center-update rule. The feasible set also includes interpolation constraints for \(f\), model-fidelity inequalities linking \(m_k\) to sampled values or subgradients, and initialization bounds. The PEP value is the supremum of a designated performance measure over every function, model sequence, and trajectory satisfying these finite constraints.

children.title: Model-Fidelity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural effects of exact, lower, or approximate local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Model-Fidelity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classifies exact, one-sided, and inexact model fidelity through explicit inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For an anchor \(y\in C\), a convex model \(m(\cdot;y)\) is globally exact lower-fidelity for \(f\) when \(m(x;y)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(m(y;y)=f(y)\). It has two-sided \((L,\delta)\)-fidelity relative to a norm when
\[m(x;y)\le f(x)\le m(x;y)+\frac{L}{2}\|x-y\|^2+\delta\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\]
The case \(\delta=0\) is an exact quadratic-fidelity regime; \(\delta>0\) is an inexact regime. A model-based PEP must impose the regime selected for every model anchor, since changing \(L\) or \(\delta\) changes its feasible trajectories and worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Model fidelity is exact when the model touches and globally underestimates the objective; quadratic upper error and additive error define progressively weaker regimes.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) and every model \(m(\cdot;y)\) are finite on the points under consideration.
\(L\ge0\), \(\delta\ge0\), and \(\|\cdot\|\) is a norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\delta=0\) yields exact quadratic fidelity, whereas \(\delta>0\) permits uniformly bounded model error.

notation.meaning: model value at x anchored at y

children.title: Momentum PEPs
children.top_down_role: Worst-case performance of methods carrying inertial state across iterations.

knowledge_statements.title: Momentum PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP representation of the heavy-ball momentum recurrence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\), fixed parameters \(\alpha>0\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), and initialization \(x_{-1}=x_0\), a horizon-\(N\) momentum PEP introduces samples \((x_i,f_i,g_i)\) satisfying \(g_i=\nabla f(x_i)\) and
\[x_{i+1}=x_i-\alpha g_i+\beta(x_i-x_{i-1}),\qquad i=0,\ldots,N-1.\]
It maximizes a prescribed terminal measure over these recurrences, an initial radius or function-gap bound, and interpolation constraints for the selected objective class. In a Euclidean formulation, all recurrence and performance expressions reduce to linear constraints in sampled values and affine expressions in the Gram matrix of iterates and gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A momentum PEP maximizes terminal error over interpolable objective samples constrained by the heavy-ball two-step recurrence and a prescribed initialization bound.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) belongs to a specified differentiable objective class with valid finite-sample interpolation conditions.
\(\alpha>0\), \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\), and \(N\ge1\).
The initial state satisfies \(x_{-1}=x_0\) and a stated radius or gap bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The heavy-ball worst case is the supremum of the selected terminal criterion over all samples satisfying interpolation and the two-step recurrence.

children.title: Extrapolation PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation for methods evaluating beyond the current iterate.

knowledge_statements.title: Extrapolation PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for gradient evaluation at an extrapolated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable. An extrapolation-method PEP with parameters \(\theta_k\) and step sizes \(\alpha_k>0\) introduces base iterates \(x_k\), extrapolated points \(y_k\), and oracle samples \((y_k,f(y_k),g_k)\) constrained by
\[y_k=x_k+\theta_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k-\alpha_k g_k,\qquad g_k=\nabla f(y_k).\]
With a specified initialization for \(x_{-1},x_0\), the PEP maximizes a chosen terminal criterion subject to these affine method relations and interpolation constraints for \(f\). The distinction between \(x_k\) and \(y_k\) is essential because the oracle is queried at the extrapolated point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extrapolation PEP keeps separate base and query points, enforces extrapolation followed by a gradient step, and applies interpolation at the query points.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) belongs to a differentiable class admitting finite-sample interpolation.
\(\alpha_k>0\), and the real parameters \(\theta_k\) are prescribed.
\(x_{-1}\) and \(x_0\) satisfy a specified initialization condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle interpolation is imposed at \(y_k\), while the method constraints link \(y_k\) affinely to \(x_k,x_{k-1}\) and \(x_{k+1}\).

children.title: Coupled Inertial Regimes
children.top_down_role: PEP structure when momentum is combined with extrapolated evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Inertial Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified two-sequence representation coupling momentum and extrapolated oracle evaluation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A coupled inertial first-order scheme is represented by
\[y_k=x_k+a_k(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=x_k+b_k(x_k-x_{k-1})-\alpha_k\nabla f(y_k),\]
with prescribed real coefficients \(a_k,b_k\) and \(\alpha_k>0\). Its PEP treats both \(x_k\) and \(y_k\) as sampled vectors, imposes objective interpolation at every oracle point \(y_k\), and maximizes a chosen terminal criterion under initialization constraints. The regime \(a_k=0\) gives gradient evaluation at the base point with momentum \(b_k\); the regime \(b_k=a_k\) gives a gradient step from the extrapolated point. Independent coefficients encode the genuinely coupled regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled inertial PEPs use separate coefficients for the oracle extrapolation and iterate momentum, containing base-point momentum and extrapolated-gradient schemes as special cases.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) belongs to a differentiable class with finite-sample interpolation conditions.
\(a_k,b_k\in\mathbb{R}\), \(\alpha_k>0\), and the coefficient sequences are prescribed.
The two initial states satisfy a stated boundedness condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a_k=0\) recovers base-point momentum, while \(b_k=a_k\) recovers stepping from the extrapolated point.

children.title: Inertial Stability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Parameter regions where acceleration loses stability or worst-case benefit.

knowledge_statements.title: Inertial Stability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp scalar-quadratic stability boundary for constant-parameter heavy-ball iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Apply \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1})\) to \(f(x)=\lambda x^2/2\), where \(\lambda>0\), \(\alpha>0\), and \(0\le\beta<1\). The error recurrence has characteristic polynomial
\[p(r)=r^2-(1-\alpha\lambda+\beta)r+\beta.\]
Both characteristic roots lie strictly inside the unit disk exactly when
\[0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta).\]
At \(\alpha\lambda=2(1+\beta)\), the polynomial has the root \(r=-1\), so generic trajectories do not converge. For \(\alpha\lambda>2(1+\beta)\), at least one root has modulus greater than one, furnishing a divergent quadratic instance and a sharp inertial stability failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a scalar positive quadratic, heavy-ball is stable exactly below the step threshold; equality creates a persistent minus-one mode, and larger steps diverge.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\lambda x^2/2\) with \(\lambda>0\).
The heavy-ball parameters are constant with \(\alpha>0\) and \(0\le\beta<1\).
The initial pair is not chosen to cancel every unstable or unit-modulus mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The strict stability region is \(0<\alpha\lambda<2(1+\beta)\); the upper equality is a nonconvergent boundary and larger products admit divergence.

notation.meaning: characteristic polynomial of the error recurrence

knowledge_statements.title: Optimized-Coefficient Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint PEP design of fixed first-order coefficients and a certified worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a horizon \(N\), choose coefficients \(h_{k,i}\) in the fixed-step scheme \[x_{k+1}=x_0-\frac{1}{L}\sum_{i=0}^{k}h_{k,i}g_i,\qquad g_i=\nabla f(x_i).\] Normalize \(\|x_0-x_\star\|^2\le R^2\), introduce function values \(f_i\) and Gram matrix \(G\) of the vectors \(x_0-x_\star,g_0,\ldots,g_N\), and impose the smooth-convex interpolation inequalities for every sampled pair. Minimize \(\tau\) jointly over admissible coefficients and a valid dual PEP certificate subject to \(f_N-f_\star\le \tau LR^2\). The returned coefficients define the method; dual feasibility certifies its normalized worst-case guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize the method coefficients together with a dual performance-estimation certificate; the feasible dual bound rigorously controls the method’s worst-case final objective error.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a real Hilbert space.
\(x_\star\in\operatorname*{argmin} f\) and \(\|x_0-x_\star\|\le R\).
The coefficients are fixed independently of oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_N)-f_\star\le \tau LR^2\) for every admissible instance whenever the designed dual certificate is feasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Accelerated Proximal PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Proximal Fixed-Point Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Translation between proximal oracle samples and resolvent fixed-point samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proper closed convex function \(f\), set \(A=\partial f\) and fix \(\lambda>0\). Then \[p=\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p=J_{\lambda A}(y)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a=\frac{y-p}{\lambda}\in\partial f(p).\] Moreover, \(p=y\) holds exactly when \(0\in\partial f(y)\), equivalently when \(y\) minimizes \(f\). Thus a proximal-method PEP can be expressed as a fixed-point PEP for the firmly nonexpansive resolvent, while retaining function-value variables and cyclic-subgradient interpolation when the performance measure involves objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proximal call is exactly a resolvent fixed-point call, with its displacement encoding a subgradient; fixed points coincide with minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is proper, closed, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
\(A=\partial f\) and \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{prox}_{\lambda f}=J_{\lambda\partial f}\) and \(\operatorname{Fix}(J_{\lambda\partial f})=\operatorname*{argmin}f\).

knowledge_statements.title: Acceleration Failure Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unrestricted inertial extrapolation even for a proximal fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Acceleration is not universally stable under unrestricted inertial coefficients. On \(\mathbb{R}\), take \(f=\delta_{\{0\}}\), so \(T=\operatorname{prox}_{f}\equiv0\), and apply \[y_k=x_k+\beta(x_k-x_{k-1}),\qquad x_{k+1}=y_k+\alpha(Ty_k-y_k).\] With \(\alpha=2\), the state recurrence is \(x_{k+1}=-(1+\beta)x_k+\beta x_{k-1}\). Its characteristic polynomial is \(q^2+(1+\beta)q-\beta\), which has a root of modulus greater than one for every \(\beta>0\). Hence a valid firmly nonexpansive proximal map can produce divergent accelerated iterates when overrelaxation and inertia are combined without a stability restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a constant proximal map diverges under a simple overrelaxed inertial scheme, so nonexpansiveness alone cannot justify arbitrary acceleration.
assumptions_latex: The iteration uses constant inertia \(\beta>0\) and relaxation \(\alpha=2\).
Initial data have a nonzero component along the unstable scalar recurrence mode.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|x_k|\to\infty\) for generic initial data although \(T\) is firmly nonexpansive and has a fixed point.

notation.meaning: indicator function of the singleton containing zero

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating-Projection PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-set projection certificate retaining both families of normal-cone constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\) be nonempty closed convex sets with \(C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), and generate \(u_{k+1}=P_C(v_k)\), \(v_{k+1}=P_D(u_{k+1})\). Define \(a_{k+1}=v_k-u_{k+1}\in N_C(u_{k+1})\) and \(b_{k+1}=u_{k+1}-v_{k+1}\in N_D(v_{k+1})\). Pairwise normal inequalities within each set, the alternating recurrences, a common point \(x_\star\in C\cap D\), an initial constraint, and Gram-matrix positivity form an alternating-projection PEP. A feasible dual aggregation proving \(\|v_N-x_\star\|^2\le B_N\), or a stated feasibility-residual bound, certifies that inequality for every compatible pair \((C,D)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separate normal-cone interpolation for both sets, coupled by alternating updates, gives a finite certificate for distance or feasibility residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are nonempty closed convex sets in a real Hilbert space with nonempty intersection.
All projections are exact.
The initial condition and chosen performance measure are Gram-representable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible dual aggregation yields the selected universal bound, such as \(\|v_N-x_\star\|^2\le B_N\).

notation.meaning: alternating projected points in the two sets
projection displacements belonging to the respective normal cones
