children.title: Projection Geometry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Effects of set geometry on projection-based worst-case performance.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Geometry Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric regularity predicates used to stratify projection-method performance bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For closed convex sets \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) with intersection \(S=\bigcap_{i=1}^m C_i\), bounded linear regularity on a set \(B\) is the existence of \(\kappa_B<\infty\) such that \[d(x,S)\le \kappa_B\max_{1\le i\le m}d(x,C_i)\qquad\text{for all }x\in B.\] Global linear regularity means the same inequality holds with \(B\) equal to the ambient space and a single constant \(\kappa\). A projection PEP must declare whether no regularity, bounded regularity, or global regularity is imposed, because the corresponding interpolation constraints and attainable contraction factors describe different geometric regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection analyses separate arbitrary convex geometry from bounded or global linear regularity, each encoded by a distance-to-intersection error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(C_1,\ldots,C_m\) are nonempty closed convex sets with \(S\ne\varnothing\).
Distances are induced by the Hilbert-space norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The value and domain of \(\kappa_B\) specify the projection-geometry regime available to a performance-estimation model.

notation.meaning: distance from a point to a set

review_flags: Standard definition supplied without a matching local source locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the geometry-regime leaf, and the distinction between bounded and global linear regularity is standard and precisely stated. However, the record supplies no source locator for the definition or for its asserted role in projection PEP constraints.

children.title: Feasibility Interaction Effects
children.top_down_role: Performance consequences arising from interactions among projected sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Interaction Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How mutual set geometry enters alternating-projection contraction certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C,D\) be closed convex sets with \(S=C\cap D\ne\varnothing\), and assume linear regularity \(d(x,S)\le\kappa\max\{d(x,C),d(x,D)\}\) on a region containing the iterates. For \(x\in C\), set \(y=P_Dx\) and \(z=P_Cy\). Projection Pythagorean inequalities give \[d(z,S)^2\le d(x,S)^2-\|x-y\|^2-\|y-z\|^2.\] Thus the two projection decreases interact additively, while regularity links at least one feasibility residual to distance from \(S\). A PEP that omits the common-point and regularity constraints cannot generally certify a uniform strict contraction from convexity alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Alternating projections accumulate two geometric decreases; a regularity error bound converts these decreases into contraction, while convexity alone does not.
assumptions_latex: \(C,D\) are closed convex sets with nonempty intersection \(S\).
The pair is linearly regular with modulus \(\kappa\) on the iterate region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable contraction certificate depends on interaction constraints coupling distances to \(C\), \(D\), and \(S\).

notation.meaning: successive projections onto the two sets

review_flags: The geometric decrease is standard, but no supplied source supports the PEP interaction claim

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property role fits the interaction-effects leaf, and the chained projection decrease is mathematically plausible under the stated convex-set assumptions. No source supports either the displayed geometric inequality in this formulation or the stronger PEP claim about regularity constraints and uniform strict contraction.

knowledge_statements.title: Basic Conditional-Gradient PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon certificate for the basic conditional-gradient oracle and update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be compact and convex, let \(f\) be convex and \(L\)-smooth, and generate \[s_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in C}\langle g_k,s\rangle,\qquad g_k=\nabla f(x_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=(1-\gamma_k)x_k+\gamma_k s_k.\] A conditional-gradient PEP uses smooth-convex interpolation for the sampled triples, affine update equations, diameter constraints \(\|u-v\|\le D\) for sampled feasible points, and oracle inequalities \(\langle g_k,s_k-u\rangle\le0\) for every sampled \(u\in C\), including an optimizer. Together with Gram-matrix positivity, feasible dual multipliers yielding \(f(x_N)-f_\star\le B_N\) constitute a verifiable worst-case certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Smooth interpolation, feasible-set diameter, linear-minimization inequalities, and affine updates certify the basic conditional-gradient method’s finite-horizon error.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, compact, convex, and has diameter at most \(D\).
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood of \(C\).
The step sizes satisfy \(0\le\gamma_k\le1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible dual PEP certificate establishes \(f(x_N)-f_\star\le B_N\) for every modeled instance.

notation.meaning: upper bound on the feasible-set diameter

review_flags: No supplied locator directly supports conditional-gradient PEP interpolation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate role fits the basic conditional-gradient PEP leaf, and the linear-minimization oracle inequalities are standard. No source or locator supports the proposed finite interpolation/Gram formulation or its dual-certificate conclusion. A direct conditional-gradient PEP reference is required.

children.title: Away-Step PEPs
children.top_down_role: Worst-case analysis of conditional-gradient schemes permitting away directions.

knowledge_statements.title: Away-Step PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP representation for deterministic away-step conditional-gradient iterations on compact polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(V)\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) belong to a prescribed convex smooth function class, and write \(x_k=\sum_{v\in S_k}\alpha_{k,v}v\). Select \(s_k\in\arg\min_{v\in V}\langle\nabla f(x_k),v\rangle\) and \(a_k\in\arg\max_{v\in S_k}\langle\nabla f(x_k),v\rangle\). Choose either \(d_k=s_k-x_k\) or \(d_k=x_k-a_k\), with the corresponding feasible upper step \(\gamma_k^{\max}\), and set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+\gamma_kd_k\), where \(0\leq\gamma_k\leq\gamma_k^{\max}\). The horizon-\(N\) away-step PEP is the supremum of a specified terminal criterion over all dimensions, admissible \(f,C,V\), oracle selections, active-set coefficients, and trajectories satisfying these relations and the class interpolation constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The away-step PEP maximizes a terminal error over every admissible function, polytope, active-set representation, oracle choice, and feasible away-step trajectory.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
\(f\) belongs to the smooth convex class fixed by the PEP.
The step rule and terminal performance criterion are fixed for the horizon \(N\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:\text{all stated interpolation, oracle, active-set, and update constraints hold}\}\).

notation.meaning: active vertex set representing the current iterate

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the Away-Step PEPs leaf and is mathematically plausible, but no evidence is supplied for the exact PEP formulation. The performance criterion, function class, direction-selection policy, step policy, and interpolation system remain family parameters, so source uncertainty affects the precise feasible problem.

children.title: Corrective-Variant PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation for partially or fully corrective variants.

knowledge_statements.title: Corrective-Variant PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for fully or partially corrective conditional-gradient variants with explicit active-hull constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\operatorname{conv}(V)\subset\mathbb{R}^d\), let \(f\) lie in a prescribed convex function class, and let \(S_k\subset V\) be the active set. After obtaining \(s_k\in\arg\min_{v\in V}\langle\nabla f(x_k),v\rangle\), choose a revised set \(S_{k+1}\subseteq S_k\cup\{s_k\}\) and require \(x_{k+1}\in\operatorname{conv}(S_{k+1})\). A fully corrective step additionally satisfies \(x_{k+1}\in\arg\min_{x\in\operatorname{conv}(S_k\cup\{s_k\})}f(x)\); a partial correction replaces this equality by its specified verifiable decrease or stationarity condition. The associated horizon-\(N\) PEP maximizes the terminal criterion over all interpolable samples and all active-set revisions satisfying the selected correction regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A corrective-variant PEP adds active-hull membership and exact or approximate correction constraints to the conditional-gradient performance-estimation problem.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty compact polytope.
The function class admits finite interpolation constraints.
One exact or approximate correction rule is fixed throughout the PEP.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{corr}}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:\text{interpolation, linear-oracle, revision, and correction constraints hold}\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the corrective-variant leaf, but no source supports the proposed PEP constraints. In particular, a partial correction is left as an unspecified decrease or stationarity predicate, so the mathematical formulation cannot be reviewed as one definite variant.

children.title: Active-Set Revision Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural comparison of local active-set removal or recombination.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Revision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility predicates distinguishing add, drop, swap, and corrective active-set revisions inside conditional-gradient PEPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_k=\sum_{v\in S_k}\alpha_{k,v}v\), where \(\alpha_{k,v}>0\) and \(\sum_{v\in S_k}\alpha_{k,v}=1\), and let \(s_k\in V\) be a new oracle atom. An admissible revision is encoded by coefficients \(\alpha_{k+1,v}\geq0\) satisfying \(x_{k+1}=\sum_{v\in S_k\cup\{s_k\}}\alpha_{k+1,v}v\) and \(\sum_v\alpha_{k+1,v}=1\), with \(S_{k+1}=\{v:\alpha_{k+1,v}>0\}\). It is an add regime when no old positive coefficient vanishes, a drop regime when at least one does, a swap regime when a dropped atom is replaced by \(s_k\), and a corrective regime when the coefficients satisfy an additional prescribed optimality or decrease condition over the active hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Revision regimes are determined by which active coefficients remain positive and whether the new coefficients obey an additional correction condition.
assumptions_latex: \(V\) is the vertex set of a polytope.
\(S_k\) is a finite positive-coefficient representation of \(x_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_{k+1}=\{v\in S_k\cup\{s_k\}:\alpha_{k+1,v}>0\}\), with the regime classified by the stated support transition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition role fits the leaf, but the add, drop, swap, and corrective labels are not made mutually precise and may overlap; for example, the stated swap condition does not specify whether exactly one old atom is removed or how the incoming atom's positive coefficient is enforced. A source defining the intended active-set taxonomy is required.

children.title: Face-Identification Effects
children.top_down_role: Worst-case consequences of identifying a lower-dimensional feasible face.

knowledge_statements.title: Face-Identification Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of certified optimal-face identification on the feasible set and value of a conditional-gradient PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F_\star\) be a face of a polytope \(C\) containing every optimizer relevant to the PEP, and let \(\mathcal{F}_N\) denote the feasible transcript set of an unrestricted horizon-\(N\) conditional-gradient PEP. If face identification is certified at index \(K\), impose \(x_k\in F_\star\), \(S_k\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(F_\star)\), and all subsequently selected active atoms in \(F_\star\) for \(k\geq K\). The resulting transcript set \(\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{face}}_{N,K}\) is contained in \(\mathcal{F}_N\). Consequently, for the same maximized terminal criterion \(\mathcal{E}_N\), the face-aware PEP value cannot exceed the unrestricted value; strict improvement is possible because post-identification geometric constants may be computed on \(F_\star\) rather than on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certified identification restricts later transcripts to the optimal face, so the face-aware worst-case value cannot exceed the unrestricted PEP value.
assumptions_latex: \(F_\star\) is a face of \(C\) containing the relevant solution set.
Identification at iteration \(K\) is imposed as a valid certificate.
Both PEPs maximize the same terminal criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{face}}_{N,K}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_N\) and \(\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{F}^{\mathrm{face}}_{N,K}}\mathcal{E}_N(\tau)\leq\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{F}_N}\mathcal{E}_N(\tau)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Transcript-set restriction does imply the displayed weak inequality for a common maximized criterion, and the property role fits the leaf. However, no source supports the face-identification model or the additional claim that strict improvement may follow from face-local geometric constants; that claim is variant-dependent.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation-Oracle Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transcript-based PEP representation for first-order methods accessing a convex feasible set through separating hyperplanes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. At a query \(z_k\), a separation oracle either certifies \(z_k\in C\) or returns \((a_k,b_k)\) such that \(\langle a_k,x\rangle\leq b_k<\langle a_k,z_k\rangle\) for every \(x\in C\). Fix a deterministic method whose next query is a prescribed function of previous first-order data and oracle replies. Its horizon-\(N\) PEP is the supremum of a chosen terminal error over all dimensions, admissible objectives and sets, sampled first-order data, queries, and separating cuts satisfying objective interpolation, cut validity, and the method's update equations. Thus the cuts constitute finite, directly checkable feasibility certificates within the performance-estimation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The PEP maximizes terminal error over all objective samples and valid separation-oracle transcripts consistent with the method's query rule.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
The objective class and deterministic query rule are fixed.
Each negative membership reply supplies a strongly separating affine cut.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{sep}}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:\text{interpolation, cut-validity, and query-update constraints hold}\}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The separation-oracle transcript representation fits the topic, but it has no citation and does not instantiate the objective class, query rule, normalization, terminal criterion, or finite encoding of global cut validity. Source uncertainty therefore affects the claimed PEP formulation.

children.title: Resolvent-Iteration PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation for iterations driven by resolvent evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent-Iteration PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Gram representation of proximal-point performance estimation for maximal monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) be maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space, let \(\lambda_k>0\), and generate \(x_{k+1}=J_{\lambda_kA}x_k\). Introduce \(u_{k+1}=(x_k-x_{k+1})/\lambda_k\), so \(u_{k+1}\in Ax_{k+1}\). For sampled pairs, monotonicity gives \(\langle x_i-x_j,u_i-u_j\rangle\geq0\), including a solution pair \((x_\star,0)\). Any terminal criterion expressible through inner products of sampled points and values can therefore be maximized over their Gram matrix subject to these inequalities, the linear resolvent updates, the initial-radius constraint, and positive semidefiniteness. This semidefinite problem is the resolvent-iteration PEP for the selected criterion and step sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resolvent PEPs encode proximal-point iterates as sampled graph pairs and maximize performance over a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix satisfying monotonicity.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
\(0\in Ax_\star\) for some \(x_\star\).
The steps satisfy \(\lambda_k>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:G\succeq0,\ x_k-x_{k+1}=\lambda_ku_{k+1},\ \langle x_i-x_j,u_i-u_j\rangle\geq0\}\).

sampled value with u_k in A x_k

children.title: Fixed-Point Iteration PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Point Iteration PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gram-matrix PEP for Picard iteration of a nonexpansive mapping with a fixed point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space, let \(x_\star=Tx_\star\), and generate \(x_{k+1}=Tx_k\) for \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\). Writing \(y_i=Tx_i\), finite nonexpansive interpolation is expressed by \(\|y_i-y_j\|^2\leq\|x_i-x_j\|^2\) for every sampled pair, together with \(y_\star=x_\star\). If the initial condition is \(\|x_0-x_\star\|\leq R\), the worst value of any terminal criterion built from sampled inner products, such as \(\|x_N-Tx_N\|^2\), is the optimum of a positive-semidefinite Gram problem containing these interpolation inequalities and the linear identities \(x_{k+1}=y_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed-point PEP maximizes a sampled terminal criterion subject to nonexpansive interpolation, Picard updates, a fixed point, and an initial-radius bound.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is nonexpansive on a real Hilbert space.
\(\operatorname{Fix}(T)\neq\varnothing\).
\(\|x_0-x_\star\|\leq R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:G\succeq0,\ x_{k+1}=y_k,\ \|y_i-y_j\|^2\leq\|x_i-x_j\|^2,\ y_\star=x_\star\}\).

children.title: Resolvent Operator Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural transfer between resolvent representations plus fixed-point representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Resolvent Operator Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minty correspondence between maximal monotone operators and everywhere-defined firmly nonexpansive resolvents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space. If \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) is maximal monotone, then \(J_A=(I+A)^{-1}:H\to H\) is single-valued and firmly nonexpansive, and \(u=J_Ax\) holds exactly when \(x-u\in Au\). Conversely, if \(T:H\to H\) is firmly nonexpansive, define the relation \(A=T^{-1}-I\), meaning \(a\in Au\) exactly when \(u=T(u+a)\). Then \(A\) is maximal monotone and \(T=J_A\). Hence a resolvent sample \((x,u)\) is equivalently the graph sample \((u,x-u)\) of a maximal monotone operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximal monotone operators correspond exactly to full-domain firmly nonexpansive maps through the resolvent transformation.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
Operators may be set-valued, while the firmly nonexpansive map is defined on all of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A\text{ maximal monotone}\Longleftrightarrow J_A\text{ firmly nonexpansive on }H\), with \(u=J_Ax\Longleftrightarrow x-u\in Au\).

notation.meaning: resolvent of A, equal to the inverse relation of identity plus A
relation assigning a to u when u equals T applied to u plus a

children.title: Averagedness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance distinctions across contractive, nonexpansive, or averaged operator settings.

knowledge_statements.title: Averagedness Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent inequality characterizing averaged operators and the limiting firmly nonexpansive and nonexpansive regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(0<\alpha<1\). A mapping \(T:H\to H\) is \(\alpha\)-averaged precisely when there exists a nonexpansive \(R:H\to H\) such that \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\). Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in H\), \[\|Tx-Ty\|^2+\frac{1-\alpha}{\alpha}\|(I-T)x-(I-T)y\|^2\leq\|x-y\|^2.\] The case \(\alpha=1/2\) is firm nonexpansiveness. At the boundary \(\alpha=1\), the residual term vanishes and the condition reduces to nonexpansiveness, although the usual definition of an averaged map takes \(\alpha<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An averaged map is a convex combination of identity and a nonexpansive map, equivalently satisfying a strengthened nonexpansive inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T=(1-\alpha)I+\alpha R\) for some nonexpansive \(R\) if and only if the displayed averagedness inequality holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Forward-Backward PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for deterministic forward-backward splitting with a cocoercive forward operator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(B:H\to H\) be \(\beta\)-cocoercive, and choose \(0<\gamma<2\beta\). Forward-backward splitting applies \(x_{k+1}=J_{\gamma A}(x_k-\gamma Bx_k)\). With \(b_k=Bx_k\) and \(a_{k+1}=(x_k-x_{k+1})/\gamma-b_k\), the update is equivalent to \(a_{k+1}\in Ax_{k+1}\). A horizon-\(N\) PEP maximizes a chosen terminal criterion over a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix subject to these linear identities, monotonicity inequalities for the sampled graph of \(A\), cocoercivity inequalities \(\langle b_i-b_j,x_i-x_j\rangle\geq\beta\|b_i-b_j\|^2\), a sampled solution satisfying \(0\in(A+B)x_\star\), and the initial condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The forward-backward PEP combines resolvent identities, monotone interpolation for the backward operator, and cocoercive interpolation for the forward operator.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is maximal monotone and \(B\) is \(\beta\)-cocoercive.
\(0<\gamma<2\beta\).
\(0\in(A+B)x_\star\) for some \(x_\star\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{FB}}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:\text{the stated Gram, update, monotonicity, cocoercivity, and initial constraints hold}\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Reflected-Splitting PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for the Douglas–Rachford reflected-resolvent fixed-point map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A,B:H\rightrightarrows H\) be maximal monotone, let \(\gamma>0\), define \(R_{\gamma A}=2J_{\gamma A}-I\) and \(R_{\gamma B}=2J_{\gamma B}-I\), and set \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}=\tfrac12(I+R_{\gamma A}R_{\gamma B})\). Douglas–Rachford iteration is \(z_{k+1}=T_{\mathrm{DR}}z_k\). Introduce each intermediate resolvent image and its graph residual; then every iteration is represented by linear identities, while sampled values of \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy their respective monotonicity inequalities. A horizon-\(N\) reflected-splitting PEP maximizes a selected residual or solution criterion over the corresponding positive-semidefinite Gram matrix, the two families of monotonicity constraints, the update identities, and the initial bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reflected-splitting PEP expands Douglas–Rachford steps into two resolvent samples and enforces monotonicity through a common Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(B\) are maximal monotone on a real Hilbert space.
The fixed-point set of \(T_{\mathrm{DR}}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{DR}}_N)=\sup\{\mathcal{E}_N:\text{Gram positivity, two resolvent graphs, monotonicity, updates, and the initial bound hold}\}\).

children.title: Splitting-Map Comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Splitting-Map Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP comparison principle based on inclusion between feasible transcript sets for splitting maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a horizon \(N\), an initial-condition normalization, and a terminal criterion \(\mathcal{E}_N\). For splitting maps \(T_1\) and \(T_2\), let \(\mathcal{F}_1\) and \(\mathcal{F}_2\) be the PEP transcript sets produced by their update identities and operator interpolation constraints. If every transcript feasible for \(T_1\) can be transformed without changing \(\mathcal{E}_N\) into a transcript feasible for \(T_2\), then \(\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{F}_1}\mathcal{E}_N(\tau)\leq\sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{F}_2}\mathcal{E}_N(\tau)\). In particular, adding valid structural assumptions or interpolation inequalities to the same splitting-map model can only decrease its worst-case PEP value. Equality requires feasible extremizers to survive the restriction or a value-preserving correspondence in both directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Splitting-map worst cases compare by feasible-transcript inclusion: stronger valid constraints cannot increase the maximized PEP value.
assumptions_latex: Both PEPs use the same horizon, normalization, and terminal criterion.
A value-preserving map sends every transcript in \(\mathcal{F}_1\) into \(\mathcal{F}_2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{F}_1\hookrightarrow\mathcal{F}_2\Longrightarrow\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_1)\leq\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}_2)\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The supremum comparison under a value-preserving transcript map is correct and the property kind fits the comparison leaf. However, no evidence or standard-field rationale is supplied, and no concrete correspondence between splitting-map transcript sets is instantiated; the final equality discussion is also only a general sufficient-condition description.

children.title: Cocoercivity Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits imposed by insufficient regularity of the explicit operator component.

knowledge_statements.title: Cocoercivity Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between monotonicity, Lipschitz continuity, and cocoercivity in forward-step certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an operator \(B:H\to H\) on a real Hilbert space, \(\beta\)-cocoercivity requires \[\langle Bx-By,x-y\rangle\geq \beta\lVert Bx-By\rVert^2\qquad(x,y\in H).\] Monotonicity and \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity do not imply this condition: the rotation \(R(u_1,u_2)=(-u_2,u_1)\) is monotone and \(1\)-Lipschitz, but \(\langle Ru-Rv,u-v\rangle=0\) while \(\lVert Ru-Rv\rVert^2>0\) whenever \(u\neq v\). Consequently, no positive cocoercivity parameter can be imposed on that class, and forward-step PEP constraints relying on such a parameter are invalid without an additional assumption such as gradient structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotone Lipschitz operator need not be cocoercive; a planar rotation is a concrete counterexample, so cocoercivity-based forward-step certificates require an extra structural assumption.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a real Hilbert space.
\(B\) is assumed only monotone and Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotonicity plus Lipschitz continuity alone does not imply \(\beta\)-cocoercivity for any \(\beta>0\).

notation.meaning: single-valued operator used in the forward step

children.title: ADMM PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation for alternating direction multiplier schemes.

knowledge_statements.title: ADMM PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP representation for two-block convex ADMM with a fixed penalty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) and \(g\) be proper closed convex functions and consider \(\min\{f(x)+g(z):Ax+Bz=c\}\). For penalty \(\rho>0\), ADMM generates \(x^{k+1}\), \(z^{k+1}\), and \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho(Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c)\) by the two exact augmented-Lagrangian minimizations. A horizon-\(N\) ADMM performance-estimation problem for criterion \(\Phi_N\) is \[\sup\ \Phi_N\] over sampled iterates, function values, subgradients, and their Gram matrix, subject to the ADMM optimality equalities, convex interpolation inequalities for \(f\) and \(g\), the initial normalization, and positive semidefiniteness of the Gram matrix. Every feasible point represents admissible finite ADMM data; its optimum is the corresponding worst-case bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ADMM PEP maximizes a terminal criterion over finite ADMM trajectories satisfying update equations, convex interpolation constraints, normalization, and a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(\rho>0\), and both ADMM subproblems attain minimizers.
A finite initial-data normalization is specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PEP optimum equals the worst value of \(\Phi_N\) among trajectories represented by its interpolation model.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal-Dual Splitting PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpolation-based PEP for fixed-step primal-dual proximal splitting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_x f(x)+g(Kx)\), consider the fixed-step iteration \[y^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\sigma g^*}(y^k+\sigma K\bar x^k),\qquad x^{k+1}=\operatorname{prox}_{\tau f}(x^k-\tau K^*y^{k+1}),\qquad \bar x^{k+1}=x^{k+1}+\theta(x^{k+1}-x^k).\] A horizon-\(N\) primal-dual PEP maximizes a prescribed criterion \(\Phi_N\) over sampled primal-dual points, subgradients, values, and inner products, subject to these update relations, interpolation inequalities for \(f\) and \(g^*\), an initial normalization, and a positive-semidefinite Gram matrix. Under the selected interpolation class, the optimum is the worst-case value represented by the model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual splitting PEP encodes proximal updates and convex interpolation for both primal and dual functions, then maximizes a finite-horizon performance criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex.
\(K\) is bounded linear, with \(\tau>0\), \(\sigma>0\), and fixed \(\theta\).
All displayed proximal points exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The finite-dimensional PEP represents the worst modeled value of \(\Phi_N\) for the stated primal-dual iteration.

children.title: Dual-Splitting Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural links between ADMM representations plus dual splitting maps.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Splitting Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence of ADMM and Douglas–Rachford splitting on the Fenchel dual inclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min_{x,z}\{f(x)+g(z):Ax+Bz=c\}\), define dual functions \(F(y)=f^*(-A^*y)+\langle c,y\rangle\) and \(G(y)=g^*(-B^*y)\). With compatible sign, scaling, and initialization conventions, exact two-block ADMM with penalty \(\rho>0\) induces Douglas–Rachford splitting with stepsize \(\rho\) for \[0\in\partial F(y)+\partial G(y).\] The ADMM multiplier and residual data are obtained by an affine reconstruction from the Douglas–Rachford state and its resolvent points. Hence a performance criterion invariant under this reconstruction can be transferred between the ADMM PEP and the dual Douglas–Rachford PEP after applying the same scaling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact two-block ADMM is Douglas–Rachford splitting on an associated Fenchel-dual inclusion, allowing compatible PEP criteria and certificates to be transferred by affine reconstruction.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are proper, closed, and convex, and strong duality holds.
The required primal and resolvent subproblems are solvable.
ADMM and Douglas–Rachford use compatible scaling and initialization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: ADMM trajectory data and dual Douglas–Rachford data correspond affinely, so invariant performance criteria have equivalent PEP representations.

notation.meaning: ADMM penalty and corresponding splitting stepsize

children.title: Penalty Sensitivity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Worst-case effects of penalty or preconditioning choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Penalty Sensitivity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling law governing how ADMM PEPs depend on the penalty parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In unscaled ADMM, the multiplier update is \(y^{k+1}=y^k+\rho r^{k+1}\), where \(r^{k+1}=Ax^{k+1}+Bz^{k+1}-c\). Introducing \(u^k=y^k/\rho\) gives \(u^{k+1}=u^k+r^{k+1}\), but the primal subproblems retain the quadratic weight \(\rho\). Therefore two penalties \(\rho_1\) and \(\rho_2\) define equivalent normalized PEPs only when the function class, initial conditions, and performance criterion are rescaled consistently. If objective curvature, residual norms, or dual distances are fixed in physical units, changing \(\rho\) changes the feasible PEP and may change its worst-case value; penalty independence cannot be inferred from the scaled multiplier update alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling the ADMM multiplier removes the penalty from its update, but not from the primal subproblems; PEP bounds are penalty-invariant only under consistent data and criterion rescaling.
assumptions_latex: Exact two-block ADMM uses a constant \(\rho>0\).
The PEP fixes a function class, initial normalization, and performance criterion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Penalty changes preserve a PEP only under a compatible scaling transformation; otherwise the worst-case value can depend on \(\rho\).

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Coordinate PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation-valued PEP for independent randomized block-coordinate fixed-point updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\), let \(T:H\to H\), and sample \(i_k\) independently with \(\mathbb P(i_k=i)=p_i>0\). The coordinate iteration is \[x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k U_{i_k}\bigl(Tx^k-x^k\bigr),\] where \(U_i\) embeds block \(i\). A horizon-\(N\) randomized coordinate PEP maximizes \(\mathbb E[\Phi_N]\) over branchwise sampled points and values, subject to the update on every sampling history, interpolation constraints describing \(T\), probability-weighted Gram consistency, and an expected or deterministic initial normalization. Its optimum is the worst expected criterion over trajectories represented by those constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A randomized-coordinate PEP branches over sampled blocks, enforces each coordinate update and operator interpolation constraints, and maximizes an expected finite-horizon criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite orthogonal product of Hilbert spaces.
The indices \(i_k\) are independent with fixed probabilities \(p_i>0\).
The operator class of \(T\) admits finite interpolation constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PEP optimum represents the worst modeled value of \(\mathbb E[\Phi_N]\).

children.title: Stochastic-Gradient PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Stochastic-Gradient PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon expected-performance model for unbiased stochastic-gradient iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and consider \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\gamma_k g_k\), where \(\mathcal F_k\) contains the history through \(x^k\). An unbiased bounded-variance stochastic-gradient PEP maximizes \(\mathbb E[\Phi_N]\) over sampled points, function values, true subgradients \(s_k\), noises \(\xi_k=g_k-s_k\), and their moments, subject to convex interpolation and \[\mathbb E[\xi_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=0,\qquad \mathbb E[\lVert\xi_k\rVert^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\leq\sigma^2,\qquad x^{k+1}=x^k-\gamma_k(s_k+\xi_k).\] Together with a positive-semidefinite moment matrix and initial normalization, these constraints define the admissible finite-horizon model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stochastic-gradient PEP combines convex interpolation, the iterative update, conditional unbiasedness, a variance bound, moment consistency, and an initial normalization to optimize expected performance.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is convex and admits the sampled subgradients.
\(\gamma_k\geq0\) is fixed in advance.
The oracle noise is conditionally unbiased with conditional second moment at most \(\sigma^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PEP optimum is the worst expected value of \(\Phi_N\) within the stated oracle model.

children.title: Incremental-Method PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental-Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP representation for cyclic or prescribed-order finite-sum incremental updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), with each \(f_i\) convex. For a prescribed index sequence \((i_k)_{k=0}^{N-1}\), the incremental method satisfies \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\gamma_k g_{i_k}^k\), where \(g_{i_k}^k\in\partial f_{i_k}(x^k)\). Its horizon-\(N\) PEP maximizes a criterion \(\Phi_N\) over component values, subgradients, and a Gram matrix, subject to every incremental update, separate convex interpolation inequalities for each \(f_i\), an initial normalization, and Gram positive semidefiniteness. Because component gradients are evaluated at different intermediate points, they may not be replaced by a full subgradient of \(F\) at a common iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An incremental-method PEP enforces componentwise interpolation and each ordered update; intermediate component subgradients cannot generally be collapsed into one full-gradient observation.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), with every \(f_i\) convex.
The index sequence and stepsizes \(\gamma_k\geq0\) are prescribed.
A finite initial normalization is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The PEP optimum gives the worst modeled \(\Phi_N\) for the specified incremental schedule.

children.title: Sampling Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Sampling Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability constraints distinguishing independent, without-replacement, and importance-sampled PEP models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite-sum indices \(i_k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), the sampling regime is part of the PEP oracle specification. Independent sampling requires \(\mathbb P(i_k=i\mid\mathcal F_k)=p_i\) with fixed \(p_i>0\). Importance sampling uses the same condition with nonuniform \(p_i\) and an estimator scaled by \((np_{i_k})^{-1}\) to preserve conditional unbiasedness. Without-replacement epoch sampling requires each block \((i_{qn},\ldots,i_{qn+n-1})\) to be a permutation of \(\{1,\\ldots,n\}\); conditional probabilities then depend on previously drawn indices. These predicates define different feasible moment sets and must not be interchanged within one PEP certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent, importance, and without-replacement sampling impose different conditional laws; each produces a distinct feasible PEP moment model.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F_k\) records all samples and iterates available before drawing \(i_k\).
Every importance-sampling probability satisfies \(p_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chosen conditional sampling law must be encoded explicitly because different regimes yield different PEP feasible sets.

children.title: Finite-Sum Oracle Comparisons

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Sum Oracle Comparisons
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Non-equivalence of component, full-gradient, and generic unbiased-oracle PEP information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\), a full-gradient oracle returns \(
abla F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i
abla f_i(x)\), whereas a component oracle returns \((i,
abla f_i(x))\). Under uniform sampling, the latter is conditionally unbiased, but it additionally reveals a component label and must satisfy interpolation constraints shared across repeated queries to that component. A generic unbiased oracle constrained only by \(\mathbb E[g\mid x]=
abla F(x)\) and a moment bound need not admit any fixed finite-sum decomposition. Thus the corresponding PEP feasible sets generally differ; bounds are comparable only after explicitly mapping oracle information, sampling laws, and evaluation cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full-gradient, labeled component, and generic unbiased oracles expose different information, so their PEP bounds are comparable only under an explicit oracle and cost mapping.
assumptions_latex: \(F=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i\), and all required gradients exist.
Component indices are sampled uniformly when unbiasedness is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unbiasedness alone does not make a generic stochastic oracle equivalent to a finite-sum component oracle or a full-gradient oracle.

knowledge_statements.title: Variance-Reduced Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: State-augmented PEP for finite-sum estimators with stored or snapshot information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x)\). A variance-reduced method forms an estimator \(v_k\) from a sampled component gradient and auxiliary state \(s_k\), then updates \(x^{k+1}=x^k-\gamma_k v_k\) and \(s_{k+1}=\mathcal U(s_k,i_k,x^k)\). Its horizon-\(N\) PEP maximizes \(\mathbb E[\Phi_N]\) over iterates, component gradients, auxiliary states, and moments, subject to componentwise interpolation, the exact estimator and state-update identities, the sampling law, initial normalization, and positive-semidefinite moment consistency. Retaining \(s_k\) is essential: imposing only unbiasedness and a uniform variance bound discards the temporal correlations that constitute variance reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A variance-reduced PEP must track snapshots or gradient memory together with component interpolation and sampling; a generic bounded-variance oracle omits the defining temporal correlations.

The estimator formula, state update \(\mathcal U\), and sampling law are fixed.
A finite initial normalization is supplied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented PEP represents worst-case expected performance while preserving the method's state-dependent variance-reduction mechanism.

children.title: Asynchronous PEPs

knowledge_statements.title: Asynchronous PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Delay-augmented PEP for asynchronous coordinate updates with stale reads.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T:H_1\oplus\cdots\oplus H_m\to H\). At iteration \(k\), an asynchronous coordinate method reads a stale vector \(\hat x^k\) with blocks \(\hat x_j^k=x_j^{k-d_{k,j}}\), selects \(i_k\), and updates \[x^{k+1}=x^k+\lambda_k U_{i_k}\bigl(T\hat x^k-hat x^k\bigr).\] A horizon-\(N\) asynchronous PEP maximizes an expected criterion over iterates, delayed reads, indices, and delays, subject to this update, the operator's interpolation constraints, the prescribed joint law or deterministic bounds for \((i_k,d_k)\), causality, initial history, and positive-semidefinite moment consistency. The delay variables must remain explicit because stale evaluations are generally correlated with the trajectory.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asynchronous PEP augments coordinate-update constraints with explicit stale reads, delays, causality, and their probability law or deterministic bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is a finite product Hilbert space.
Every delay satisfies \(0\leq d_{k,j}\leq\tau\), or a specified delay law replaces this bound.
The selection-delay process obeys the stated causality assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented feasible set represents asynchronous trajectories without replacing stale evaluations by current-iterate evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Delayed-Information PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP with boundedly stale first-order information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a horizon \(N\), delay bound \(D\), function class \(\mathcal F\), and performance functional \(\Phi\). Thus the oracle datum used at iteration \(i\) may have been generated at \(x_{i-\tau_i}\).

children.title: Delay-Distribution Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions among bounded, random, or adversarial delays.

knowledge_statements.title: Delay-Distribution Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility conditions for deterministic and stochastic delay laws in PEPs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For delays \((\tau_i)_{i=0}^{N-1}\) adapted to a filtration \((\mathcal G_i)\), three standard admissible regimes are: bounded delay, \(0\leq\tau_i\leq D\) almost surely; conditionally independent delay, \(\mathbb P(\tau_i=d\mid\mathcal G_i)=p_{i,d}\) with prescribed probabilities; and moment-controlled delay, \(\mathbb E[\tau_i^q\mid\mathcal G_i]\leq m_q\). A delay-distribution PEP imposes exactly one declared regime, together with support constraints \(0\leq\tau_i\leq i\), before taking its worst case or expected performance objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Delay-aware PEPs must declare whether delays are adversarially bounded, conditionally distributed, or controlled only through moments; these regimes define different feasible trajectory sets.
assumptions_latex: \(\tau_i\) is integer-valued and \(\mathcal G_i\)-measurable when chosen adversarially, or sampled after conditioning on \(\mathcal G_i\).
The support condition \(0\leq\tau_i\leq i\) holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal D\in\left\{\mathcal D_D^{\mathrm{bd}},\mathcal D_p^{\mathrm{law}},\mathcal D_{q,m_q}^{\mathrm{mom}}\right\}\quad\text{is an explicit component of the PEP specification}.\]

notation.meaning: information available before the delay at iteration i is determined
upper bound on the conditional q-th delay moment

children.title: Concurrency Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Execution conditions where parallelism destroys a performance guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Concurrency Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of finite worst-case guarantees under unrestricted stale updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and the stale-gradient update \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma x_{k-\tau_k}\), with \(\gamma>0\). For any proposed horizon-independent guarantee based only on \(f(x_0)-f_\star\), allowing unbounded adversarial delays admits \(\tau_k=k\), hence \(x_{k+1}=x_k-\gamma x_0\) and \(x_k=(1-k\gamma)x_0\). Consequently \(f(x_k)=(1-k\gamma)^2f(x_0)\), which diverges quadratically. A finite concurrency PEP therefore requires a delay, overlap, consistency, or probabilistic-control assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even on a scalar quadratic, unrestricted adversarial staleness can make fixed-step stale-gradient iteration diverge; finite concurrency guarantees need an explicit control assumption.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0\neq0\) and \(\gamma>0\).
The adversary may choose any integer delay satisfying \(0\leq\tau_k\leq k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{k\geq0}\frac{f(x_k)-f_\star}{f(x_0)-f_\star}=+\infty.\]

notation.meaning: staleness of the gradient used at iteration k

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed scalar recurrence directly identifies the failure mechanism.
An authoritative asynchronous-optimization source is still required for promotion.

children.title: Approximate-Oracle PEPs
children.top_down_role: Worst-case performance under inaccurate function, gradient, or operator information.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximate-Oracle PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon PEP incorporating deterministic inexact first-order oracle outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a function class \(\mathcal F\), horizon \(N\), and error sets \(E_i\). An approximate-oracle PEP maximizes a performance functional \(\Phi\) over \(f\in\mathcal F\), iterates \(x_i\), exact sampled data \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and reported data \((\widetilde f_i,\widetilde g_i)\), subject to interpolation for \((x_i,f(x_i),g_i)\), algorithmic updates formed from the reported data, and \((\widetilde f_i-f(x_i),\widetilde g_i-g_i)\in E_i\). Absolute, relative, and biased-oracle models correspond to different declared choices of \(E_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An approximate-oracle PEP optimizes over exact and reported oracle data simultaneously, constraining their discrepancy by a specified error set and running the method on reported data.
assumptions_latex: The exact sampled data satisfy a finite interpolation characterization of \(\mathcal F\).
Each error set \(E_i\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathcal H\) is specified in advance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{oracle}}_N)=\sup\{\Phi:\text{interpolation, update, initialization, and oracle-error constraints hold}\}.\]

notation.meaning: admissible value-and-gradient error set at iteration i
oracle data reported to the algorithm

REQUEST_SOURCES: authoritative inexact-oracle PEP reference required.

children.title: Inexact-Subproblem PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation when internal optimization subproblems are solved approximately.

knowledge_statements.title: Inexact-Subproblem PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP model for algorithms whose proximal or implicit subproblems are solved inexactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For composite minimization \(F=f+h\), let a method request the proximal point of \(v_i=x_i-\gamma_i g_i\). An inexact-subproblem PEP replaces the exact condition by variables \(x_{i+1}\), \(s_{i+1}\in\partial h(x_{i+1})\), and residual \(r_{i+1}\) satisfying \(r_{i+1}=x_{i+1}-v_i+\gamma_i s_{i+1}\) and a declared criterion such as \(\|r_{i+1}\|\leq\eta_i\). The PEP maximizes its performance functional over interpolable data and residuals satisfying the initialization, update, and error criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact-subproblem PEP introduces residual variables for approximate proximal or implicit solves and maximizes performance over all interpolable trajectories satisfying the chosen residual criterion.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) belong to declared interpolable function classes.
\(\gamma_i>0\) and \(\eta_i\geq0\) are prescribed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{val}(\mathrm{PEP}^{\mathrm{sub}}_N)=\sup\{\Phi:r_{i+1}=x_{i+1}-v_i+\gamma_i s_{i+1},\ \|r_{i+1}\|\leq\eta_i,\ \text{and all interpolation constraints hold}\}.\]

notation.meaning: first-order residual of the approximate subproblem solution

children.title: Mixed Error Channels
children.top_down_role: Structural interaction between oracle error plus subproblem error.

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed Error Channels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unified PEP representation of simultaneous oracle, update, and subproblem errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A mixed-error first-order trajectory can be represented by \(z_{i+1}=A_i(z_0,\ldots,z_i;\widetilde o_i)+B_i e_i\), where \(\widetilde o_i=o_i+\delta_i\) is an approximate oracle output, \(e_i\) is an update or subproblem residual, and \((\delta_i,e_i)\in E_i\). The associated PEP includes exact-data interpolation constraints, this affine error-channel equation, and the declared joint set \(E_i\). A product set models separately bounded channels; a nonproduct set records correlation or a shared error budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixed-error PEPs represent oracle inaccuracies and computational residuals jointly; product uncertainty sets impose separate budgets, while coupled sets encode correlation or shared budgets.
assumptions_latex: The exact oracle data \(o_i\) satisfy the interpolation constraints of the declared problem class.
The maps \(A_i\), \(B_i\), and uncertainty sets \(E_i\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal T_N(E_0,\ldots,E_{N-1})=\{(z,o,\delta,e):\widetilde o_i=o_i+\delta_i,\ z_{i+1}=A_i(z_{0:i};\widetilde o_i)+B_i e_i,\ (\delta_i,e_i)\in E_i\}.\]

notation.meaning: update or subproblem error at iteration i

review_flags: The unified mixed-channel representation is not supported by the supplied locator hints.
REQUEST_SOURCES: robust or inexact PEP reference with coupled error channels required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits the leaf, but the affine channel equation is a particular modeling choice rather than a general representation of mixed oracle and subproblem errors. The spaces and types of the oracle outputs, states, errors, and maps are also not introduced. A source is needed to determine a defensible formulation.

children.title: Error-Accumulation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Worst-case consequences of persistent, summable, relative, or adaptive error.

knowledge_statements.title: Error-Accumulation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon classifications determined by weighted cumulative error budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a PEP analysis yields \(\Phi_N\leq B_N^{(0)}+\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}w_{N,i}\varepsilon_i\), with \(w_{N,i}\geq0\) and error magnitudes \(\varepsilon_i\geq0\). The errors are nonaccumulating when \(\sup_N\sum_i w_{N,i}\varepsilon_i<\infty\), vanishing when \(\sum_i w_{N,i}\varepsilon_i\to0\), linearly accumulating when the sum is \(\Theta(N)\), and destabilizing when it is unbounded relative to the target scale \(B_N^{(0)}\). The applicable regime is therefore defined by the weighted, not merely unweighted, error sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Error accumulation is classified by the weighted error term appearing in the performance certificate: it may vanish, remain bounded, grow linearly, or dominate the error-free target scale.
assumptions_latex: \(w_{N,i}\geq0\) and \(\varepsilon_i\geq0\).
The same performance normalization is used for \(B_N^{(0)}\) and the accumulated error term.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[S_N:=\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}w_{N,i}\varepsilon_i\quad\text{determines the error-accumulation regime through its asymptotic behavior}.\]

notation.meaning: error-free component of the performance bound
sensitivity weight of error i at horizon N

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: additive perturbation certificates are naturally classified by their weighted cumulative term.
Terminology for the four regimes requires alignment with an authoritative robustness source.
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate, but the proposed regimes are not a clean classification: vanishing is a special case of bounded nonaccumulation, while domination of the target scale can overlap bounded, vanishing, or linear behavior depending on the scale. An authoritative robustness source is needed to select terminology and precise boundaries.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Misspecification Robustness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Robustness criterion for PEP bounds under incorrect algorithmic parameter estimates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta\in\Theta\) denote the true problem parameters and let a method use estimates \(\widehat\theta\). Write \(V_N(\theta,\widehat\theta)\) for the corresponding worst-case PEP value and \(V_N^\star(\theta)=\inf_{\vartheta\in\Theta}V_N(\theta,\vartheta)\). The method is \(C\)-robust on a misspecification set \(M\subseteq\Theta\times\Theta\) if it remains well-defined and \(V_N(\theta,\widehat\theta)\leq C V_N^\star(\theta)\) for every \((\theta,\widehat\theta)\in M\) and every declared horizon \(N\). An additive version replaces the right side by \(C V_N^\star(\theta)+b_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Parameter-misspecification robustness means that using an inaccurate parameter estimate increases the worst-case PEP value by at most a declared multiplicative or additive amount.
assumptions_latex: \(V_N(\theta,\widehat\theta)\) uses the true class indexed by \(\theta\) and the algorithm tuned with \(\widehat\theta\).
\(V_N^\star(\theta)>0\) when the multiplicative criterion is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{N}\sup_{(\theta,\widehat\theta)\in M}\frac{V_N(\theta,\widehat\theta)}{V_N^\star(\theta)}\leq C.\]

notation.meaning: parameter vector used to tune the method
declared set of admissible true-and-estimated parameter pairs

review_flags: The multiplicative robustness convention is locally defined but not selected by the supplied sources.
REQUEST_SOURCES: PEP treatment of tuning-parameter misspecification required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the topic, but the benchmark defined by optimizing the tuning parameter over all of Theta and the requirement of one horizon-uniform multiplicative constant are noncanonical choices. Without a source, it is unclear that this is the intended parameter-misspecification robustness notion for PEPs.

children.title: Parameter-Free Method PEPs
children.top_down_role: Performance estimation for methods avoiding prescribed problem parameters.

knowledge_statements.title: Parameter-Free Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP for methods whose updates do not receive unknown class constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}\) be problem classes indexed by unknown constants. A parameter-free method PEP fixes update maps \(A_i\) that depend only on the observed transcript \(\mathcal T_i=(x_0,o_0,\ldots,x_i,o_i)\) and declared numerical constants independent of \(\theta\). For each \(\theta\), its value is the supremum of \(\Phi_N\) over functions in \(\mathcal F_\theta\) and transcripts satisfying interpolation and \(x_{i+1}=A_i(\mathcal T_i)\). The same maps \((A_i)\) must be used for every \(\theta\in\Theta\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-free PEP evaluates one transcript-driven method across a parameterized family of function classes without supplying the unknown class parameter to its updates.
assumptions_latex: Each class \(\mathcal F_\theta\) has a declared interpolation model.
The update maps are measurable functions of the observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[V_N^{\mathrm{pf}}(\theta)=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_\theta}\Phi_N(f,A_0,\ldots,A_{N-1}),\qquad A_i\ \text{is independent of}\ \theta.\]

notation.meaning: problem class indexed by an unknown parameter
oracle transcript observed through iteration i
worst-case value of the fixed parameter-free method

children.title: Universal-Method PEPs
children.top_down_role: Worst-case analysis for methods adapting across regularity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Universal-Method PEPs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: PEP evaluating one adaptive method over a scale of regularity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal F_\alpha)_{\alpha\in I}\) be a nested or otherwise jointly specified family of regularity classes. A universal-method PEP fixes one adaptive update-and-acceptance rule, independent of \(\alpha\), and for each \(\alpha\) maximizes a performance functional over \(f\in\mathcal F_\alpha\), oracle transcripts, and any admissible line-search decisions. Universality is certified when the resulting values satisfy \(V_N^{\mathrm{univ}}(\alpha)\leq C_\alpha R_N^\star(\alpha)+b_N(\alpha)\) simultaneously for every \(\alpha\in I\), where \(R_N^\star(\alpha)\) is a declared class-specific benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A universal-method PEP tests one adaptive rule on every class in a regularity scale and compares each worst-case value with that class's benchmark rate.
assumptions_latex: Every \(\mathcal F_\alpha\) and benchmark \(R_N^\star(\alpha)\) is explicitly specified.
The update-and-acceptance rule does not receive \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\alpha\in I,\qquad V_N^{\mathrm{univ}}(\alpha)\leq C_\alpha R_N^\star(\alpha)+b_N(\alpha).\]

notation.meaning: PEP value of the universal method on class alpha

review_flags: The regularity scale and benchmark convention are not determined by the supplied locators.
REQUEST_SOURCES: authoritative universal first-order method and PEP formulation required.

children.title: Knowledge-Agnostic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Performance distinctions arising from unavailable smoothness or curvature data.

knowledge_statements.title: Knowledge-Agnostic Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Information restrictions defining which problem constants a method may use.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be the vector of problem-class constants and let \(S\) index the constants revealed to the algorithm. A knowledge-agnostic regime is specified by the information condition \(x_{i+1}=A_i(\mathcal T_i,K_S,U_i)\), where \(U_i\) is internal randomness and \(A_i\) is independent of the hidden coordinates \(K_{S^c}\). Fully agnostic, partially agnostic, and horizon-agnostic regimes correspond respectively to \(S=\varnothing\), a proper nonempty subset \(S\), and exclusion of the horizon \(N\). The PEP adversary may vary every hidden coordinate within its declared domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A knowledge-agnostic regime is defined by which class constants are hidden from the update rule; hidden constants remain free adversarial variables in the PEP.
assumptions_latex: The revealed index set \(S\) and domain of each hidden constant are declared before optimization.
Internal randomness \(U_i\) is independent of hidden constants conditional on the observed transcript.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[A_i\perp K_{S^c}\mid(\mathcal T_i,K_S,U_i),\qquad K_{S^c}\ \text{remains variable in the PEP}.\]

notation.meaning: problem constants revealed to the algorithm
problem constants hidden from the algorithm

children.title: Universality Overhead
children.top_down_role: Worst-case cost associated with adaptation across problem classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Universality Overhead
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle-complexity penalty relative to class-tuned benchmark methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each class index \(\alpha\), let \(T_\star(\varepsilon,\alpha)\) be the minimum declared oracle complexity of a method tuned to \(\alpha\), and let \(T_U(\varepsilon,\alpha)\) be the complexity of one universal method that is not given \(\alpha\). Its multiplicative universality overhead on \(I\) is \(H(\varepsilon)=\sup_{\alpha\in I}T_U(\varepsilon,\alpha)/T_\star(\varepsilon,\alpha)\). A bound \(H(\varepsilon)\leq h(\varepsilon)\) certifies that universality costs at most the factor \(h(\varepsilon)\) in oracle calls at accuracy \(\varepsilon\), under the same initialization and success criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Universality overhead is the worst ratio between the oracle complexity of one parameter-agnostic method and the corresponding class-tuned benchmark complexity.
assumptions_latex: \(T_\star(\varepsilon,\alpha)>0\) for every \(\alpha\in I\).
Both complexities count the same oracle and use the same accuracy and success conventions.
The universal method is not supplied \(\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\sup_{\alpha\in I}\frac{T_U(\varepsilon,\alpha)}{T_\star(\varepsilon,\alpha)}\leq h(\varepsilon).\]

notation.meaning: universal-method oracle complexity on class alpha

children.title: Comparison Normalizations

children.title: Common Problem Class
children.top_down_role: Shared structural class used to make method comparisons commensurate.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Problem Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the shared instance family required for worst-case method comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space and let \(\mathcal F\) be a specified class of proper functions on \(X\). The common problem class is \[\mathcal P(\mathcal F,X)=\{(f,X):f\in\mathcal F,\ \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}f(x)\neq\varnothing\}.\] Two methods are compared on this class only when their guarantees quantify over the same members of \(\mathcal P(\mathcal F,X)\), with identical structural parameters such as smoothness, convexity, and domain restrictions. Their worst-case performances therefore take suprema over one common admissible instance set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Methods share a problem class when their worst-case guarantees range over exactly the same feasible domains, objectives, solutions, and structural parameter restrictions.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty subset of a real Hilbert space.
Every \(f\in\mathcal F\) is proper and attains its minimum on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P(\mathcal F,X)\) is the common instance set over which both methods are evaluated.

children.title: Common Initial Data
children.top_down_role: Shared initialization information used across competing performance estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Initial Data
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a shared admissible initialization set for worst-case comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each problem \(p=(f,X)\in\mathcal P(\mathcal F,X)\), let \(\mathcal I(p)\) be a set of admissible initial data, such as points and numerical bounds. A comparison uses common initial data when both methods begin from the same \(i_0\in\mathcal I(p)\) and every declared bound in \(i_0\), including a radius bound \(\lVert x_0-x_\star\rVert\le R\) or an objective-gap bound \(f(x_0)-f_\star\le\Delta\), has the same value and interpretation for both methods. The joint instance is then \((p,i_0)\).

\(\mathcal I(p)\) is specified independently of the method being compared.

children.title: Initialization Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Conditions under which distinct initial descriptions support the same comparison.

knowledge_statements.title: Initialization Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States when two initialization descriptions induce the same normalized instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal I_1(p)\) and \(\mathcal I_2(p)\) be two initialization descriptions for every \(p\in\mathcal P(\mathcal F,X)\). They are initialization-equivalent if there are mutually inverse maps \(T_p:\mathcal I_1(p)\to\mathcal I_2(p)\) such that \(i\) and \(T_p(i)\) contain the same starting iterate and define the same admissible set of underlying problems. Equivalently, for every \(i\in\mathcal I_1(p)\), \[\{q:q\text{ satisfies }i\}=\{q:q\text{ satisfies }T_p(i)\}.\] Under this condition, replacing one description by the other leaves every normalized worst-case supremum unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two initialization formats are equivalent when a reversible translation preserves the starting iterate and exactly the same admissible underlying instances.
assumptions_latex: Both initialization descriptions refer to the same common problem class.
The translations \(T_p\) are defined for every admissible problem \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equivalent descriptions induce identical normalized instance sets and hence identical worst-case suprema.

children.title: Normalization Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Comparison failures caused by incompatible classes or initialization records.

knowledge_statements.title: Normalization Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exhibits failure of comparison when distance and objective-gap initializations are interchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f_a(x)=a x^2/2\) on \(\mathbb R\), where \(a>0\), with minimizer \(x_\star=0\). If initialization is normalized by \(|x_0-x_\star|\le R\), then \(f_a(x_0)-f_a(x_\star)\le aR^2/2\). Conversely, a fixed gap bound \(f_a(x_0)-f_a(x_\star)\le\Delta\) permits \(|x_0-x_\star|\le\sqrt{2\Delta/a}\). Because these conversion factors are unbounded as \(a\) varies, a distance-normalized guarantee and a gap-normalized guarantee are not uniformly comparable unless the problem class supplies common curvature bounds controlling \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance and objective-gap initializations are incomparable without shared curvature bounds; a quadratic scaling family makes either conversion factor unbounded.
assumptions_latex: The compared problem class does not bound \(a\) above and below by common positive constants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No uniform equivalence exists between the normalizations \(|x_0-x_\star|\le R\) and \(f_a(x_0)-f_a(x_\star)\le\Delta\).
review_flags: elementary counterexample is self-contained but lacks a supplied source locator

children.title: Common Oracle Strength

knowledge_statements.title: Common Oracle Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines equality of information available per oracle query.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a problem \(p\) and query \(x\), let an oracle be a response relation \(\mathcal O_p(x)\subseteq\mathcal Y\). Two methods use common oracle strength when they query the same relation \(\mathcal O\) and receive responses from the same response space under the same adversarial or deterministic convention. For example, a first-order oracle for a convex function may return \((f(x),g)\) with \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Neither method may access additional derivatives, proximal points, hidden parameters, or exact subproblem solutions unless those data are included in the common response relation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Oracle strength is common when each query gives both methods exactly the same types of information under the same response convention.
assumptions_latex: Both methods operate on the same problem class.
Oracle responses obey one fixed deterministic or adversarial convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every permitted query exposes the same information relation \(\mathcal O_p(x)\) to both methods.

notation.meaning: set of admissible oracle responses at a query
