children.title: Distribution-Dependent Behavior
children.top_down_role: Typical-performance conclusions whose meaning depends on an explicit instance distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Dependent Behavior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records how typical-case performance varies with the instance law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) and \(Q\) be probability measures on the same measurable instance space \((\mathcal I,\mathscr F)\), and let \(R_N:\mathcal I\to\mathbb R\) be measurable and integrable under both laws. The expectations \(\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\) and \(\mathbb E_Q[R_N(I)]\), as well as the corresponding performance quantiles, may differ even when the algorithm, horizon, and admissible instance set are unchanged. If a uniform bound \(R_N(I)\le W_N\) holds for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), then \(\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\le W_N\) for every probability law \(P\) on \((\mathcal I,\mathscr F)\) under which \(R_N\) is integrable. Thus a distribution-free worst-case bound controls, but does not determine, distribution-dependent performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the instance distribution can change expectations and quantiles. A uniform worst-case bound controls all integrable supported distributions but does not determine their typical behavior.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal I,\mathscr F)\text{ is a measurable space}
P,Q\text{ are probability measures on }(\mathcal I,\mathscr F)
R_N\in L^1(P)\cap L^1(Q)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall I\in\mathcal I,\ R_N(I)\le W_N\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\le W_N

notation.meaning: alternative probability laws on the same measurable instance space

children.title: Cross-Regime Inference Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on using extremal results to predict typical behavior or vice versa.

knowledge_statements.title: Cross-Regime Inference Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates valid worst-to-average implications from invalid average-to-worst inference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a probability measure on a measurable instance space \((\mathcal I,\mathscr F)\), and let \(R_N:\mathcal I\to[0,+\infty]\) be measurable. If \(R_N(I)\le U_N<+\infty\) for every \(I\in\mathcal I\), then \(R_N(I)\le U_N\) almost surely and \(\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\le U_N\). The converse fails. For any \(M>0\) and \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\), take two admissible instances \(I_0,I_1\), assign probabilities \(P(\{I_1\})=\varepsilon\) and \(P(\{I_0\})=1-\varepsilon\), and set \(R_N(I_1)=M\) and \(R_N(I_0)=0\). Then \(\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]=\varepsilon M\), while \(\sup_{I\in\{I_0,I_1\}}R_N(I)=M\). Consequently, an expected or high-probability bound cannot by itself be promoted to a class-wide worst-case certificate; additional support, tail, or uniformity hypotheses are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case bounds imply supported average-case bounds, but small expectations or high-probability bounds do not control rare admissible worst cases.
assumptions_latex: (\mathcal I,\mathscr F,P)\text{ is a probability space}
R_N:\mathcal I\to[0,+\infty]\text{ is measurable}
U_N\in[0,+\infty)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(\forall I\in\mathcal I,\ R_N(I)\le U_N\bigr)\Rightarrow\mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\le U_N,\qquad \mathbb E_P[R_N(I)]\le U_N\not\Rightarrow\sup_{I\in\mathcal I}R_N(I)\le U_N

notation.meaning: probability law on the admissible instance space
instances in the explicit two-point counterexample

children.title: Numerical Evidence
children.top_down_role: Computed objectives, residuals, spectra, and solver outputs supporting empirical confidence.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Evidence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the evidentiary status of floating-point PEP outputs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Numerical PEP evidence consists of computed primal or dual variables, reported objective values, and residual diagnostics obtained in finite precision. For a maximization PEP and its dual, approximate values \(p_{\mathrm{num}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm{num}}\) support the conjecture \(p^\star\approx p_{\mathrm{num}}\approx d_{\mathrm{num}}\) when the observed gap and residuals are small. Unless feasibility and objective inequalities are validated with rigorous error bounds, however, neither \(d_{\mathrm{num}}\) nor solver status alone proves \(p^\star\le d_{\mathrm{num}}\). Numerical evidence therefore suggests a bound or sharp example but is not, by itself, a formal certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small solver residuals and primal-dual gaps support a conjectured PEP value, but floating-point output is not a proof without rigorous feasibility validation.
assumptions_latex: p^\star\text{ is the value of a maximization PEP}
p_{\mathrm{num}},d_{\mathrm{num}}\in\mathbb R
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{small numerical residuals and }d_{\mathrm{num}}-p_{\mathrm{num}}\not\Rightarrow p^\star\le d_{\mathrm{num}}

notation.meaning: exact optimal value of the primal PEP

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role is defensible for this leaf and the distinction is mathematically plausible, but no source supports the claims about floating-point primal-dual output, residuals, solver status, and rigorous validation. A precise validated-numerics or PEP implementation source is required.

children.title: Formal Certificates
children.top_down_role: Checkable proof artifacts supporting a mathematically valid performance bound.

knowledge_statements.title: Formal Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the dual-feasibility mechanism behind a rigorous PEP upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a primal maximization PEP with exact value \(p^\star\) and a weakly dual conic formulation with dual feasible set \(\mathcal D\) and dual objective \(D\). An explicitly represented \(y\in\mathcal D\), together with exact verification of every equality, cone-membership, and sign constraint, is a formal upper-bound certificate:
\[p^\star\le D(y).\]
If an admissible primal construction \(z\) is also supplied and satisfies \(P(z)=D(y)\), then weak duality yields \(P(z)=p^\star=D(y)\), certifying sharpness. Approximate feasibility is insufficient unless rigorous residual-to-bound corrections are incorporated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exactly feasible dual point formally upper-bounds a maximization PEP. A matching feasible primal construction also certifies that the bound is sharp.
assumptions_latex: \sup_{z\in\mathcal P}P(z)\le\inf_{y\in\mathcal D}D(y)
y\in\mathcal D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^\star\le D(y);\qquad z\in\mathcal P\ \land\ P(z)=D(y)\Rightarrow P(z)=p^\star=D(y)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate content kind exactly fits the terminal container, and the weak-duality mechanism is stated coherently. However, no authoritative conic-duality or PEP-certificate source and locator is supplied.

children.title: Certificate Recovery Gap
children.top_down_role: Cases where a convincing numerical result does not yield a stable, replayable certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Recovery Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies the gap between a numerical dual solution and an exact certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widetilde y\) be a floating-point approximation to a dual PEP certificate and let \(\rho(\widetilde y)\ge0\) measure violation of its exact affine, sign, and cone constraints. Even when \(\rho(\widetilde y)\) is small, weak duality does not establish \(p^\star\le D(\widetilde y)\) unless \(\rho(\widetilde y)=0\) is rigorously verified. Certificate recovery closes this gap by producing an exactly feasible \(y\) or by proving a correction \(\Delta(\rho)\) satisfying
\[p^\star\le D(\widetilde y)+\Delta(\rho(\widetilde y)).\]
Without such recovery or correction, the reported numerical bound retains evidentiary rather than formal status.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nearly feasible numerical dual point is not automatically a certificate. Exact recovery or a rigorous residual correction is needed for a valid bound.
assumptions_latex: \widetilde y\text{ is a finite-precision dual candidate}
\rho(\widetilde y)\ge0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho(\widetilde y)\approx0\not\Rightarrow p^\star\le D(\widetilde y)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits, but the residual measure and correction mechanism are formulation-dependent, and no validated-numerics or certificate-recovery source is supplied. Source uncertainty is material to the hypotheses under which a correction Delta exists.

children.title: Evidentiary Status Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on presenting numerical agreement as a formally certified conclusion.

knowledge_statements.title: Evidentiary Status Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates empirical, numerical, and formally certified PEP conclusions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a maximization PEP, a sampled feasible instance with value \(L\) proves only \(p^\star\ge L\). A floating-point dual candidate with reported value \(U\) suggests, but does not prove, \(p^\star\le U\) unless exact dual feasibility or a validated correction is established. An exactly feasible dual certificate proves \(p^\star\le U\); matching certified bounds \(L=U\) prove the exact value. Accordingly, empirical lower evidence, unvalidated numerical upper evidence, rigorous one-sided certificates, and sharp two-sided certificates are distinct statuses and must not be interchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible examples certify lower bounds; only validated dual feasibility certifies upper bounds. Equality of certified lower and upper bounds establishes sharpness.
assumptions_latex: p^\star=\sup_{z\in\mathcal P}P(z)
\text{weak duality holds for }(\mathcal P,\mathcal D)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: z\in\mathcal P\Rightarrow P(z)\le p^\star;\qquad y\in\mathcal D\Rightarrow p^\star\le D(y)

notation.meaning: objective value of a certified feasible primal construction
objective value of a certified feasible dual point

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits and the primal-lower/dual-upper distinction follows the intended maximization convention, but the record has no citation for its PEP-specific evidentiary classification or validation requirements.

children.title: Class-Wide Guarantees
children.top_down_role: Uniform bounds over every admissible instance represented by the modeled class.

knowledge_statements.title: Class-Wide Guarantees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a guarantee quantified uniformly over a prescribed PEP instance class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal I\) contain every problem, oracle realization, initialization, and parameter choice admitted by the model. A class-wide guarantee at horizon \(N\) is a bound \(B_N(\theta)\) such that
\[\forall I\in\mathcal I(\theta),\qquad R_N(I)\le B_N(\theta).\]
The parameters \(\theta\) may encode declared class constants such as smoothness, convexity, or initial radius, but \(B_N(\theta)\) cannot depend on undeclared features of the particular instance. A valid upper-bound PEP certificate establishes this universal statement only for the class and performance criterion actually encoded by that PEP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A class-wide guarantee bounds every encoded instance using only declared class parameters. It says nothing about instances outside the modeled class.
assumptions_latex: N\in\mathbb N
\mathcal I(\theta)\ne\varnothing
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall I\in\mathcal I(\theta),\ R_N(I)\le B_N(\theta)

notation.meaning: declared parameters defining the instance class
all instances satisfying those declared parameters

children.title: Instance-Level Predictions
children.top_down_role: Expected or inferred behavior for a particular problem instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Instance-Level Predictions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a prediction conditional on one specified optimization instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a particular instance \(I_0\), including its objective, feasible set, oracle behavior, initialization, and algorithmic parameters. An instance-level prediction is a statement about \(R_N(I_0)\), for example \(R_N(I_0)\le b_N(I_0)\), obtained from instance-specific information. It is not a universal statement over the ambient class \(\mathcal I\). Conversely, a class-wide worst-case bound \(R_N(I)\le B_N\) for all \(I\in\mathcal I\) applies to \(I_0\in\mathcal I\) but generally does not predict that \(R_N(I_0)\) is close to \(B_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An instance-level prediction concerns one fully specified problem. A worst-case class bound applies to it but need not accurately predict its realized performance.
assumptions_latex: I_0\in\mathcal I
N\in\mathbb N
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R_N(I_0)\le b_N(I_0)\text{ does not by itself imply }\forall I\in\mathcal I,\ R_N(I)\le b_N(I_0)

children.title: Uniformity Scope
children.top_down_role: Parameters, initializations, dimensions, and oracle behaviors covered uniformly by a guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformity Scope
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Specifies the quantifier condition required for a genuinely uniform guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Theta\) be a parameter set, let \(\mathcal I(\theta)\) be an instance class for each \(\theta\in\Theta\), and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb N\times\Theta\). A bound has uniformity scope \(S\) when \[\forall (N,\theta)\in S\;\forall I\in\mathcal I(\theta),\qquad R_N(I)\le B(N,\theta),\] where \(B\) depends only on the displayed indices and declared class parameters. Uniformity over instances at a fixed horizon and parameter value does not by itself imply uniformity over horizons or parameter values. Likewise, exchanging a limit in \(N\) with a supremum over instances or parameters requires additional hypotheses that justify that exchange, such as an applicable uniform-convergence or domination condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniformity is determined by explicit quantifiers. Uniformity over instances alone does not provide uniformity over horizons or parameters, and limit exchanges require separately justified hypotheses.
assumptions_latex: \Theta\text{ is a parameter set}
S\subseteq\mathbb N\times\Theta
\mathcal I(\theta)\ne\varnothing\text{ for every relevant }\theta
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall (N,\theta)\in S\ \forall I\in\mathcal I(\theta),\ R_N(I)\le B(N,\theta)

notation.meaning: horizon-parameter scope of the uniform claim
instance class associated with parameter value theta
bound independent of the particular instance

children.title: Prediction Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits on treating a class-wide extremal bound as a precise forecast for one instance.

knowledge_statements.title: Prediction Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes a uniform worst-case PEP guarantee from instance prediction and transfer beyond the modeled class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F\) be a function class, \(M\) a fixed first-order method and oracle protocol, and \(P(M,f)\) its performance after a prescribed number of oracle calls. A certified inequality \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}P(M,f)\leq U\] transfers to every instance represented by the same class, initialization constraints, oracle, and performance criterion. It does not imply that \(P(M,f)\) is close to \(U\) for a particular \(f\), nor does it apply to an enlarged class \(\widetilde{\mathcal F}\). Transfer fails whenever some \(\tilde f\in\widetilde{\mathcal F}\setminus\mathcal F\) satisfies \(P(M,\tilde f)>U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A PEP bound is uniform only over its modeled class and protocol; it neither predicts typical instance performance nor transfers automatically to a broader class.
assumptions_latex: \(M\), the oracle protocol, initialization constraints, and the evaluation horizon are fixed.
\(P(M,f)\) is the same performance functional used by the certificate.
Every transferred instance satisfies the interpolation and side constraints defining \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(M,f)\leq U\) holds for all \(f\in\mathcal F\), but no instance-level tightness or out-of-class guarantee follows.

notation.meaning: Function class represented in the performance-estimation problem.
Fixed first-order method together with its oracle interaction rules.
Certified performance criterion for method M on instance f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary content kind fits the terminal container, and the fixed-class versus instance-level distinction is mathematically plausible. However, the record has no citation or inspectable locator. Source support is required for the PEP interpretation and for the precise transfer boundary. The phrase that the certificate “does not apply” to an enlarged class should also be checked against the intended weaker claim that applicability is not implied automatically.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle Lower-Bound Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates method-specific PEP extremizers from oracle-complexity lower bounds quantified over all admissible algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathfrak M_k\) be the admissible algorithms using at most \(k\) calls to an oracle \(\mathcal O\), and let \(P(M,f)\) be an error criterion. A PEP extremizer for one fixed method \(M_0\) can establish \[\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}P(M_0,f)\geq L,\] but this alone does not establish the oracle lower bound \[\inf_{M\in\mathfrak M_k}\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}P(M,f)\geq L.\] The latter requires a hard-instance distribution, resisting oracle, or indistinguishability construction valid uniformly against every \(M\in\mathfrak M_k\), with oracle replies consistent with some member of \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A worst case for one algorithm is not an oracle lower bound; minimax complexity requires a valid hard construction against every admissible algorithm.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal F\), \(\mathcal O\), and the admissible algorithm family \(\mathfrak M_k\) are fixed.
Oracle transcripts used by a lower-bound construction are consistent with functions in \(\mathcal F\).
The same error criterion \(P\) and call budget \(k\) are used on both sides.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A method-specific extremizer supplies only a fixed-method lower witness unless it extends to the minimax quantifiers over \(\mathfrak M_k\).

notation.meaning: Admissible algorithms making at most k oracle calls.
Optimization error evaluated for method M and instance f.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle content kind fits this external-theory interface, and the distinction between a fixed-method extremizer and a minimax oracle lower bound is appropriate. No cited source or specific locator supports the oracle-complexity quantifiers. Moreover, the admissible family does not specify whether algorithms are deterministic or randomized, while a hard-instance distribution generally requires an expectation convention and an appropriate minimax argument. A source is needed to determine the correct hypotheses and formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat-Minima Generalization Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that perfect empirical flatness alone does not control the population generalization gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(n\geq1\), \(p\in(0,1)\), and \(B>0\). Let data take values in \(\{0,1\}\) with \(\mathbb P(Z=1)=p\), and define the loss by \(\ell(w,0)=0\) and \(\ell(w,1)=B\) for every parameter \(w\). On the event that a sample \(S=(Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\) contains only zeros, which has probability \((1-p)^n>0\), the empirical risk is identically zero. Hence every local oscillation, gradient, Hessian, and neighborhood sharpness certificate is zero, while \[R(w)-\widehat R_S(w)=pB\] for every \(w\). Taking \(B\) arbitrarily large disproves any distribution-free generalization bound derived solely from such empirical flatness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An empirical objective can be perfectly flat while its population gap is arbitrarily large, so flatness alone is not a generalization certificate.
assumptions_latex: The flatness statistic depends only on the empirical risk as a function of the parameter.
No bounded-loss, stability, PAC-Bayesian, or distributional assumption independently controls generalization.
The observed sample contains only outcomes \(Z_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Zero empirical flatness does not imply any finite distribution-free upper bound on \(R(w)-\widehat R_S(w)\).

notation.meaning: Empirical average of the loss over sample S.
Loss assigned to the unobserved outcome one.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A counterexample is a suitable mathematical role for demonstrating the non-implication boundary represented by this interface. The construction is plausible, but no source or inspectable locator is supplied. The domain of the parameter w is also not introduced, which is material to the claims about gradients, Hessians, neighborhoods, and sharpness. Source support and an explicit parameter space are needed before the record can pass review.
